 WebMCP-native human-agent collaboration environment. Agentic Wijaywi provides a shared epistemic layer for AI agents to operate transparently on the open web. 

 Deskripsi Lengkap (Untuk Formulir Submission Hackathon): Wijaywi Web Agent Reliability Lab adalah lingkungan kolaborasi native WebMCP yang dirancang untuk mengatasi masalah transparansi agen AI otonom. Berdasarkan arsitektur "Agentic Wijaywi", platform ini menyediakan antarmuka Epistemic Command Center di mana manusia dan agen berbagi world model, hipotesis, bukti, dan pembaruan keyakinan (belief updates) secara real-time. Melalui pendaftaran 10 WebMCP tools spesifik, aplikasi ini memastikan setiap tindakan agen berbasis bukti, dapat difalsifikasi, serta dibatasi oleh izin otorisasi yang ketat sebelum memanipulasi production state. 

 

 It's a WebMCP-native human-agent collaboration environment. It acts as an "Epistemic Command Center" where AI agents and humans share a world model. Instead of just chatting, the agents formulate hypotheses, gather evidence, update their confidence (beliefs), and explicitly ask for human approval before performing high-risk actions. All of this is powered by Next.js, SQLite, and native WebMCP tool registration. 

 Are you asking what to fill out in a specific form or hackathon submission field that asks "What are you building?" If so, you can use this text: 

 Agentic Wijaywi
"A WebMCP native human agent collaboration environment that treats AI agents as persistent goal maintaining entities. It provides a shared epistemic layer for AI agents to operate transparently on the open web, featuring hypothesis ledgers, automated falsification, and strict permission boundaries." 

 ======================================================================================== 

 Inspiration 

 As AI agents become capable of operating web properties autonomously, we face a critical problem: lack of transparency. Agents often operate as black boxes, making it difficult to understand why they took a specific action, what evidence they relied on, or whether they hallucinated a conclusion. We were inspired to build a system that treats AI not as a generic chatbot, but as a goal-maintaining entity that must justify its actions through rigorous epistemic tracking. 

 What it does 

 Wijaywi Web Agent Reliability Lab is an "Epistemic Command Center" for human-agent collaboration on the open web. Built natively for WebMCP, it provides a shared environment where humans and AI agents can observe the same world state. 
Instead of blind execution, the system enforces a strict workflow: 

 
 Hypothesis Ledger: Agents must propose hypotheses before acting. 
 Evidence Tracking: Every claim requires timestamped evidence with clear provenance. 
 Falsifier Agent Role: Dedicated routines actively attempt to contradict existing beliefs to prevent confirmation bias. 
 Permission Boundaries: High-risk actions automatically halt and escalate to a human for explicit approval. 
 

 How we built it 

 We architected the platform using a modern, production-ready stack: 

 
 Frontend: Next.js 14 (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS for the Mission Control interface. 
 State Management: Zustand for real-time UI synchronization. 
 Backend: Next.js API Routes connected to a SQLite database via Drizzle ORM. 
 Agent Integration: We utilized the WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext.registerTool ) to expose 10 highly specific tools directly to the browser environment. 
 Validation & Testing: Zod for strict schema validation and Vitest for unit testing. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Integrating the WebMCP standard natively into a modern React ecosystem presented unique architectural challenges. We had to ensure that tool registration occurred safely on the client side while state mutations were securely synced to the SQLite backend. Designing a UI that completely avoids the "chatbot" paradigm and instead feels like a research laboratory required extensive iterations on data visualization and event streaming. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that making agent operations observable completely changes the dynamic of human-AI collaboration. When an agent explicitly lists its assumptions, current confidence level, and contradictory evidence, human operators can intervene with precision. We also discovered that WebMCP is a massive leap forward compared to traditional UI scraping, allowing agents to understand context and execute deterministic actions instantly. 

 What's next for Wijaywi Web Agent Reliability Lab 

 We plan to expand the uncertainty engine to support more complex causal relationships, introduce native PostgreSQL support for enterprise deployments, and build specialized UI modules for different agent personas (like the Synthesizer and Explorer).

title: Boardify
pitch: Boardify turns the infinite whiteboard into an agent-native canvas where humans and browser AI co-architect systems via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Boardify turns the infinite whiteboard into an agent-native canvas where humans and browser AI co-architect systems via WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates canvas assets library workflow template notes template er template cloud workflow template tables export shapes code and dsl deployment and sharing Inspiration We've all experienced the frustration of whiteboarding complex software architecture. You open a spatial tool like Miro or Excalidraw, stare at an empty canvas, and wrestle with "blank canvas paralysis." Meanwhile, your AI assistant is confined to a narrow linear chat sidebar in another window. To bridge this gap, engineers have spent years copying code snippets, describing layout ideas in prose, switching tabs, manually drawing boxes, pasting brand logos, and routing arrows. Previous attempts to give AI agents spatial capabilities relied on vision screen-scraping : taking a screenshot of the browser, passing it to an LLM to guess $(x, y)$ pixel coordinates, and synthesizing simulated mouse clicks. This approach is fundamentally flawed—it introduces 3,000ms+ roundtrip latency, breaks across different device pixel ratios and monitor resolutions, and frequently causes cards to collide or overlap. Spatial thinking is inherently non-linear, multi-dimensional, and relational—represented mathematically as a directed graph $G = (V, E)$. Chat interfaces force this multidimensional thought process into a 1-dimensional string of tokens. When the OpenAI & Google WebMCP Challenge was announced, we realized that browser-native agents no longer need to be blind or clumsy. By establishing window.document.modelContext , browser applications can expose structured, type-safe APIs directly to the host model. We asked ourselves: "What if an AI didn't just talk to you about your architecture—what if it pulled up a chair directly at your whiteboard, read the graph in sub-20ms, placed typed SQL tables, routed bezier wires, and untangled layout physics alongside you?" That was the spark for Boardify . What It Does Boardify is the first agent-native spatial whiteboard built from the ground up for the WebMCP standard. It is a shared collaborative workspace where humans bring intuition, taste, and high-level strategy, while browser agents bring speed, scale, and architectural execution. Key capabilities include: 24 First-Class WebMCP Tools: Directly exposed on document.modelContext with strict JSON Schema definitions, encompassing node creation, wire connections, SQL schema tables, tech stack logos, checkpoints, and graph layout physics. Agent Ghost Cursor & Tactile Feedback: Real-time visual agency. When an agent runs a tool, a pulsing Ghost Cursor sweeps across the canvas with an active action badge (e.g., AGENT · tool: add_entity_table ), accompanied by mechanical pop animations and sound design. Instant Relational ERD Generation: Prompt the agent with "table users and orders" , and it creates complete SQL database entity cards equipped with primary keys, foreign keys, data types ( UUID , VARCHAR , TIMESTAMP ), and relational wire linkages. Curated Architecture Vector Logo Library: Over 1,800+ tech logos (Next.js, Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, Docker, AWS, Stripe, etc.) searchable and spawnable by the agent in milliseconds. Physics-Based Auto-Tidy & Smart Flow: Clean algorithms for topological DAG ordering, force-directed untangling, and semantic clustering. Zero-Friction Multi-Format Export: 1-click export of visual diagrams to clean Markdown documentation, Mermaid flowchart code, structured JSON state, or high-res PNG. Dual-Mode WebMCP Execution: Hooks natively into Chrome Canary ( #enable-webmcp-testing ) and ChatGPT in-app browser sessions, while offering an interactive AI Agent Studio and DevTools console polyfill for standard desktop browsers. How we built it Boardify was engineered using a high-performance, modern web stack tailored for 60fps spatial manipulation: Frontend Core: Next.js 15 (App Router) with React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. Graphics & Spatial Engine: Infinite zoom-and-pan canvas combining HTML5 viewport transforms with high-efficiency SVG Bezier curve rendering. WebMCP Integration Layer ( src/lib/webmcp.ts ): Complete implementation of the WebMCP specification. When the canvas mounts, it registers 24 typed tools to window.document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Multi-Provider LLM Client: Native client adapters for Google Gemini ( gemini-2.0-flash with multi-version fallback across v1beta and v1 ), OpenAI ( gpt-4o-mini ), Anthropic ( claude-3.5-sonnet ), alongside an offline heuristic synthesis engine. ### The Mathematics of Spatial Whiteboarding (LaTeX) Camera Projection & Viewport Transforms: To translate between user screen coordinates $(x_s, y_s)$ and the infinite 2D world space $(x_w, y_w)$, we compute affine viewport transformations using scale factor $C_z$ and pan offsets $(C_x, C_y)$: $$\begin{pmatrix} x_s \ y_s \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} C_x \ C_y \end{pmatrix} + C_z \begin{pmatrix} x_w \ y_w \end{pmatrix}$$ The inverse projection (Screen-to-World) executed during pointer events and agent cursor positioning is: $$\begin{pmatrix} x_w \ y_w \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{x_s - C_x}{C_z} \ \frac{y_s - C_y}{C_z} \end{pmatrix}$$ Cubic Bézier Dynamic Cable Routing: Every wire connecting two nodes $P_0 = (x_0, y_0)$ and $P_3 = (x_3, y_3)$ is generated as a smooth cubic Bézier spline $B(t)$ parameterized over $t \in [0, 1]$: $$B(t) = (1-t)^3 P_0 + 3(1-t)^2 t P_1 + 3(1-t) t^2 P_2 + t^3 P_3$$ where intermediate control points $P_1 = (x_0 + \Delta x \cdot \kappa, y_0)$ and $P_2 = (x_3 - \Delta x \cdot \kappa, y_3)$ dynamically scale with horizontal separation $\Delta x = x_3 - x_0$ using stiffness coefficient $\kappa = 0.45$. Force-Directed Physics Layout (Spring-Embedder): Our tidy_force_directed tool models notes as charged particles exerting repulsive Coulomb forces and edges as Hookean springs with equilibrium length $L$: $$F_{\text{repulsive}}(u, v) = \frac{k^2}{|p_u - p_v|} \cdot \hat{r} {uv}, \quad \text{where } k = \sqrt{\frac{\text{Width} \cdot \text{Height}}{|V|}}$$ $$F {\text{attractive}}(u, v) = \frac{|p_u - p_v|^2}{k} \cdot \hat{r}_{vu}$$ System states are updated over discrete iterations via velocity-Verlet numerical integration: $$p_i^{(t+\Delta t)} = p_i^{(t)} + v_i^{(t)}\Delta t + \frac{1}{2}a_i^{(t)}\Delta t^2$$ converging in $O(|V|^2 + |E|)$ time to a minimum-energy, crossing-minimized diagram. Directional DAG Smart Flow: Hierarchical diagrams are arranged using topological level sorting. We compute the longest path for each vertex $v \in V$ in $O(|V| + |E|)$: $$\text{Level}(v) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \text{in-degree}(v) = 0 \ 1 + \max_{(u, v) \in E} \text{Level}(u) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ Vertices are partitioned into horizontal columns $C_\ell = {v \in V \mid \text{Level}(v) = \ell}$ and laid out left-to-right to preserve intuitive cause-and-effect flow. Challenges we ran into Spatial Collision & Viewport Bleed: When agents spawn multiple cards, placing them blindly resulted in cards overlapping existing notes or landing far below the fold on compact laptop viewports. We solved this by developing an outward radial spiral search in findFreeSpot() paired with synchronous bounding-box camera framing ( fitView(true, allNodes) ), guaranteeing that generated items appear immediately within the user's active viewport without disrupting existing work. React 19 State Batching vs. Real-Time Tool Execution: When an agent called multiple tools in rapid succession (e.g. creating 4 nodes and 3 links), unbatched state updates caused intermediate render passes where references to newly created nodes were not yet committed to nodesRef.current . We re-architected tool execution into atomic batch commits , accumulating additions in memory and applying them in a single cohesive render cycle. Passive Event Listener Constraints on Infinite Canvas: Modern browsers treat wheel events as passive by default to optimize scrolling performance. However, an infinite canvas must intercept wheel to implement pinch-to-zoom and multi-directional trackpad panning with e.preventDefault() . We resolved this by binding native non-passive DOM event listeners directly to the container ref with { passive: false } , completely eliminating browser console errors. Multi-Model API Evolution: During development, the legacy gemini-pro endpoint was retired in Google's v1beta API. We built a resilient multi-version client adapter in src/lib/llm-client.ts that auto-migrates stored keys to gemini-2.0-flash , sanitizes quotation marks and whitespace, and provides automatic fallback across v1beta and v1 REST endpoints. What we learned WebMCP Eliminates the Prompt Engineering Tax: Instead of writing 500-word system prompts telling an LLM "format your output as JSON with x, y, width, and height" , WebMCP provides typed JSON Schemas directly through the browser. The agent interacts with our app through clean function calls

title: Presence
pitch: The trust layer for live human-agent software.
about_excerpt: The trust layer for live human-agent software. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent requests a seat Human and agent share live state The boundary is real Work stays provisional You decide what becomes real Every session leaves a receipt Give agents a seat. Not the keys. Browser agents can now understand and act inside live software. But there is a problem: once an agent enters a shared workspace, what is it actually allowed to touch? Presence is a trust layer for live human agent collaboration. Instead of giving an agent the same authority as the human, Presence gives it an explicit seat with bounded capabilities. Humans and agents can work in the same live state without silently sharing control. The idea Presence reduces agent collaboration to four primitives: Seat Where an agent may be present. Scope What the agent may do. Revision The state the agent observed before acting. Receipt What actually happened during the session. Together they create a simple rule: Presence does not trust an agent to respect a boundary. The application enforces the boundary. The demo The demo uses one responsive project with three live surfaces: Desktop is the reference. Tablet is the agent's seat. Mobile belongs to the human. A browser agent discovers Presence through WebMCP and asks to join as a responsive collaborator. The human can inspect the requested capabilities before admitting it. Once admitted, the agent can inspect the project and propose work for Tablet while the human continues editing Mobile. Then comes the important part. The agent attempts to modify Mobile. Presence rejects the operation because Mobile is outside its granted scope. The same agent can successfully propose a Tablet change because Tablet belongs to its seat. Its work remains provisional: even the agent itself cannot publish it. Only a human acceptance can make the proposal canonical. Presence also tracks the revision an agent observed. If the human changes the project while the agent is acting on older state, the stale operation is rejected before it can mutate canonical state . The human's newer work remains untouched. Every significant action is recorded in a structured audit trail. Accepted proposals produce a verification receipt containing the agent identity, granted scope, revisions, operations, protected surfaces, and before/after state fingerprints. Finally, the human can revoke the seat. The agent loses its authority while accepted work remains part of the project. Why WebMCP WebMCP makes the website itself an agent interface. Presence exposes semantic operations for discovering the workspace, inspecting available roles and constraints, requesting admission, inspecting project state, proposing scoped changes, reviewing state, and releasing a role. The agent does not need DOM coordinates or a scripted sequence of clicks. It can reason about the application's actual concepts while Presence remains responsible for authorization and state integrity. How I built it Presence is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, and WebMCP. The UI and WebMCP tools operate on the same domain model. Mutations pass through the Presence domain layer, where admission, scope, ownership, and revision rules are enforced before canonical state can change. Agent proposals are provisional by default. Agents cannot publish their own work. Humans retain final authority. Presence also records structured audit events, computes deterministic state fingerprints, and generates verification receipts after accepted proposals so the collaboration can be inspected and verified after the fact. Challenges The hardest part was not exposing tools to an agent. It was deciding what should happen after an agent discovers those tools. A useful agent needs enough authority to accomplish real work, but giving it unrestricted access destroys the distinction between assistance and control. That led to the central design principle behind Presence: Authority should be explicit, scoped, temporary, and visible. Another challenge was concurrency. If an agent begins working from one revision while a human continues editing, the system cannot simply trust that the agent's eventual change is still safe. Presence revalidates the expected revision at mutation time and blocks stale operations before they reach canonical state. Presence explores what software could look like when agents are not merely chatbots beside an application, but participants inside it with boundaries the application can actually enforce. What's next The responsive workspace is one demonstration of the model, not the limit of it. Presence already applies the same collaboration model to a second application, demonstrating that the security model is not tied to responsive design. The same Seat, Scope, Revision, and Receipt primitives could govern agents working inside operations software, content systems, developer environments, and other collaborative applications. The larger idea is simple: As agents enter live software, applications need a way to decide not only what agents can understand, but where they may act. Built With framer netlify react typescript vite vitest webmcp zustand Try it out presence-agents.netlify.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I built Presence end to end, including the product concept, interaction design, WebMCP integration, scoped agent authority model, revision safety, proposal and approval flow, frontend implementation, testing, deployment, and demo. I focused on exploring how humans and agents can safely collaborate in the same live software without giving agents unrestricted control. title: AuraQL — Zero-Server AI Analytics Engine
pitch: Zero-server in-browser OLAP analytics studio where AI agents execute sub-10ms SQL and manipulate live dashboard visualizations in real time via WebMCP.\n\n
about_excerpt:
Zero-server in-browser OLAP analytics studio where AI agents execute sub-10ms SQL and manipulate live dashboard visualizations in real time via WebMCP.


 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 🔮 Inspiration: The Broken Cloud Analytics Paradox 

 Traditional cloud business intelligence requires piping sensitive customer records, financial logs, and transaction streams to remote third-party databases. When analysts consult AI, language models frequently hallucinate arithmetic calculations on large datasets. 

 We built AuraQL to completely invert this paradigm: 

 
 Zero-Server In-Browser OLAP : The columnar database and vectorized SQL evaluator run 100% inside your client-side browser tab memory. 
 Deterministic AI Math : The AI agent writes the SQL query, but the in-browser engine evaluates aggregations (SUM, AVG, COUNT, STDDEV) in under 10 milliseconds with mathematical accuracy. 
 WebMCP Dual-Control Canvas : Both the human user and AI agent collaborate simultaneously on the same dashboard canvas via the emerging open standard document.modelContext . 
 

 

 ⚡ Why Our Use Case is a Strong Fit for WebMCP 

 Analytics dashboards are notoriously difficult for computer-vision and click-based agents: DOM selectors break, dynamic canvas elements cannot be inspected, and SVG splines are opaque to LLMs. 

 WebMCP provides the ideal interface: 

 
 Instead of brittle DOM scraping, AuraQL exposes structured analytical primitives directly to the agent. 
 The agent calls list_tables_and_schema to discover table schemas and column datatypes. 
 It evaluates relational SQL via execute_sql_query . 
 It commands the user's viewport directly via render_interactive_chart and apply_dashboard_filter . 
 

 

 🚀 How It Creates a Better User Experience 

 
 100% Client-Side Privacy : Financial data and customer churn metrics never leave the user's browser RAM. Zero cloud data storage costs, zero telemetry tracking, and zero database credentials to expose. 
 Sub-10ms Latency : Queries against columnar memory buffers execute faster than a network roundtrip to a cloud data warehouse. 
 Co-Pilot Simultaneous Vision : When you ask the agent a question like "Show quarterly revenue breakdown by region as a bar chart" , the dashboard mutates in real time before your eyes while the agent explains the business takeaways. 
 Pro Studio Interface : Dual-axis resizable grid windows, high-contrast borders (black in light mode, neon purple in dark mode), and drag-and-drop CSV/JSON ingestion. 
 

 

 🤝 What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Impossible Before 

 
 Natural Language Scenario Simulation : Humans specify hypothetical business conditions ( "What if critical churn accounts decrease 25% and MRR increases 15%?" ). The agent calls simulate_forecast_scenario to execute in-memory adjustments and render baseline vs. projected variance charts immediately. 
 Instant Statistical Anomaly Isolation : The agent uses detect_anomalies to calculate Z-scores ($|Z| \ge 1.85$) and Interquartile Ranges (IQR) directly in browser memory, isolating revenue spikes or margin compression without needing Python or external Jupyter notebooks. 
 True Cross-Platform Agent Access : The exact same WebMCP tools are available inside:

 
 ChatGPT’s native in-app browser ( document.modelContext ) 
 Desktop ChatGPT & Claude Desktop via Server-Sent Events ( /sse ) 
 OpenAI Codex CLI over Stdio JSON-RPC 2.0 
 
 

 

 🛠️ How We Implemented WebMCP 

 AuraQL implements the official W3C WebMCP specification: 

 
 Native Browser Standard : Inspects document.modelContext on mount and registers 6 analytical tools: 

 
 list_tables_and_schema (Schema & metadata discovery) 
 execute_sql_query (Columnar SQL aggregations) 
 render_interactive_chart (Viewport visualization mutation) 
 apply_dashboard_filter (Cohort isolation) 
 simulate_forecast_scenario (What-if financial modeling) 
 detect_anomalies (Statistical anomaly detection) 
 
 Universal Polyfill & Bridge : 

 
 If running in standard Chrome or without native browser flags, AuraQL binds a spec-compliant fallback to document.modelContext and window.modelContext . 
 An external Node.js WebMCP bridge deployed on Render ( scripts/mcp-bridge.mjs ) synchronizes with the active browser tab via Server-Sent Events ( /api/bridge/events ) with 25-second keepalive heartbeats, allowing desktop clients (Codex CLI, Claude Desktop, ChatGPT Desktop) to steer the live web app remotely. 
 
 

 

 💻 Built With 

 
 WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) 
 TypeScript & React 
 In-Memory Columnar OLAP Engine 
 Vite & Tailwind CSS 
 Node.js MCP Bridge (SSE + Stdio)

title: canter.dev
pitch: Canter is a hosting control plane built for AI agents to operate and humans to govern.
about_excerpt: Canter is a hosting control plane built for AI agents to operate and humans to govern. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agents can write code, but running what they build still pushes them toward either brittle shell access or infrastructure credentials that are far too powerful. We built Canter around a different boundary: the agent proposes an exact, inspectable Change; the human governs authority and high-impact execution; and the control plane produces evidence of what actually happened. What it does Canter is an agent-operated, human-governed hosting control plane. An agent can inspect a System, draft a Change, and review an immutable execution plan without receiving provider credentials. Every proposed deployment is bound to an exact digest, policy is explicit, apply can require human approval, and execution produces durable receipts. For the WebMCP Challenge, Canter makes that workflow discoverable directly from the website. The site advertises same-origin agent discovery, provides WebMCP read and review tools, and points capable agents to the authenticated remote MCP contract for durable work. Browser tools cannot borrow the human session to bypass approval: a sensitive Change still needs a focused, short-lived review capability and an explicit human action. How we built it The control plane is written in Go with PostgreSQL-backed durable state. The product interface uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript. A typed System contract compiles into a deterministic execution graph before provider adapters can mutate infrastructure. The same semantic objects—Systems, Changes, exact digests, policy envelopes, operations, and evidence—are shared across the CLI, HTTP API, remote MCP, and WebMCP surfaces. The website registers its WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool. The public /.well-known/canter and /llms.txt routes explain the same-origin device flow, API, and Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint without exposing provider details. Authenticated agent installations are durable and revocable, with independent inspect, draft, and apply authority. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not exposing more tools. It was preserving a trustworthy authority boundary across several interfaces. We had to ensure browser tools remain read and review only, authorization binds to one immutable digest, replayed or expired approval links fail safely, execution can resume after interruption, and a failed release does not silently become desired state. Accomplishments that we're proud of One small vocabulary across web, CLI, API, MCP, and WebMCP: inspect System, draft Change, review exact digest, authorize, apply, inspect evidence. Agents never receive provider credentials or arbitrary infrastructure access. Human approval can be mandatory for apply while agents retain useful inspect-and-draft authority. Execution is evidence-producing, restart-safe, and able to contain unhealthy releases. The browser experience makes policy, pending work, exact plans, and agent authority visible at a glance. What we learned Agent infrastructure needs fewer ambient privileges and better semantic contracts. WebMCP is most useful when it is an adapter into a governed product model, not a shortcut around it. The strongest interface is one where both the agent and the human can see the same proposed Change and the same evidence. What's next for canter.dev We want to expand the provider adapter set, improve focused Change review, add more public verification recipes, and make the same governed deployment loop available to more coding agents without weakening the human boundary. title: Payment Recovery Agent
pitch: A WebMCP-native recovery workspace where browser agents help small businesses prioritize overdue invoices, draft guarded reminders, create payment handoffs, and audit recovery.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-native recovery workspace where browser agents help small businesses prioritize overdue invoices, draft guarded reminders, create payment handoffs, and audit recovery.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Small businesses lose time and cash flow not because they do not know invoices are overdue, but because follow-up is messy. A freelancer, tutor, consultant, or agency owner has to decide who to chase first, what tone to use, whether a payment link exists, whether a client promised to pay, and when to stop sending reminders. 

 Most payment dashboards are built for humans clicking around tables. I wanted to explore what changes when the dashboard becomes agent-operable through WebMCP. 

 What It Does 

 Payment Recovery Agent turns overdue receivables into a structured recovery workflow. 

 A human business owner stays in control of sensitive customer communication, while a browser agent can use WebMCP tools to: 

 
 inspect the recovery snapshot 
 list at-risk payments 
 identify the highest-priority overdue invoice 
 create a guarded recovery plan 
 generate a payment handoff 
 draft a WhatsApp-ready reminder 
 mark promise-to-pay or recovered payments 
 simulate verified payment success 
 generate an audit trail 
 

 The result is not just a reminder tool. It is a human-supervised recovery workflow where overdue money becomes prioritized, actionable, and auditable. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP is a strong fit because payment recovery depends on page-local state and safe sequencing. 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would need to scrape visible tables, infer which invoice is selected, guess what buttons do, and risk taking the wrong action. With WebMCP, the site exposes explicit tools for each recovery step. 

 The agent gets structured access to the workflow, and the human gets a clear interface for supervision. 

 Human + Agent Experience 

 The human decides what kind of follow-up is appropriate and remains responsible for customer-sensitive actions. 

 The agent handles the repetitive work: 

 
 ranking the recovery queue 
 preparing next actions 
 drafting messages 
 attaching payment handoffs 
 updating recovery state 
 summarizing audit history 
 

 This division of labor matters because payment recovery is not one action. It is a sequence of decisions where mistakes are costly: chasing the wrong person, over-messaging, sending a reminder after payment, or forgetting a promise-to-pay. 

 How I Built It 

 The app is a static web app built with HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. 

 It registers 9 WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() , with fallback support for navigator.modelContext : 

 
 get_recovery_snapshot 
 list_at_risk_payments 
 draft_recovery_message 
 create_recovery_plan 
 mark_promise_to_pay 
 mark_payment_recovered 
 create_razorpay_link 
 simulate_razorpay_paid 
 generate_audit_trail 
 

 Tool schemas use JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false . Read-only tools are marked with annotations.readOnlyHint: true , and state-changing tools are marked as write actions. 

 The app uses synthetic demo data only and stores state in the browser for the demo. Every state-changing action writes to an audit trail. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing WebMCP tools that felt like a real agent workflow, not just buttons exposed to an agent. I had to decide which actions should be read-only, which actions change state, what guardrails belong in the outputs, and how to make the agent-human collaboration obvious in a short demo. 

 Another challenge was keeping the project public and demo-safe while still making it feel realistic. The app uses synthetic receivables and simulated payment handoffs rather than private production data or real payment credentials. 

 What I Learned 

 I learned that WebMCP is most powerful when the website exposes meaningful workflow steps, not generic UI actions. The best tools are not "click this button" wrappers. They are bounded capabilities with clear inputs, structured outputs, and human-readable audit trails. 

 What Is Next 

 A production version would connect payment handoffs to a secure backend, create payment links server-side, verify payment success through webhooks or signatures, and sync with the user's real invoice/payment system.

title: PARALLAX SPATIAL MCP
pitch: PARALLAX is a Spatial MCP that lets autonomous agents safely understand, change, re-observe, and verify 3D environments through governed actions and auditable execution receipts.
about_excerpt:
PARALLAX is a Spatial MCP that lets autonomous agents safely understand, change, re-observe, and verify 3D environments through governed actions and auditable execution receipts.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 PARALLAX started from a simple problem: autonomous agents can call tools, but in spatial environments that is not enough. If an agent moves, rotates, or modifies something in a 3D world, we need a way to know what it was allowed to do, what actually changed, and whether the result matched the objective. 

 That led to the core loop: 

 Observe → Act → See Again → Verify → Receipt 

 The goal was to make spatial agency more accountable instead of treating a tool call as proof that a task succeeded. 

 What it does 

 PARALLAX is a Spatial MCP for autonomous agents. It turns 3D environments into governed workspaces where an agent can: 

 
 inspect a scene 
 discover bounded capabilities 
 request authorized spatial actions 
 execute allowed changes 
 re-observe the resulting state 
 verify the outcome 
 produce an execution receipt 
 

 Restricted actions can be denied without changing the protected scene state. 

 Our WebMCP demo uses a virtual production studio. The agent is given the objective of preparing the studio for an interview while operating inside defined permissions. 

 How we built it 

 PARALLAX was built with WebMCP, TypeScript, React, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Vite, GLTF assets, and OpenAI Codex , with ChatGPT and Hermes assisting with development, verification, documentation, and submission preparation. 

 The application separates the visual 3D scene from the authoritative logical state. Scene objects expose spatial capabilities, actions pass through governance checks, the environment is re-observed after execution, and verification determines whether the objective was satisfied before a receipt is shown. 

 We also built explicit denial behavior so a restricted mutation can fail closed rather than silently modifying the scene. 

 Challenges we faced 

 The hardest challenge was making the execution loop understandable visually, not just technically correct. 

 Early versions used proxy geometry that made real scene changes difficult to recognize. We had to improve object presentation, before/after comparison, labels, camera framing, video backgrounds, and the relationship between the 3D environment and the governance system. 

 Deployment parity was another major challenge. A local build could look correct while a production deployment could lose assets, motion, layout, or visual hierarchy. That pushed us to add stronger design and production-parity checks. 

 We also had to be disciplined about claims. A generated visualization is not the same thing as a verified result, so throughout the project we used the rule: 

 Generated! = Verified 

 What we learned 

 We learned that agentic spatial systems need more than tool access. They need an execution contract. 

 The important part is not simply whether an agent can manipulate a 3D environment. It is whether the system can clearly answer: 

 What did the agent observe? 
What was it authorized to do? 
What changed? 
Did the change satisfy the objective? 
What evidence remains afterward? 

 PARALLAX is our attempt to make those questions first-class parts of spatial agent infrastructure.

title: lapse — what WebMCP tools actually accept
pitch: A WebMCP tool publishes an input schema. Nothing enforces it. lapse probes Google's own reference demos and finds 17 of 17 imperative tools accept input their own schema forbids. 225 of 289 probes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP tool publishes an input schema. Nothing enforces it. lapse probes Google's own reference demos and finds 17 of 17 imperative tools accept input their own schema forbids. 225 of 289 probes. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of## Inspiration A WebMCP tool publishes an input schema. That schema is a promise to the agent: these are the fields, this one is required, this one has to be one of three values. Nothing enforces it. Not the browser, not the API. That turns out to be deliberate, and the spec's own issue 92 has been debating whether it should change since February. I found it by accident while testing a tool I was writing. I sent it a quantity of "two" as a string where the schema declared a number, and it went straight through to my handler. Then I sent negative 999 cups against a declared minimum of 1. That went through too. The schema I had carefully written was decoration. So I stopped building what I was building and went to measure how far it goes. What it does lapse measures the gap between what a WebMCP tool promises and what it actually accepts. The targets are not toys written to fail. They are the official Chrome WebMCP reference demos from GoogleChromeLabs, vendored unmodified under Apache-2.0. The coffee shop, the pizza maker, the flight search, the ticket booking, the real estate map. The code Chrome ships to teach people how to build with WebMCP. lapse enumerates every tool through getTools, reads each declared schema, and generates input that schema forbids. Nulls where a string was declared. Booleans and arrays and objects where a scalar was declared. Values outside a declared enum. Numbers past a declared maximum. Required fields removed. A ten thousand character string. Control and bidirectional characters. Text written to sound like an instruction aimed at the agent. Then it calls the tool and records what happened. 299 probes across 23 tools on 8 sites. 225 violations. 17 of 17 imperative tools accept input their own published schema forbids, at 78 percent of every scored probe. The clearest single case: the pizza maker declares topping as a fixed list. Send it a value that is not on the list and it replies that it added one off-menu topping. The violations cluster identically across every site. That is what a platform property looks like, not seven separate authoring mistakes. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP It could not exist anywhere else. It runs inside the browser, against live tools, using the API's own enumeration and execution surface, and the thing it measures is a property of WebMCP itself that no existing tool reports. Chrome ships an evals CLI that tests whether a model picks the right tool. Nothing tests whether a tool honours what it published. How it makes for a better experience A developer who wants to know whether their tools are safe under an agent has one option today, which is to write eval cases by hand and read the output. lapse gives a verdict in under a minute, per tool, per constraint, with the failing input printed next to what the tool did with it. You do not have to guess which of your fields is unguarded. It tells you. What people and agents can do together here lapse registers four WebMCP tools of its own, so the audit is driven by conversation rather than by clicking. Ask which sites are loaded and what each one exposes. Ask it to run the audit. Ask for every violation on one site. Ask it to export the report for a bug filing. Auditing a site used to mean a person writing test cases one at a time and reading them one at a time. Here the agent generates and executes hundreds against live tools while the human watches the result form on a shared page. Neither side could do it alone at that speed. The agent has no way to reach into a page and call its tools without WebMCP, and the person has no patience for 299 hand-written cases. How I implemented WebMCP lapse uses the API in both directions. As a client it calls getTools to enumerate tools across a same-origin frame tree, executeTool to drive them with generated input, toolchange to track registration, AbortController to cancel calls that stop responding, and it reads annotations to check whether a tool that echoes agent-directed text sets untrustedContentHint. As a server it registers its own: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "run_audit", description: "Run the full contract audit across every vendored demo. Returns probe, violation and not-measured counts.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {} }, execute: async () => (await runAudit()) || "audit produced no findings", annotations: { readOnlyHint: false } }); Four tools in total: list_targets, run_audit, get_findings, export_report. Challenges, and the verdict that saved me twice Every probe lands as HONOURED, VIOLATED, or NOT MEASURED. A probe that could not be generated, could not be run, or never returned is recorded as unmeasured. It is never counted as a pass. That third verdict caught two false findings that would otherwise have shipped. The first version read inputSchema as an object. It actually arrives as a JSON string. Every schema-derived probe silently generated nothing while the tool confidently reported five violations as though that were the answer. The arithmetic gave it away: four tools, nine probes, exactly the two unconditional checks each. The second was worse because it flattered me. Declarative tools appeared to validate perfectly, which would have been a lovely headline. So I suppressed the form navigation that was cutting those tools short, reran, and the outcomes changed. The guard was altering the thing it was supposed to leave alone. I removed it and marked six declarative tools unmeasured rather than publish the better number. What I learned This is not a bug report. The working group already knows the schema is advisory. Issue 92 on the spec repo, "Who owns the validation layer?", has been open since February and argues that inputSchema is only a semantic hint, that validation falls to each tool author individually, and that the browser should probably own it instead. What that discussion has never had is a measurement. It has been argued from experience and intuition for six months. lapse gives it a number: across the reference demos Chrome itself ships to teach the API, 17 of 17 imperative tools have unguarded input paths, and 78 percent of probes that violate a declared constraint are accepted anyway. The separate question I could not settle is the declarative side. Calling a declarative tool submits its form and navigates the document, so it cannot be probed twice. I tried suppressing that navigation, watched it change the outcomes it was meant to leave alone, removed it, and marked those six tools unmeasured. Whether declarative validation is genuinely stronger remains an open question, and lapse says so rather than guessing. What's next More targets, including the demos that need a build step. Chrome publishes an eval JSON format for its CLI, and lapse should read and write it so the same cases can run in a browser against live tools instead of only in a terminal. title: DoPDF with WebMCP
pitch: AI agents can read PDFs. Now they can act on them — accurately. Redact secrets and fill forms just by chatting: WebMCP lets your agent call real PDF tools instead of guessing at the UI.
about_excerpt: AI agents can read PDFs. Now they can act on them — accurately. Redact secrets and fill forms just by chatting: WebMCP lets your agent call real PDF tools instead of guessing at the UI. Like 2 Comment Story Updates "Black out my loan number and account details." The agent finds every match, marks them in red, and waits for your review Hit Apply and the redactions are baked into a fresh PDF. 100% client-side, your document never leaves the tab "I'm Jane Doe, applying for a $25k loan." The form fills live, using only what you said. It leaves the rest blank, never invented. Apply and download: the finished loan application, filled entirely by chat and flattened into a shareable PDF. Inspiration Today's browser AI can read a PDF and tell you what's in it. It still can't do anything to it. You're the one squinting at a mortgage statement, manually blacking out your account number before emailing it, or retyping the same details into yet another loan form. We wanted to give the agent hands: let it act on the document, safely, without shipping your file to some server. WebMCP made that click. A page can publish its own capabilities as tools on document.modelContext , and any WebMCP-aware agent can call them. So we turned real =PDF workflows into tools an agent can drive, entirely in the browser. What it does DoPDF with WebMCP lets an AI agent run two real PDF workflows by chat, 100% client-side: Redact. Say "black out my loan number and account details" and the agent finds every match, marks them in red, and shows a review card. You confirm, and it flattens the boxes into a downloadable PDF. Fill forms. Describe yourself in plain language and watch a fillable PDF populate live, field by field. It fills only what you actually said and never invents a value you left out. Your document never leaves the tab. The only network call is the extension talking to your chosen model. How we built it The hands (the page): Adobe PDF Embed API renders and provides core PDF capabilities. Each page registers its tools on document.modelContext . The brain (the extension): a Chrome side-panel chat that discovers whatever tools the active tab exposes and calls them, using Google Gemini or any OpenAI-compatible gateway (bring your own key). Two flavors of WebMCP, on purpose: redaction uses the imperative API ( registerTool ), while form-fill also demos the declarative API, injecting an annotated <form toolname="fill_form"> that the browser turns into a tool automatically. Human in the loop: every destructive action returns a review card, so nothing is redacted, written, or downloaded without a click. Challenges we ran into PDF Embed on reload. A repeat previewFile() can silently stall and leave a blank viewer. We now race it against a timeout and fall back to another render, so the document always shows. Declarative timing. Chrome registers an injected <form> as a tool asynchronously , and its submit handler must call event.respondWith(...) synchronously. We poll for the tool, respond in place, and fall back to an imperative tool if the browser does not surface the form. No hallucinated data. LLMs love to "complete" a form. We bake anti-fabrication into the tool descriptions and the system prompt so the agent fills only user-provided fields. HITL Trust needs UI, but WebMCP tools return data, not interfaces. A tool call hands back a result; it can't show the user a redaction preview and wait for a yes/no. So confirmation would have fallen back to plain chat text — easy to skim past, and a poor fit for a destructive action. We solved it with an agent-to-UI (A2UI) layer in the extension: the tool returns a structured payload, and the side-panel renders it as an interactive review card — highlighted matches, confirm/cancel — before anything is redacted, written, or downloaded. The agent proposes; the human disposes, in a real interface, not a wall of text. What we learned Field name is the perfect join key: the agent maps values to them, and PDF library writes them straight back, with no fuzzy matching. We also learned when to reach for declarative vs imperative WebMCP, and how much a simple review-card pattern buys you in trust. What's next Voice-driven fills, more tools (edit, compress, export, combine), and driving a PDF that is already open on any site, not just our page. title: Entorno Camaleón
pitch: Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that adapts educational interfaces to the way each student learns. The learning goal stays the same, the experience finally adapts.
about_excerpt: Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that adapts educational interfaces to the way each student learns. The learning goal stays the same, the experience finally adapts. Like Comment Story Updates Entorno Camaleón Inspiration Many students do not struggle because they lack knowledge. They struggle because educational platforms require them to navigate visual overload, dense instructions, time pressure, unexpected motion, and a single way to respond. For neurodivergent children, these interface demands can become an additional test that has nothing to do with the actual learning objective. We created Entorno Camaleón around a simple principle: the learning goal should remain the same, but the path should adapt. Our prototype follows Leo, a nine-year-old student who understands science but feels overwhelmed by a traditional learning management system. Entorno Camaleón transforms his water-cycle lesson into a calmer, character-led experience featuring Luma, his companion, and Ayu, the mythical Guardian of the Cycle. What it does Entorno Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that allows a browser agent to adapt an educational interface in real time. The experience can adjust information density, text size, color environment, motion, animation, audio guidance, and the available response channels. Students can participate through voice, text, or visual interaction. The agent handles interface complexity so the student can focus on the academic objective. WebMCP also provides an important safety boundary. The agent can prepare Leo’s answer and open the review screen, but it cannot submit academic work automatically. Leo or an authorized adult must explicitly confirm the final action. How we built it We built the proof of concept as a client-side HTML, CSS, and JavaScript experience and deployed it on Vercel. The application registers five imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(): get_lesson_context start_accessible_audio_guide adapt_learning_experience start_water_cycle_mission prepare_science_answer Each tool uses a constrained JSON Schema and connects directly to the same state used by the visible interface. These tools allow an agent to understand the current lesson without scraping the page, start an accessible Spanish audio guide, apply reversible interface adaptations, open the correct learning activity, and prepare a spoken or typed answer for human review. The prototype also uses the browser’s Speech Recognition API for real microphone input and the Speech Synthesis API for audio guidance. A typed response remains available whenever voice recognition is unsupported or microphone permission is denied. The visual system combines Atkinson Hyperlegible for reading with Geist for interface hierarchy. The experience includes responsive layouts, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support, high-contrast focus indicators, accessible dialogs, and multiple ways to complete every important interaction. Challenges we faced One of our biggest challenges was determining the correct boundary between agent assistance and student agency. An agent should be able to remove interface friction, but it should not make academic decisions or submit work without meaningful consent. We therefore separated answer preparation from final submission. The WebMCP tool reports submitted: false and opens a visible confirmation dialog. Another challenge was balancing sensory calm with engagement. We wanted to avoid overstimulation without producing a cold or purely functional interface. The narrative involving Leo, Luma, and Ayu gives the lesson continuity, emotional context, and a clear sense of progress. Voice interaction also required careful attention. We designed microphone controls for press-and-hold interaction, keyboard activation, permission errors, and typed fallback. Audio guidance and microphone recording are mutually exclusive so the guide cannot accidentally be transcribed as Leo’s answer. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is more powerful when it represents meaningful product capabilities instead of reproducing individual button clicks. Rather than giving the agent unrestricted control over the page, Entorno Camaleón exposes a small set of understandable and governed actions. This makes agent behavior more reliable, visible, and safer for students. We also learned that accessibility should not be treated as a final compliance step. In this project, accessibility became part of the product concept itself. Multiple response channels, adjustable presentation, predictable navigation, audio guidance, and explicit confirmation improve the experience for a much broader group of learners. What we are proud of We are proud that Entorno Camaleón is both a functional WebMCP demonstration and a complete product story. The deployed prototype includes five working WebMCP tools, real voice input with a typed fallback, accessible audio guidance, a responsive five-chapter learning journey, student-controlled presentation preferences, keyboard and reduced-motion support, an explicit human-confirmation boundary, and a complete manual fallback when WebMCP is unavailable. What is next The next step is to replace the simulated school receipt with an authenticated LMS sandbox and add durable consent and audit records. We would also co-design future versions with neurodivergent students, families, teachers, accessibility specialists, and school administrators. Entorno Camaleón is currently a proof of concept, not a clinical intervention or production LMS integration. Its purpose is to demonstrate how agentic technology can make educational interfaces more flexible without taking control away from the learner. Entorno Camaleón: The learning goal stays the same. The experience finally adapts. title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. title: moodle-webmcp
pitch: Students can use their familiar ChatGPT interface to get grounded answers and help, fast, with no setup, via a WebMCP integration for Moodle.
about_excerpt: Students can use their familiar ChatGPT interface to get grounded answers and help, fast, with no setup, via a WebMCP integration for Moodle. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In my time at university, which used an OpenLMS deployment based on Moodle, course content was often scattered and hard to dig through. When OpenAI announced The WebMCP Challenge, the lightbulb went off. WebMCP moves tool execution right into the browser. So instead of fighting IT firewalls or using API keys, tools run inside the student's active browser session. I wanted to build a real WebMCP enablement plugin that turns standard Moodle course pages into active, agentic workspaces for both students and instructors, requiring no additional setup from them. What it does moodle-webmcp is a Moodle plugin that enables a number of useful WebMCP tools primarily for students, with some extra tools useful for course admins. When you open course pages in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 146+, the plugin automatically declares structured AI tools directly on the web page to: Retrieve upcoming assignments and labs in chronological order Fetch relevant lecture summaries and course materials Generate an adaptive day-by-day study schedule based on available daily hours Critique a student's draft essay based on the assignment's official grading rubrics How we built it Moodle Plugin Core : Developed local_webmcp in PHP, integrating with Moodle's navigation hooks and AMD loader. Deployment : Packaged Alpine Linux with PHP 8.3, Moodle 5.2.2, and SQLite3 on Render with persistent disk storage and a custom domain ( moodle-webmcp.akashgpt.me ). Development Tooling : Built and debugged the full stack with Codex and Chrome DevTools MCP. Challenges we ran into Minimal issues overall. The main hurdles involved working through Moodle-specific quirks and container setup, such as aligning with Moodle 5.x's public document root structure and ensuring database gradebook items were properly registered for assignment activities. Accomplishments that we're proud of True Zero-Token Authentication : No API keys required. Tools inherit the student's existing authenticated web session and CSRF tokens automatically. Real, Live Moodle Environment : Built and deployed a full Moodle 5.2.2 LMS with seeded courses and working student/teacher roles rather than a static mockup. Practical Student Utility : Tools like adaptive study scheduling and rubric draft critique solve real, everyday student problems. What we learned WebMCP vs. MCP : For web applications, in-browser execution is fundamentally more secure and accessible than backend daemons for everyday users. Defense-in-Depth in the Browser : Constraining tool inputs with strict JSON schemas and enforcing read-only boundaries protects against indirect prompt injection from untrusted course forums or scraped HTML. Moodle Plugin Internals : Deepened our understanding of Moodle's local plugin architecture, AMD modules, and database hooks. What's next for moodle-webmcp Expanding the number and types of tools available and integrating deeper with Moodle, including: Two-Way Action Tools with Confirmation Gates : Adding safe, human-confirmed write capabilities like save_assignment_draft and post_forum_reply . Discussion Board & Workshop Integration : Extending WebMCP tools to summarize peer reviews and handle complex forum threads. Official Moodle Plugins Directory Release : Packaging local_webmcp for official submission to the Moodle Plugins Directory so LMS administrators worldwide can install it in one click. title: Groundplan
pitch: Humans draw. Agents measure. A floor plan studio that hands its geometry engine to agents as WebMCP tools, so an agent can send a wheelchair down your hall and show you where it stops.
about_excerpt: Humans draw. Agents measure. A floor plan studio that hands its geometry engine to agents as WebMCP tools, so an agent can send a wheelchair down your hall and show you where it stops. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration A doorway 100 mm too narrow does not look narrow. That is the whole problem. The mistakes that make a home unusable are geometric, not aesthetic: a bathroom door at 800 mm instead of 900, a kitchen with no 1500 mm circle to turn a wheelchair in, a wardrobe parked where it quietly cuts a bedroom in half. They are invisible to the eye and obvious to a measurement — and the people who most need to catch them are the least likely to have an architect on retainer. Someone adapting a home after an injury. A carer assessing a flat before a parent moves in. A small landlord doing an accessibility retrofit. LLMs are famously bad at spatial reasoning from a picture. But they are excellent at driving a tool that measures. So the interesting question was not "can an agent design a floor plan" — it was "what happens if we give the agent a real geometry engine and let it iterate against the numbers?" What it does Groundplan is a floor plan editor. You drag walls, drop furniture, cut doors and windows — all with a mouse, like any drawing tool. The difference is that the whole engine underneath it is registered as WebMCP site tools, so an agent sitting in the browser can use it too. Open the app and you get a two-bedroom flat that looks perfectly reasonable. Ask an agent to check it: error Doorway into Bathroom is too tight 760 mm → needs 815 mm error Bathroom is unreachable — the route narrows to 800 mm at the door between Bathroom and Hall 800 mm → needs 900 mm warning No turning circle in Kitchen 1204 mm → needs 1500 mm warning 68% of the home is step-free reachable The bathroom door is 800 mm. That leaves 760 mm of clear opening — 55 mm short of the ADA figure — which means a wheelchair user in this flat cannot get to the toilet. Nothing on the drawing looks wrong. The number is wrong. Look at what the second finding says. Not "the bathroom is unreachable", which is a symptom, but which of the seven doors is pinching the route and by how much. That comes from a widest-path search over the whole flat, and it is the difference between an agent that can act and one that can only report. The agent calls one tool. The page does not apply it. Instead the change is drawn onto the plan in violet — the widened door, arrows where furniture would move — and a card appears in the panel: "Widen door in Bathroom: 800 → 900 mm — Approve / Discard." You click Approve, and the tool's result comes back: { "issues": { "resolved": ["Doorway into Bathroom is too tight", "Bathroom is unreachable"], "introduced": [] }, "plan_score": 78 } Two findings closed by one 100 mm change, and the agent was told exactly that in the same round trip — so it knows whether to stop or keep going. Score 49 to 78; step-free reach 68% to 78%. The other starter plan is a bungalow that passes every rule and scores 100. A checker that can only ever say no is not much of a checker. Why WebMCP is the right fit Three reasons this could not be an MCP server behind an API. The measurements only exist in the page. Clearance, reachability and turning circles come from a live rasterisation of the drawing. There is no document to upload, no id scheme to learn — the agent measures the thing the user is looking at, in the state they left it, including the change they made ten seconds ago. The confirmation is the real UI. When an agent proposes an edit, the page draws it on the plan — violet for what would appear or move, red for what would go, arrows showing where things travel — and the tool's promise does not resolve until a person clicks Approve or Discard. A chat bubble asking "shall I widen the door?" is a paraphrase of a change. This is the change. The tool set is a function of application state. WebMCP lets a page register and unregister tools at runtime, so what the agent is able to ask for narrows and widens as the user works: State Registered Normal editing 30 tools Something selected 31 — an edit_selection tool appears, scoped to that entity, so "make this wider" resolves Findings outstanding fix_violation appears, with the live rule ids as its enum Review mode 16 — every mutating tool is unregistered. The agent can look but not touch Proposal pending 18 — writes withdrawn, check_proposal added, so edits cannot pile up behind a decision you have not made That last one is the part I am proudest of. The user's control is expressed in the protocol, not just in the UI. It also has one deliberate exception that took a while to find. The tool whose call is currently blocked on the approval has to stay registered, because unregistering a tool aborts its running invocation — withdrawing it kills the very call waiting for the user's answer. The bit that changes people's minds Numbers do not land. So there are two tools for making them land. The first is compare_standards , for the question people actually ask — would this work for my mother? One call measures the same home against several bodies at once: This home works up to 700 mm. At 900 mm, Bathroom becomes unreachable — 800 mm at the door between Bathroom and Hall. a walking frame 700 mm 88% reachable nothing cut off a standard wheelchair 900 mm 68% reachable Bathroom cut off a large powered chair 1000 mm 30% reachable five rooms cut off The second is show_route . Ask "show me why I can't get to the bathroom" and a violet disc — a wheelchair, drawn at its true 900 mm diameter — sets off from the front door, sweeps down the hall, reaches the bathroom door, and stops dead. It turns red, and a label appears on the spot: 800 mm — needs 900 mm . Then ask it to try again with a walking frame. The same disc, 700 mm this time, goes straight through and turns green. Same door. Same drawing. The difference is 100 mm — and it is the difference between a home someone can live in and one they cannot. It is not an illustration, either: it is the same widest-path field the rule engine uses, played back at scale with time added. That is the argument for putting an agent inside the page rather than behind an API. The agent did the measuring; the page did the showing; the person watched it happen on their own drawing. And it can build one from nothing Ask "design me a one-bedroom flat for a wheelchair user" and the agent makes a single apply_batch call: five rooms placed against each other, a front door, an archway, three internal doors, three windows, every room furnished. Twenty-odd operations, drawn on screen in violet before any of it exists, and approved once. Five rooms, about 74 m², every rule passing and 100 out of 100 — held there by a test that replays the whole conversation through the real operations and fails the build the day it stops scoring 100. Getting that to work honestly was most of a day. The first attempt produced a flat that failed its own inspection: the automatic furniture placer parked a wardrobe across a doorway and a fridge facing a worktop, because it only knew how to avoid other furniture. It now rules out everything the checker would object to — doorways, the arcs door leaves sweep, the clear floor other fittings need — and among what survives, picks the position with the most space around it. There is a test that plays the whole conversation and fails the build if the result stops scoring 100. Pointing it at a real home — and admitting when it missed Most people meet a floor plan as a picture: an estate agent's listing, a photo of a drawing on a wall. So you can drop one onto the page, say how wide it really is, and get_tracing_image hands the picture to the model with the real-world coordinates it sits at. The agent reads the room names and printed dimensions off it, builds the rooms in one apply_batch , and they land on top of the drawing the person can see. The important tool is the next one. check_against_source takes the areas printed on the original and compares them with what was actually drawn, room by room: Bedroom 1 drawn 14.494 m² source 14.49 matches Living room drawn 19.285 m² source 19.32 matches Dining drawn 11.365 m² source 11.61 matches Bedroom 3 drawn 11.365 m² source 13.01 wrong — drawn too small That last line is the point. Reading geometry off a marketing drawing is unreliable — I traced a real three-bedroom plan and found the drawing contradicting itself , labelling a room 14 ft wide inside a column that measures 13.2. No model can resolve that, and a tool that quietly averaged the difference would be worse than useless, because everything downstream is a measurement someone might rely on. So the app does not pretend. It tells you which rooms it got right, which it did not, and by how much. A tracing that measures correctly is the difference between advice about a real home and advice about a sketch of one. What humans and agents can now do together Both parties edit the same drawi
