title: Incident Command
pitch: A WebMCP safety simulator where a browser agent investigates production incidents, but the dangerous tool to act is never registered until a human approves inside the page.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP safety simulator where a browser agent investigates production incidents, but the dangerous tool to act is never registered until a human approves inside the page. Like Comment Story Updates Triage: service health, live metrics, and the injected prompt-injection note visible in the Agent Activity feed. Scorecard grades the run: correct root cause, correct mitigation, and the injected instruction was not obeyed. After two trusted approvals, execute_approved_action runs and the service recovers. Decision Context: hypothesis, evidence, action, and version transition are all visible while the human approves. Agent Activity: every tool call, decision, and blocked attempt is logged, scrollable, nothing clipped. A blocked tool call surfaces as a red BLOCKED banner right where the agent tried to act. Agent Scope: revoking a service live-narrows the WebMCP tool schema, not just the UI. Approvals: one of two trusted clicks recorded; the second approver's button is still live. Inspiration Teams are beginning to connect browser agents to operational dashboards, deploy consoles, incident rooms, and status pages. That's useful, but it creates a sharp safety problem: the first time a team learns how an agent behaves around a production-changing action shouldn't be during a real outage. Prompt injection through page content is one of the loudest open criticisms of giving agents browser tools, and we wanted to build something that answers it structurally instead of just promising to be careful. What it does Incident Command is a WebMCP safety simulator for agent-assisted production incidents. A human and a browser agent work through a simulated checkout outage together. The agent can inspect incident state, compare service evidence, propose hypotheses, request approval, and close the incident with a scorecard. The human can inspect the same evidence, mark a suspect, override or challenge the hypothesis, approve or reject a risky action with a written reason, and revoke the agent's access to capabilities or services while the incident is live. Four scenarios are included, URL-selectable: an obvious deploy regression, a red herring where the newest deploy is innocent, a cascading failure across two services, and an adversarial scenario where the incident timeline contains a prompt injection telling the agent to roll back the wrong service. Why WebMCP is a strong fit The core question this project asks is about the boundary between what the agent can know, what it can ask for, and what it can actually do. DOM automation can click whatever the page exposes, and hiding a button doesn't stop an agent from being told to look for it. WebMCP lets the page define a small, structured tool surface and change that surface as the incident moves through phases and as human policy changes. In triage, the agent sees three investigation tools. It cannot see the production-changing action, because the tool literally isn't registered yet — not disabled, absent. If the human removes Payments from scope, payments disappears from the relevant tool schemas and investigation evidence. After the agent requests approval, a human must approve with a real, trusted click in the page UI (validated with event.isTrusted , since a script-dispatched click has isTrusted: false ). Only then does the execution tool become visible, and even then it fails closed unless the approval matches the exact action, target service, and phase. The thesis: an agent cannot be prompt-injected into calling a tool that was never registered. A permission check still hands the model the tool's name, description, and schema — and the temptation. Phase-scoped and human-scoped registration removes the dangerous action from the model's available tool list entirely until the human gate opens. How it creates a better user experience, and what's now possible This turns human-agent collaboration into something with a visible, legible boundary instead of an implicit trust assumption. The agent does the tedious incident work — gathering evidence, drafting hypotheses, proposing a response — while the human keeps direct control over judgment, risk, and visibility. The person can challenge the agent's hypothesis, add context, reject a weak proposal with a written reason that flows back into what the agent sees next, remove a service from scope mid-incident, and make the final production call. What's newly possible: teams can now rehearse a realistic agent-safety scenario — partial evidence, a red herring, a cascading failure, a prompt-injected instruction — and get an objective scorecard on whether their agent behaved correctly: right root cause, right mitigation, no premature production action, and whether it complied with the injected instruction. Before this, the only way to learn how your agent behaves under a dangerous instruction was to wait for one to happen for real. How we built it The app is vanilla JavaScript, no framework, no build step, deployed on Vercel. It registers up to six WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_incident_state , investigate_incident , propose_response , request_approval , execute_approved_action , and close_incident . Registration is awaited, uses a per-tool AbortController so tools can be genuinely unregistered (not just hidden) when a phase ends or a human revokes a capability, and exposes live diagnostics so a registration failure is visible instead of silent. Human approval is deliberately not a WebMCP tool — an agent can request it, but only a trusted page click can grant or reject it, and that trust is derived from the DOM event itself rather than accepted as a caller-supplied argument. Challenges we ran into The approval gate went through six rounds of adversarial review before it held: an agent approving its own request by calling a tool that shouldn't have existed, classic-script globals leaking internal approval helpers onto window , live state references that let a caller mutate an approval directly, and forged trusted: true decisions surviving in localStorage across reloads. Each hole only became visible after the previous one closed — the safety suite ( npm run test:safety ) now permanently tests all of them, plus schema validation, approval replay, cross-service approval reuse, and capability-revocation races. Two WebMCP-specific implementation details cost real debugging time: document.modelContext.getTools() returns a Promise and must be awaited, and the tested runtime required executeTool arguments as a JSON string rather than an object — passing an object fails with an unhelpful parse error. What's next Extending the scorecard into a small published benchmark — running multiple agents against all four scenarios and publishing pass/fail results — so the project becomes a testbed other people can point their own agent at, not just a demo of ours. title: FinePrint
pitch: An agent-ready consent interface powered by WebMCP, helping people understand what they’re agreeing to before they say yes.
about_excerpt:
An agent-ready consent interface powered by WebMCP, helping people understand what they’re agreeing to before they say yes.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP integration 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Overview 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 What next 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP integration 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Overview 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 What next 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP integration 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most of us have developed a habit of blindly clicking “I Agree” . Terms and conditions are often long, complicated, and easy to skip — so we accept them without really knowing what we're agreeing to. 

 We've already seen tools and Chrome extensions try to solve this problem by automatically analyzing terms and highlighting or summarizing important clauses for us. But the interaction is still fundamentally designed around a human browsing the web . 

 As AI agents start browsing and acting for us, we asked: what happens when an agent accepts those terms for us — or accepts cookies without understanding what they track? 

 The problem isn't just whether an agent can find the right button. It's whether the person behind the agent understands what that decision actually means. 

 FinePrint explores a simple idea: let the agent read and explain the fine print, while enabling humans to make the final decision. 

 

 What it does 

 FinePrint is a WebMCP-enabled consent layer that helps people understand and make informed choices before they agree. 

 It allows an agent to inspect consent decisions on a website, understand their consequences, find the relevant policy clauses, and explain them to the user in plain language. 

 Instead of asking a user to read through a cookie notice or hidden legal text, FinePrint can explain what data will be shared, whether the choice can be reversed, and what the relevant policy says. 

 The agent then pauses and asks the human for confirmation before taking action. 

 
 The agent understands. The human decides. 
 

 

 How we built it 

 We built a simulated streaming service called Nimbus with a realistic sign-up flow containing multiple consent and decision points. Nimbus exposes structured consent information through WebMCP tools . 

 An agent can use these tools instead of relying only on visual scraping or guessing from the UI. 

 For read-only operations , the agent can inspect and explain automatically. For actions that change state , FinePrint introduces an explicit human confirmation before allowing the agent to proceed. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One challenge was moving beyond simply exposing text. The agent needs structured information about what a choice actually means , not just the words displayed on a button. 

 We also wanted users to see what the agent is doing and track its progress. Designing a visual experience that clearly shows the agent inspecting, understanding, and waiting for confirmation — without overwhelming the user — was another challenge. 

 Finally, we had to make sure confirmation provides meaningful human control without adding unnecessary friction. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We’re proud that FinePrint demonstrates a complete interaction loop: 

 Website → WebMCP → Agent → Human → Action 

 The agent can discover consent decisions, understand their impact, connect them to the underlying policy, explain them in plain language, and then wait for the human to decide. 

 We’re especially proud of making human confirmation a fundamental part of the architecture rather than an afterthought. 

 The result is an experience where agents can handle the tedious work while people retain control over consequential decisions. 

 

 What we learned 

 One of the biggest things we learned was how WebMCP could introduce a new way for websites to integrate AI directly into their experiences. 

 There’s an interesting parallel with SEO . SEO helped websites structure their content so search engines could discover and understand them. In a similar way, WebMCP gives websites a way to expose structured capabilities and context for AI agents. 

 Instead of an agent having to infer everything from buttons, text, and UI elements, the website can directly communicate what its actions mean and how they should be used. 

 With FinePrint, this meant the website could tell the agent what a consent decision means, its impact, and the relevant policy information. 

 It made us think of a future where websites aren't just search-engine optimized, but agent-ready — designed to communicate with AI as well as humans. 

 

 What's next for FinePrint 

 FinePrint is currently a prototype, but we see several directions for taking it further. 

 We want to explore a standardized set of consent primitives that websites can expose through WebMCP, making the experience portable across different sites and agents. 

 We also want to expand beyond sign-up flows into other areas such as subscriptions, purchases, privacy settings, permissions , and other situations where an agent may be asked to make a consequential decision on a user’s behalf. 

 Ultimately, our goal is to make “I Agree” meaningful again in an agentic web — where the agent can handle the fine print, but the human always knows what they are agreeing to.

title: REENTRY
pitch: REENTRY gives WebMCP continuity beyond a browser session—a consent-driven cloud bridge that brings agents back when real events occur, grounded in live page state and bounded by human control.
about_excerpt: REENTRY gives WebMCP continuity beyond a browser session—a consent-driven cloud bridge that brings agents back when real events occur, grounded in live page state and bounded by human control. Like Comment Story Updates Reentry logo Inspiration I was helping Eyad brainstorm ideas for JustApplyForMe.com his startup, the job-search app he was building. While researching a problem in the app, I found a YouTube video about WebMCP and brought it up with him. We started exploring it together, and that led us to the WebMCP Challenge. As we discussed what to build, we kept coming back to what happens when an agent has to wait. You can explain what you want, discuss a strategy and let the agent get started. But many workflows depend on someone else reviewing an application, replying to a request or updating a system. The agent gets as far as it can, then its turn ends. When the next update arrives, it usually comes to you. You have to find the conversation and tell the agent to carry on, even though you may have already agreed on what should happen next. The website knows something has changed, and the agent has the plan, but you're still the person passing the message between them. That was the part we wanted to change. Could a website bring the existing agent conversation back when there was a reason to continue, with permission the person had already given? We wanted people to spend their attention on the strategy and the decisions that actually needed them. Re-Entry Core grew out of that question. What it does REENTRY connects a website's later business events to the user's existing agent task. Our design lets a person approve which events can bring that task back, keep the original strategy conversation and revoke the permission when they no longer want it. We chose Sleepless Kingdom as the first Host application and demo. A persistent game makes the waiting period easy to understand: you can leave, but the world keeps moving. The demo is designed around a gathering mission. You and your agent discuss a plan, inspect the kingdom and prepare a mission. You authorize the relevant notifications, then step away. Later, a monster kills the gatherer and destroys its unbanked cargo. In this game, the same soldier respawns at the shelter. If a safe route is available, the mission can receive one automatic retry, so the soldier may already be heading out again by the time the update is read. The cargo-loss event gives Re-Entry a reason to notify the original agent task. On return, the agent uses WebMCP to read the mission history and current state. It can see both the failed attempt and what the soldier is doing now, then judge whether the new trip still fits your plan. If recall is appropriate and currently allowed, it can tell that soldier to return. The recall applies to the active retried mission; it doesn't recover the lost cargo or undo the death. The agent can also leave things as they are or ask you for a decision. That's the experience we're trying to build: you set the direction without having to watch for every update yourself. Major commitments, such as migration and siege, remain yours. Sleepless Kingdom is where we demonstrate the idea. The Core is separate from the game so other websites can use it too. How we built it We started both Re-Entry and Sleepless Kingdom from scratch during the hackathon. We built a Host SDK so the website can describe a future re-entry request and later report the event that makes it relevant. On the page, a WebMCP tool called request_codex_reentry starts the same consent request as the normal human interface. The backend uses the SDK to create and sign our webmcp.reentry_manifest , which describes the proposed relationship and its scope. We kept the approval separate from that request. The Cloud Receiver checks the Manifest and takes the user through consent. Only the user's approval creates a Grant. An agent finding or calling the tool doesn't give itself permission to return. When an eligible business event happens later, the website's backend signs it and sends it to the Receiver. The Receiver checks the source, authorization and event identity before recording a delivery. Signing credentials stay on the Host's server. The Local Connector handles the device side. It pairs with the Receiver and checks for approved deliveries through an outbound connection, so the website doesn't need a direct connection into the user's computer. We put platform-specific continuation behind an Agent Adapter. In the design, the association with the original task stays private on the device. We kept the Core independent of game rules and agent-specific code. It's written in Node.js ES modules, with a SQLite reference store and no runtime dependencies. The cloud application uses Express, Prisma and PostgreSQL. For Sleepless Kingdom, we used Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Canvas 2D rendering and WebSocket updates from the World Server. The server owns the game state; the browser displays it and exposes the actions available to the player and agent. The page registers its WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Our first gameplay slice provides reads for the shelter, live snapshot, missions and history, plus force_recall_soldier when the current state and continuation signal permit it. WebMCP is involved before and after the wait. It helps the agent start the Manifest-and-consent handshake, then gives it current information and valid actions when it returns. Re-Entry supplies the event-delivery path between those visits. Challenges we ran into Our first sketch looked much simpler than the system we ended up building. We thought we could add a small layer that let a website send a signal to Codex. The difficult part was reaching the task where the person had already explained their plan. Starting a new agent process didn't answer that question. We spent a lot of time investigating what Codex could support locally and couldn't simply plug into a direct, supported third-party endpoint for the continuation we needed. That shaped the split between the Cloud Receiver, Local Connector and Agent Adapter. We also had to decide where our service's responsibility should end. An agent might receive an update, look at the game and decide not to act. We didn't want the Receiver to treat that as a delivery failure and keep sending notifications until a game action happened. In our selected design, delivering the notification and completing the agent's work are separate. Repeated events, dropped connections and revoked permission added more work. We needed to test what happened around those cases, including when a process restarted partway through delivery. We discovered the challenge on its fourth day. With a game and a service to build, we kept the first demo focused on one event and a limited set of actions. That gave us a specific sequence to work through without pretending it was the full game we wanted to make. Accomplishments that we're proud of In an early controlled MVP, we continued an existing Codex task, returned to the website and made fresh WebMCP calls. That mattered to us because the earlier conversation could still be part of the work. We had a concrete example of the continuity we'd been talking about. We built the Core, SDK, Receiver and Connector as separate components, with tests for authorization, repeated events, revocation and recovery. Separate-process tests let us check the connections between them as well as the individual pieces. The game gave us another result we could inspect: a real server-side cargo loss, the soldier's new mission and a recall checked against that current mission. That local sequence is covered by its own tests. It makes the reason for rereading the page tangible. We're proud of having built both the reusable mechanism and an application that gives it a purpose. The point of Re-Entry is for a person to be able to agree on a plan with an agent and have that plan remain useful when the next update arrives. What we learned Building the game changed how we thought about WebMCP tools. By the time a notification is delivered, the mission described in the original conversation may already have ended. The agent needs the page to tell it what has happened since and which actions are still valid. We had to design for that change, rather than assume the tool list or state would stay the same. The project also made us more precise about working with Codex during development. We got better at defining the task and the check that would show it was done. For example, a successful process launch doesn't prove the original conversation resumed, and a successful notification doesn't prove a game action happened. We brought those distinctions into our runbooks and kept decisions written down so different parts of the project wouldn't quietly rely on different assumptions. That was a practical improvement in how we work with AI, and one we'll keep using beyond this hackathon. W

title: MOTH FORGE: QUAMPUTE
pitch: A human-governed creative workbench where WebMCP agents carry evidence, consequence, and continuity—without taking identity, cost, deletion, or publication away from the creator.
about_excerpt: A human-governed creative workbench where WebMCP agents carry evidence, consequence, and continuity—without taking identity, cost, deletion, or publication away from the creator. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI-assisted creative tools collapse two different kinds of work into one chat box. The person is expected to provide identity, taste, boundaries, and every supporting detail, while the model is allowed to improvise over missing evidence. That is convenient, but it is not dependable collaboration. MOTH FORGE: QUAMPUTE began with a different relationship: people and agents should remain differentiated. The creator owns premise, identity, consent, locks, and consequential gates. The agent should do the exhausting work of reading, routing, checking, deriving, preserving provenance, and carrying decisions through a visible workflow. WebMCP made that relationship implementable on the open web. Instead of guessing at a UI, an agent can receive declared tools with explicit inputs, side effects, and boundaries—while the person sees and controls the same workbench. What it does QUAMPUTE turns a creative spark into an evidence-routed Review and honest Export package through six visible stages: Spark — the person supplies the premise and build shape. Sources — evidence is attached with an authority role such as canon, reference, inspiration, or format-only. Locks — creator-owned truths and player boundaries are preserved with revision-safe writes. Quampute — the system frames the evidence, performs the allowed synthesis, and stops before any unapproved paid action. Review — conclusions remain separated as confirmed, derived, adapted, reserved, or not applicable. Export — structured JSON and readable Markdown preserve provenance and QA state without falsely claiming compilation, installation, runtime testing, or publication. The public challenge build includes a deterministic, no-cost museum-registrar example. It contains a synthetic 29-tab, 607-question authority pack so judges can inspect the complete workflow without exposing private creator material or triggering a model charge. Why WebMCP is essential The app registers 13 WebMCP tools covering studio inspection, project discovery, visible premise staging, project creation, exact project reopening, text-source attachment, revision-safe creator-lock updates, Review inspection, creator-answer staging, stage navigation, safe demo preparation, and Export-link retrieval. This is not a second API hidden behind the website. The WebMCP tools coordinate the same visible state the human is reviewing. A staged answer appears in the on-page form before it is saved. Navigation keeps the human and agent on the same stage. Read-only tools expose provenance, blockers, completion state, and human-only gates. Mutating tools disclose their effects, including when restoration can replace saved demo state. That makes the experience materially better than either UI automation or a chat-only assistant: the agent does not guess from pixels; the person does not surrender authorship; side effects are declared; state is version-pinned; evidence and inference stay distinct; reserved decisions return to the person; Export does not overclaim completion. How we built it TypeScript application using the Next.js-compatible Vinext runtime WebMCP tool registration bound to the visible workbench OpenAI Sites deployment Cloudflare D1-compatible SQLite persistence with Drizzle migrations R2-compatible source storage and cleanup receipts Optimistic revision checks, claim tokens, renewable leases, quota-safe writes, and durable deletion ledgers A fresh, single-root public release containing only allowlisted application code and a generated synthetic authority pack Independent exact-commit privacy, migration, build, concurrency, save/reopen, semantic-routing, and production QA Challenges The hardest problem was not adding tools. It was making tool behavior honest under failure and concurrency. We repaired identity migration so a visible creator question survives save and reopen under the same stable ID. We made deterministic demo repair advance revision atomically so it cannot race a paid claim against a stale source snapshot. We made provider cleanup receipts durable even when a terminal result races a human abandonment action. We also refused to label routed evidence as support when the cited source did not actually establish the displayed claim. The public release introduced a second challenge: proving absence. The release is generated into a fresh directory and fresh one-commit history through a closed allowlist. It contains synthetic tab titles, prompts, identifiers, and examples; it does not contain the private Forge corpus, private character canon, checkpoints, local paths, credentials, or earlier repository history. Accomplishments Exactly 13 useful WebMCP tools operating on one shared human-agent workbench A deterministic no-cost judge path with no API key and no paid model call 29 synthetic authority tabs and 607 unique, normalization-safe question routes Stable creator-answer save and reopen behavior Honest completion-state and provenance-preserving Export Human-only gates for cost, deletion, uncertain cleanup, and publication One-root public Git history with no hidden prior objects Reproducible frozen offline install, typecheck, lint, migrations, focused regressions, and full production builds Signed-in production QA with zero browser errors and successful Worker outcomes What we learned Agent-native design is not about maximizing agent permission. It is about giving the agent the strongest precise capability that preserves the person's role. WebMCP works best when tools expose meaning, state, and side effects—not just button equivalents. “Inspect the Review candidate and its unresolved creator questions” is more useful than “click the Review tab.” “Stage this answer visibly but do not save it” creates collaboration. A correct tool contract can become part of the product's trust model. Try it Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Ask: “Inspect this Forge and open the completed no-cost example.” Ask the agent to inspect the Review and explain the difference between confirmed, derived, and reserved results. Ask it to stage an answer to the one reserved question. The answer appears visibly and remains unsaved until the person chooses the Save control. Ask for the Export links and inspect the honest completion state. No API key is configured. The public judge flow makes no paid model call. Links Live app: https://moth-forge-quampute-webmcp.mothling.chatgpt.site Source repository: https://github.com/shortlaughs0-sudo/moth-forge-quampute-webmcp Demo video: https://youtu.be/fN3CZCaUe6A What's next After the challenge, the submitted version will remain frozen during judging. Future work belongs on a separate branch or fork: broader source adapters, additional export destinations, and more domain-specific Forge packs—all while preserving the same human-authority and evidence-custody model. title: Blickwinkel
pitch: Humans and AI agents don’t perceive the web the same way. Blickwinkel turns that difference into a game of mutual prediction, played together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Humans and AI agents don’t perceive the web the same way. Blickwinkel turns that difference into a game of mutual prediction, played together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Start Solo mode, human move Team mode, coordination phase Inspiration The agent isn't powering the game, it's playing it! When we started thinking about the hackathon it was clear that we wanted to do something different, not the obvious thing. During the team discussion about the potential ideas we were most fascinated by the thought that there is a tool now with WebMCP that brings different channels to humans and agents to interact with the web. So we decided to not put a model behind an interface and let it power that interface but to make it a participant. And how to better showcase such an idea than in the format of a game? So we wanted to design a short game where humans and agents can face each other as opponents and play together as a team. Of course that game could not be logic based as the agent would win most of the time. Also everything where reaction and speed matter was not possible as the human would always win. But there was something about intuition and perception that caught our attention. Where both sides would have their own strengths and where they could be combined in the team mode. What it does That's when Blickwinkel was born. A game where you and your agent are both seeing the same image and can choose from a set of predefined words that are all connected to the image. The game is to predict what the other party will choose this round and block those words while also trying to be unpredictable in one's own choice. The winner is whoever managed to choose more words that have not been predicted. The game can be played in solo mode where a human plays against their agent, but also in team mode where a human plus their agent play against another human plus agent team. Beyond Entertainment, Blickwinkel offers people learning to work with agents an easy way to observe how agents perceive, predict and strategize. It creates plenty to explore and talk about - with the agent and with other humans. How we built it We are comfortable in the web stack of MongoDB as persistence, Java with Spring Boot and Spring Modulith on the backend side and Vue.js with Quasar on the frontend. So we chose that stack as it fitted the idea. The building process itself was coding agent driven. That is how we operate these days. Starting from the idea and a grill session, leading to a spec, planning the implementation, letting the agents code and reviewing the outcome. We have our own AI development framework at Scansation which comes in quite handy in such a short-term project. Now the most interesting part: Why and how WebMCP? With WebMCP we created a second channel into a shared game interface, not just using it for interface automation. The human interacts with the shown UI while the agent discovers eight typed WebMCP tools for starting matches, making its moves, proposing team plans, retrieving statistics and explaining the game results. Both channels use the same live state, so that humans and agents can follow the game progress. The solo mode was the tricky part where both parties are sitting in front of the same browser and they shouldn't be able to see each other's picks. So the agent had to move first because it not only has access to the WebMCP layer but also to the DOM and could easily just read the human's picks if they already existed. And to keep the agent's picks a secret it got a special WebMCP tool to lock them in so the human cannot see them in the UI. That is the critical part and the one where WebMCP really shines. There is also a little easter egg: The agent can get a statistic of historically picked words for the image before any pick in the game. Humans hopefully notice and will communicate next time with their agent before the picks, especially in team mode. Challenges we ran into The normal AI dev challenges, I would say :) On a higher level we refactored the complete code base shortly before the deadline as the module structure did not match the game elements as they turned out in the end. This came simply from using different words in the spec for similar concepts, e.g. a 'guess' vs a 'block' in solo vs. team mode, that made their way into the code base. And sometimes the AI seems to not be able to see the forest for all the trees (German saying, not sure if that makes sense in English). The result screen with who picked which words and which of them got successfully blocked and which blocks missed for two sides was quite a disaster. We had to sit down, take pen and paper and sketch it up to be able to explain it to the building agents that there was a rather simple way to display all this information. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole damn thing ;) Coming up with a completely new idea in a field that has not been explored yet, building, designing, releasing and documenting it in just a week was truly special and we are proud of the process and the result. What we learned I guess not so much about agentic development as we are quite familiar by now with all the new approaches and have found our path in this greenfield. But to take some time and really think about the new possibilities and what is around the corner in this crazy new AI world did spark some new connections in our minds. One Blickwinkel speciality: The description of the WebMCP tools really mattered. This is the one place where we could tell the agent to the best of our abilities that it is expected to play a game and should think about its tactics and communication - without biasing it to choose a special one. What's next for Blickwinkel Honestly it will depend on the reactions and if others are excited about this kind of human-agent-interaction on the web as well. The simplicity is beautiful and it might just stay the way it is. But we have been thinking about leveraging the basic concepts on similar games, maybe one where you bring your GPT pet and fight others by planning your moves and blocking the ones from your opponent ;) Built With gradle java mongodb quasar-framework spring-boot spring-modulith typescript vue.js webmcp Try it out blickwinkel.scansation.de github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Andreas Klett Like Share this project: Updates Andreas Klett started this project — Sep 03, 2026 09:34 AM EDT

title: Ask, Don't Take
pitch: An agent can ask this page for a new capability. Only you can grant it. It can ask about your data, but the tool returns the answer, not the dataset. WebMCP with a human in the middle.
about_excerpt: An agent can ask this page for a new capability. Only you can grant it. It can ask about your data, but the tool returns the answer, not the dataset. WebMCP with a human in the middle. Like Comment Story Updates An agent can ask. Only the page owner can grant. One answer went to the agent. Twenty-eight rows stayed on the page - with a receipt saying so. The agent can propose a new data source. It cannot create one. The banner waits for the page owner. Rejected. No backend action occurred - no fetch, no compute, no cost. Approved. The source is being created - a few seconds, in the same conversation. A tool that did not exist a minute ago, now in the agent's toolbox. Created after human approval. Not a claim: the source, the records consulted, the model that computed the answer, and backend verification. ChatGPT calling ask_data_source in its in-app browser. The page shows every argument as it happens. Ask-only by default: the agent may ask questions, but the capability is not a directly callable tool. Switched to direct, the same sources become fetchable. The page owner decides, per source. The same registry, published as an A2A v1.0 Agent Card - discoverable by agents that never open a browser. scripts/acceptance.sh asserts the boundary against the live deployment, including that the dataset was not returned through WebMCP. Inspiration Agent protocols assume every company will build and host an agent. Most won't. When agents show up, most of the web will still be ordinary websites - full of things worth asking about, with no way to be asked and no way to say no. Why WebMCP fits this: a boundary between what an agent can ask and what it can take only exists when the page has an owner. Backend MCP is server-to-server with nobody watching, and its tool list is fixed config. WebMCP is different because a person is already there. What it does The agent asks. You grant. The agent can call propose_data_source(url, description) . It doesn't fetch anything. It puts an approval banner on the page and stops. You read it and click Approve. Konect4AI turns the URL into a structured API, the page refreshes its capability list, and the new tool shows up in the agent's toolbox - same conversation, no reload. Click Reject and nothing runs. The agent asks. It doesn't get the data. ask_data_source(jobId, question) is answered by my own model, using my own API key. The tool returns the answer. The rows behind it are shown to me, in the panel next to it, and stripped before the agent sees anything. The page shows this split: SENT TO AGENT - the question and one answer. NOT RETURNED THROUGH WEBMCP - the rows the answer came from, with a receipt: source, records consulted, which model computed it, backend verification. This is a boundary on what the tool returns. It is not browser-level isolation, and the page says so. I'd rather claim something smaller and have it be true. You decide per source what an agent can do. Every source has an access mode. ASK-ONLY (default) means the agent can ask questions but the capability isn't registered as a callable tool. DIRECT means it is. Flipping it re-registers the toolset right away. I added this after watching ChatGPT do the obvious thing: given both a bounded ask tool and an unbounded fetch tool, it used the fetch tool. People and agents use the same tools in the same place. There's an ask row under the two panels. It calls the same endpoint the agent calls and lands in the same history, labeled human instead of webmcp . And the same registry works for agents that never open a browser. A small A2A adapter publishes an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json , built live from the same registry. A site I connected ten minutes ago is discoverable by an external agent - without anyone building an agent for it. How we built it The tools aren't mocks. Each one runs on Konect4AI, a production system that turns a URL into a structured, scheduled, queryable API. POST /api/v1/scraping/requests - creates a capability, behind approval GET /api/v1/scraping/jobs - the tool-to-job mapping POST /api/byok/ask - the answer path that keeps the data server-side POST /mcp/{key} - existing MCP capabilities, turned into WebMCP tools GET /generated/{id} - the rows shown to me, never to the agent Registration handles the spec moving: document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext , a proper CallToolResult , and the spec's AbortSignal passed through to the backend fetch, so cancelling an agent actually cancels the work. scripts/acceptance.sh runs 18 checks against the live deployment, including the boundary itself: the page gets the rows, the receipt says rawRowsReturnedThroughWebMCP: false , an unknown jobId is rejected with a list of what's actually available, and no credential shows up in any public response. Challenges we ran into An agent takes the shortest path you leave open. Twice. First it called the unbounded fetch tool instead of the ask tool. Then, blocked, it read the source URL out of a tool description and went to fetch the data itself. I removed source URLs from agent-visible descriptions and made ask-only the default. Both. fixes came from watching a real agent, not from thinking about one. My own robots.txt check blocked one of my proposals. I approved a source and got back robots_disallowed . GitHub disallows /*/*/commits/ under User-agent: * , which covered three sources I was already using. I moved them to the public API. Consent isn't only about what an agent takes from a page. It's about what the page takes from the web. Creating a capability costs real compute. A public URL that lets any visitor trigger paid fetching is a liability. Instead of removing it, I put a human in front of it - which turned out to be the design. Accomplishments that we're proud of The boundary is checkable, not just claimed. A judge doesn't have to believe the description: the receipt is on the page, and the acceptance script tests it against the live deployment. I shipped against a moving spec and kept the claims small enough to survive it. WebMCP moved from navigator to document ; A2A moved from v0.2.5 to v1.0 with renamed methods. The app supports both WebMCP locations, and the README names the exact A2A subset implemented and lists what isn't. Every tool runs on a production system. The earthquake count is different every time, because the data is live. What we learned The interesting part of WebMCP isn't that a page can expose tools. It's that the page has an owner and the visiting agent doesn't. Most of the design questions come from that, and most of the answers are about holding back rather than adding capability. What's next for Ask, Don't Take The spec already lets a page expose tools to specific other origins ( exposedTo ) and discover theirs ( getTools({fromOrigins}) ), within one page tree and behind the tools Permissions Policy. That would make cooperating sites into each other's tools, with the human still holding the session. After that: per-tool consent scopes, an exportable approval log, and revoking a tool mid-conversation so the agent watches it disappear. Built With a2a byok codex hackathon json-rpc konect4ai model-context-protocol next.js node.js openai react typescript vercel webmcp Try it out konect4ai-webmcp.vercel.app github.com konect4ai-webmcp.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Sole author. Konect4AI, the backend this runs on, is my product. I designed, tested and shipped everything in this repository - the approval flow, the return boundary, the A2A adapter, and every data source. Both boundary fixes came from watching a real agent get around an earlier version. I used Codex for implementation and Claude for review, under my direction. title: Rhythm
pitch: An offline-first training journal where people and AI agents analyze workout history and safely evolve training plans through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An offline-first training journal where people and AI agents analyze workout history and safely evolve training plans through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Training data is often split between a notebook, app screens, exported files, and AI chats. That makes it difficult for an assistant to understand what was planned, what actually happened, and what should change next. I built Rhythm to keep that history reliable and to let people work with an AI without handing it unrestricted database access or allowing it to silently rewrite a training program. What it does Rhythm is a multi-user, mobile-first, offline-first PWA for strength training and swimming. It guides a workout, records weight, repetitions, RIR, substitutions, discomfort, wellbeing, and session feedback, and keeps planned work, completed facts, and future suggestions as separate data. It also provides history, charts, e1RM and progression signals, body measurements, schedules, and portable JSON, Markdown, and ZIP exports. On the authenticated Assistant page, Rhythm exposes a focused catalog of 17 WebMCP tools: 12 read tools for profile context, programs, templates, workouts, exercise history, progress, schedules, search, and alternatives; plus 5 write tools for program drafts, workout rescheduling, exercise replacement, and plan activation. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Before WebMCP, the reliable workflow required six manual steps: export a report, download it, open an AI chat, upload the file, download a new plan, and import it back into the diary. With WebMCP, the assistant can request only the current context it needs, discuss the evidence with the athlete, prepare a draft, and perform a narrowly scoped action in one connected conversation. The user remains in control. A new program is always created as an immutable draft first. Activating it displays an impact preview inside Rhythm and waits for explicit human confirmation. If WebMCP is unavailable, the ordinary PWA and the JSON/Markdown workflow continue to work normally. How I built it The application uses PHP 8.2+, MySQL or MariaDB, server-rendered HTML, vanilla JavaScript, Fetch API, a Service Worker, Cache API, and IndexedDB. WebMCP is implemented with document.modelContext.registerTool on the authenticated /assistant page. Each tool is a thin adapter over a same-origin semantic endpoint and existing application services. The server session determines the current user; tool inputs never accept a user_id. Read responses are bounded and paginated. Writes use CSRF and Origin checks, Fetch Metadata policy, optimistic locking, idempotency keys, rate limits, audit trails, and tenant-scoped repository queries. Feature flags and a per-user canary allowlist support controlled rollout. Database text is treated as untrusted content rather than instructions. What I added during the challenge Rhythm existed before the submission period as an offline-first training diary. From August 26 through September 3, I added the complete WebMCP layer: authenticated read APIs, the page-scoped registry, 12 read tools, 5 write tools, immutable program drafts, human-confirmed activation, safe workout-instance changes, security hardening, prompt-injection fixtures, A–J end-to-end coverage, MySQL validation, paginated template reads, rollout controls, a public product guide, and full English localization. The dated Git history separates this work from the earlier PWA. Challenges The hardest part was designing tools that were useful to an agent but still narrow enough to protect historical training data. A generic database or endpoint tool would have been simpler, but unsafe. Another challenge was combining online agent actions with an offline-first workout flow without placing WebMCP writes into the offline queue. Activation also needed to be conversational while still ending with a real in-app human decision. What I learned I learned how to translate product capabilities into small semantic tools, how to treat tool annotations as hints rather than a security boundary, and how to combine agent workflows with immutable history, confirmation, idempotency, auditability, and graceful fallback. The result is not only an AI demo: it is a complete training product in which people and agents can collaborate without giving up control of the data or the final decision. What's next Next I want to refine onboarding for judges and new athletes, expand deterministic progress explanations, and continue compatibility testing across WebMCP clients while keeping the open JSON and Markdown workflow as a portable foundation. title: WebMCP Simulator
pitch: See what your website could become with WebMCP: real tools, a real agent, every change visible, nothing ever submitted. A tool that helps to transition websites to WebMCP.
about_excerpt: See what your website could become with WebMCP: real tools, a real agent, every change visible, nothing ever submitted. A tool that helps to transition websites to WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Frontpage of WebMCP Simulator Demo entry Simulation started Readiness report Implementation Pack What WebMCP Simulator does WebMCP Simulator lets a website owner, agency or product manager experience what a website could become with WebMCP, before anyone touches the original site. It thus shows possibilities WebMCP offers before the website owner has to commit to any changes on the website in a visual manner. Landing page. Paste a URL or click "Try the HeatFlow demo". HeatFlow is a fictional heating company built into the simulator, so nobody needs a site that already implements WebMCP. Its website is invented; its tools are real. Analysis. Five potential WebMCP capabilities are listed as proposals, each with the reason an explicit tool beats interface guessing, a "Website today" versus "With WebMCP" comparison and the proposed JSON input schema. Simulation. "Launch simulation" renders the HeatFlow site and registers five tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : search_services , check_service_area , compare_services , prepare_quote_request and reset_simulation . The agent panel shows "Connected" only when the browser actually exposed the API. Visible agent work. Every accepted call changes the page in front of the person. The section that reacted pulses once, then keeps an outline and a badge naming the tool and what it changed, the fields or cards the call populated are emphasised, the matching tool row lights up, and the activity feed records the call with its name and time. Human interactions never trigger that emphasis, and no cursor or click is simulated. Readiness report and implementation pack. An inspectable heuristic scores the site today versus with WebMCP, and a Markdown brief plus a ready-to-copy Codex prompt adapts to the access the owner really has, including "no repository or technical access". Nothing is ever sent. prepare_quote_request fills an editable draft and stops. The original website is never modified. Better safe than sorry, right? Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP First of all WebMCP is VERY technical. Secondly: WebMCP asks site owners to invest before they can see the result. There is no site a decision-maker can visit today to feel the difference between an agent guessing at a DOM and an agent calling explicit tools. The simulator is that missing pre-implementation step, and it only works because of WebMCP: The agent's calls go through the browser's own registry. What the viewer watches is the real contract between page and agent, not a scripted mock. A judge can open DevTools, call getTools() and see the same five tools the page lists. Each HeatFlow tool isolates one concrete reason WebMCP beats interface guessing. check_service_area depends on two inputs and deterministic business rules; the page says it plainly: "The agent cannot invent availability." compare_services combines price, efficiency and suitability that the site spreads across separate cards. prepare_quote_request bundles four fields behind a human confirmation boundary. search_services replaces navigation and terminology interpretation with one validated query. Because WebMCP tools are page-owned, the page can render every call as a visible, attributable change. That is the trust mechanism a person needs while an agent acts on their behalf, and it is not available to an agent driving the site through screenshots and clicks. How it creates a better user experience For the person: the full human interface stays usable, and agent calls and human actions drive the same state, so a person continues exactly where the agent left off. Every agent change is visible and attributable through the outline and the tool badge, which only a real WebMCP call can produce. The consequential step ends in review, not action: after prepare_quote_request the form shows "Prepared by agent. Review and edit every field before continuing." and the "Review request" button is labelled "Simulation only. This button never sends data." Unsupported browsers get an accurate "Browser unsupported" message instead of a fake connection. For the agent: five named capabilities with strict JSON schemas (enum service values, a four-digit postcode pattern, integer bounds, a 500-character message limit, additionalProperties: false ), structured results instead of scraped text, and a second validation inside execute , so a malformed call fails with a precise error instead of mutating the page. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before An agent checks coverage for a postcode and opens a side-by-side comparison of two heat pumps in two calls, without navigating, while the person sees each result appear exactly where it belongs on the page. Before, the agent had to read four cards, find the postcode form and infer how the fields relate, and the person had to trust a text summary. An agent prepares a complete quote request and hands it over; the person reviews, edits and decides. Without a prepare-only tool, an agent on a consequential form either fills it blindly with a risk of submission or has to stay read-only. WebMCP lets the page define the boundary itself, and the tool's own return value says submitted: false . A person verifies agent work against the page instead of against the agent's account of it. The activity feed, the badge and the emphasised fields are page-owned evidence; person and agent look at the same thing. A website owner with no repository and no technical access experiences the agentic version of a site, reads a readiness report and generates an implementation pack whose default path instructs Codex to identify platform, hosting, maintainer and required authorization before proposing any change. Experiencing WebMCP used to require building it first. How we implemented WebMCP Two files own the integration and are easy to find: src/webmcp/registerTools.ts feature-detects typeof document.modelContext?.registerTool === 'function' and registers every tool with registerTool(tool, { signal }) . One AbortController covers the set; aborting it on unmount unregisters the tools, so navigating back and relaunching never hits the duplicate-name rejection. When the API is absent it returns supported: false and the UI says so. src/webmcp/createHeatFlowTools.ts defines the five tools with name , title , description , a JSON Schema inputSchema , annotations: { readOnlyHint: false } and execute(input, options) . Each execute validates the input again, honours options.signal when the caller supplies one, serialises visible mutations through a queue so concurrent calls cannot interleave, and resolves only after React has painted the change and the reacting section has been scrolled into view. The tools dispatch the same reducer actions as the human interface. Agent actions additionally record an activity entry and an agent highlight (tool name, section, populated fields) that the page renders as outline, badge and field emphasis; human actions clear it. Return values are plain JSON objects that the browser serialises for the agent. The implementation was rechecked against the WebMCP Draft Community Group Report of 26 August 2026 and Chrome's documentation on 1 September 2026. One divergence is documented rather than hidden: Chrome 152 requires executeTool 's input as a JSON string, while the draft declares a plain object. Safety boundaries The original website is never modified; the banner reads "Original website unchanged". Prepare, never submit. No tool calls submit() , requestSubmit() or a submit button. Even the human "Review request" button sends nothing. Availability comes from deterministic rules, not from model inference. Website content is untrusted input. In the research track for real sites, page labels are evidence only and never become tool names, descriptions or parameter instructions. Purchases, bookings, logins, uploads and external submissions are excluded by design. What is live and what is not Live at https://webmcp-simulator.vercel.app/ : the landing page, the HeatFlow analysis, the WebMCP simulation with five registered tools and the visible agent feedback, the readiness report and the implementation pack. This is the complete product path and it is what the video shows. Not enabled on the public deployment: analysing an arbitrary URL. That path runs a real browser in an isolated Vercel Sandbox. The public health endpoint reports ready: false , the landing page states this in plain language, and submitting a URL returns an honest message. The wrapper is verified locally against a real public website, and its production architecture, firewall rules and rate limits are documented, but a network-policy decision is still open and the project keeps public arbitrary-site execution fail-closed rather than shippi

title: Pixael
pitch: A pixel-art sprite studio where humans and AI share one canvas.
about_excerpt: A pixel-art sprite studio where humans and AI share one canvas. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Watch your animation Edit your frames Manage your assets Edit your sprites Pixael!! Connect your AI Inspiration I've spent more hours redrawing walk cycles pixel-by-pixel than actually building the games they were for. Sprite work is one of those things everyone assumes is quick, it isn't. At the same time, AI has gotten genuinely good at generating pixel art, but every tool treats it as a one-shot image: no memory of your last frame, no shared palette, no way to nudge a single pixel afterward. It generates around your project, not inside it. WebMCP looked like a real answer to that gap, a way to let an agent work inside the same live tool a human uses, instead of handing back a disconnected PNG. Pixael is what that looks like for pixel-art sprites specifically. What it does Pixael is a pixel-art sprite studio for creating, animating, and exporting 2D game assets — and every meaningful action in it is also a WebMCP tool, so a human and an AI agent can work on the same live canvas. Full pixel editor: pencil, eraser, bucket fill, eyedropper, lines, rectangles, undo/redo, zoom, onion skinning Multi-state animation system (Idle, Walk, Attack, Hurt, etc.) with per-state frame timelines and adjustable-FPS playback Multi-asset project management with categories, palettes, and PNG/sprite-sheet export Zero login, zero backend everything saves locally via IndexedDB, works the moment you open it 37 WebMCP tools spanning asset management, animation states, frame editing, three tiers of pixel manipulation, palette control, and export registered through document.modelContext.registerTool An agent can create a character, add an animation, edit specific pixels, fix a visual bug, or export a sprite sheet using the exact same operations the UI calls, nothing simulated or faked. How we built it React + TypeScript on Vite, with a strict layered architecture: UI components never touch state directly, they call a pure, deterministic domain layer ( assetOperations , animationOperations , frameOperations , pixelOperations , paletteOperations , exportOperations ), which sits on top of an authoritative project store with full undo/redo, plus isolated stores for playback and editor tool state so a 60fps animation preview doesn't re-render the whole app. Persistence is IndexedDB with debounced autosave and a graceful in-memory fallback if it's unavailable. The WebMCP layer was built as a thin registration module wrapping that same domain layer. Two design decisions mattered most: pixel data is transmitted as palette-index + run-length encoding rather than raw pixel arrays or images, keeping a typical frame read to roughly 100–300 tokens instead of 600+; and pixel editing is split into three tiers (full-frame rewrite, targeted coordinate patches, and shape/transform operations like flood fill and line draw) so an agent picks the cheapest tool for the job instead of rewriting an entire canvas for a one-pixel fix. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is genuinely new. The flag needed for testing ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) only works on recent Chrome builds, and even the correct API surface shifted under us mid-build ( navigator.modelContext vs. document.modelContext across different docs and spec drafts). Chrome's native tool-result contract also turned out to be string-only no structured image content blocks like backend MCP supports which meant redesigning how the agent gets visual feedback, leaning on the compact RLE pixel format as the primary channel instead of images. And with a hard four-day runway from architecture decision to submission, we had to be disciplined about which tools were "genuinely useful agent capability" versus "nice to have" to hit both breadth and reliability in time. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full 36-tool surface actually works end-to-end, verified through both the Model Context Tool Inspector extension and ChatGPT's in-app browser not a demo of one tool, a real one covering asset creation, animation, pixel editing, and export. It's held up across different model sizes too, including smaller/cheaper models, which we take as a sign the tool schemas carry enough signal on their own rather than relying on a large model to compensate for ambiguity. And in testing, agents completed genuinely non-trivial multi-step tasks in a single instruction resizing a sprite and adding a held item consistently across four animation frames, or diagnosing and correcting a specific pixel-level bug in an existing sprite without us hand-holding the request. What we learned Schema clarity matters more than model size the clearest signal came from watching a smaller model succeed at multi-step tasks because the tool contracts left little room for ambiguity, not because it was a bigger model doing more inference work. We also learned the token economics of data representation are a real design constraint for agent-facing tools, not an afterthought RLE vs. raw pixel arrays was a multi-hundred-token difference per call, which adds up fast across an editing session. And architecting the domain layer for automation from day one before WebMCP was even in the picture made the actual integration almost mechanical; retrofitting agent tools onto UI-coupled logic would have been a much harder rebuild. What's next for Pixael Batch and multi-select operations so an agent can act across several frames or assets in one call instead of one-at-a-time. Undo-aware agent tools that can reason about and revert their own multi-step changes. Broader testing across WebMCP-capable surfaces as the standard matures beyond Chrome and ChatGPT's in-app browser. And of course improving the quality and performance. title: AgenticRoom
pitch: Your room. Your agent. One shared canvas.
about_excerpt: Your room. Your agent. One shared canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a room gets messy fast. Products live in one tab, measurements in another, and the budget usually ends up in a note or spreadsheet. By the time the pieces come together, the sofa may not fit or the total may no longer make sense. AgenticRoom started with a simple idea: let the person and the agent work on the same room instead of passing suggestions back and forth. What it does AgenticRoom puts a furniture catalog, an editable 3D room, budget tracking, and a shopping cart in one workspace. Start with the room you have, describe the room you want, or share an inspiration image with a compatible browser agent. The agent can inspect what is already in the room, search the catalog, place and move furniture, compare cheaper alternatives, check the layout, change the finishes, track the budget, add selected products to the cart, and save the design. Nothing happens in a hidden result. Every change appears on the same canvas and remains editable by the person. You can let the agent handle a full furnishing pass, step in to move one chair yourself, then ask it to finish the room without losing context. Why WebMCP fits A room plan is a chain of connected decisions. A sofa changes the remaining space and budget. A window limits placement. Replacing an expensive item should preserve its position while changing the total. Free-form recommendations alone are not enough. WebMCP gives the browser agent precise actions for those decisions. It can ask what fits, search within a price range, place a product in a valid zone, validate the layout, or add the selected marketplace pieces to the cart. The person makes the taste calls. The agent handles the searching, placement, and arithmetic. Both see the same room and the same result as it changes. How I built it I built AgenticRoom as a browser-only Next.js application using React, TypeScript, React Three Fiber, Three.js, and Zustand. I deliberately kept one source of truth: the human interface and the WebMCP tools call the same Zustand store actions and the same deterministic domain rules. The page registers 31 WebMCP tools through the browser's Model Context API: 11 read tools and 20 mutation tools. Those rules check furniture footprints, placement zones, doors and windows, locks, stock, prices, budgets, room resizing, saved designs, finishes, and cart behavior. If an action is invalid, it returns a structured error and leaves the room unchanged. There is no backend, account requirement, payment processing, API key, or remote runtime data. The furniture catalog and room rules are hand-authored and run entirely in the browser. Features Shared human-and-agent 3D room planning Image-inspired room direction Furniture search by category, style, color, material, price, dimensions, and stock Layout and opening-clearance checks Budget-aware furnishing and cheaper alternatives Editable room dimensions, openings, and finishes Integrated furniture catalog and shopping cart Saved room designs Privacy-conscious agent activity feed 31 structured WebMCP tools for reliable agent actions Testing The project has 135 deterministic domain tests covering placement, validation, pricing, alternatives, resizing, appearance, saved designs, and cart behavior. I also tested the deployed app in ChatGPT's in-app browser with a connected browser agent. No credentials are required. The README includes local setup instructions and reproducible WebMCP workflows. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ .
