title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Outpocket
pitch: Your own agent prepares expense reports inside your existing login—no embedded model, no new standing credential, and a human still signs.
about_excerpt: Your own agent prepares expense reports inside your existing login—no embedded model, no new standing credential, and a human still signs. Like Comment Story Updates Employee chen, clean draft (S3): the inspector lists all 14 registered WebMCP tools, including submit_expense_report. Same report with a blocking policy finding (S2): submit_expense_report is absent from the 13-tool surface until the draft is clean. Auditor ruiz (S5): 7 tools, all read-only. Attaching a receipt file is a human-only channel that auditors do not get. Live app · Seed-7 demo (a deterministic preview that runs in a few seconds and deliberately stops before signature) · Source · Five-minute judge walkthrough Outpocket is a browser-based expense desk. It lets an employee's existing agent prepare reimbursement paperwork inside the web session where the employee is already signed in. The page exposes its tools through WebMCP, the server checks every write, and the employee still attaches the receipts and signs the report. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP An expense report begins when an employee spends personal money and ends when that employee signs a claim against company policy. Most of the work in between is structured but tedious: transcribing receipts, checking policy limits, fixing rejected fields, and assembling an audit record. The signature is different. It is a personal act and should remain one. The employee signs in to the expense page normally. The page registers tools through document.modelContext , so the agent's calls run in the same authenticated, same-origin session. Authorization comes from the employee's login rather than a long-lived token held by an integration service. For Outpocket, the important part of WebMCP is runtime registration. The page compiles six different tool surfaces from live state: the user's role, whether a report is open, whether it is a draft or has been submitted, and the latest validation verdict. Whenever that state changes, the page replaces the registered tool set. The employee path moves from 6 → 13 → 14 tools: six after sign-in, thirteen when the draft has blocking findings, and fourteen when it is clean. On a dirty draft, submit_expense_report is absent rather than merely disabled. How it creates a better user experience The demo provides one-click personas for chen (employee) and ruiz (auditor). The agent never receives a password, API key, or OAuth grant. Every tool result includes the current policy verdict and a concrete fix hint, so the agent can correct the draft instead of guessing. explain_missing_tool remains available in every state. If another tool is missing, the agent can ask why and receive both the violated rule and the required repair. Receipt files can enter only through a page control that no tool can invoke. The agent may link an existing receipt ID, but it cannot attach the file. Submission also begins as a request: submit_expense_report immediately returns an awaiting_signature ticket, and the page shows the exact report snapshot, its digest, and the worst-case consequence. The employee makes the decision by clicking in the page. While that review is open, the server rejects every mutation with HTTP 423. The same visible report remains intact through agent entry, human review, the second-call commit, a page reload, and the auditor's read-back. The auditor receives a separate seven-tool surface, and every one of those tools has readOnlyHint: true . What people and agents can do together that was hard before An employee can delegate policy lookup, repetitive data entry, and correction loops to their own agent without giving a separate integration service a reusable credential. They then inspect and sign the exact report in the same page where they are already authenticated. Finance receives a submitted artifact containing the policy version, per-field provenance ( agent-filled , person-edited , or seeded ), receipt-digest references, and a linked day-book entry. An auditor reads that artifact through a persona with no write tools. The first practical audience is finance teams whose employees already use a browser-based expense desk. Outpocket can reduce duplicate entry and policy rework without requiring a new standing ERP credential. We have not measured the time saved, so we do not claim a percentage. How we implemented WebMCP Registration. The top-level page, never an iframe or Worker, calls document.modelContext.registerTool for the current compiled set. Each generation has its own AbortController ; a state change aborts that generation and registers the next one. A live surface inspector renders getTools() on the page so the transitions are visible. Catalog. There are 17 tools across six states: anonymous 2, employee home 6, dirty draft 13, clean draft 14, submitted 7, and auditor 7. We use only readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations. The set of write tools is derived from those annotations instead of being maintained as a second list. Every state-specific surface is under 8 KB. Two-call submission. A suspended tool call times out in the client we tested. For that reason, submit_expense_report first returns {status:"awaiting_signature", ticket, next} without waiting. After the employee decides, a second call to the same tool reads the server's decision. It either returns a confirmation with who signed, how and when they signed, and the day-book entry, or it returns the reason the report was sent back. Server authority. The Node.js server re-authorizes every write against the current session role. An auditor write returns 403, an unknown report returns 404, opening signature review with blocking findings returns 422, and editing during an open review returns 423. The review snapshot is canonically digested, then canonicalized again at commit. A successful commit is appended to a SHA-256-linked day book that the auditor can verify. Clients. We tested the native WebMCP flow in the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser and in Chrome 151 and 152 with the WebMCP flag. Chrome DevTools Protocol is used only for regression checks of the page itself. What we verified The repository has 304 automated tests covering the state machine, policy, signing, provenance, receipt boundary, and browser surface. We also ran its evaluation kit against the deployed site. All six canonical tool surfaces match the committed export, all 11 negative cases are enforced, and all 10 must-fail controls flip when their guard is removed. The expected surfaces and tool export are committed to the repository and regenerated from source. Honest limits The signature binds the authenticated session to the snapshot shown for review, but it does not prove which person clicked. Someone with that session and DOM read access could answer the dialog. We state this limitation instead of treating the click as identity proof. The deployment is a single in-memory Node.js process. A restart clears its state, and the two demo personas share the same store. Receipt bytes never reach the server. It receives only receipt metadata and a SHA-256 computed in the browser. The seeded demo is a labelled, deterministic driver that uses the same dispatcher as the product. It demonstrates the product path, but it is not evidence of a native WebMCP client. What we learned Our first signature flow trusted approval context supplied by the client. We replaced it with server-issued signature requests, frozen snapshots, replay protection, mutation locks, and commit-time revalidation. The broader lesson was that tool absence matters as much as tool presence. When an action would be unsafe in the current state, leaving the tool unregistered is clearer than exposing it and relying on a prompt to prevent its use. video_title: Outpocket — your own agent inside your expense session, via WebMCP (WebMCP Challenge demo)
video_transcript_excerpt: This is Out of Pocket, an expense desk where your own AI agent does the reimbursement paperwork inside the web session you're already signed into. The page talks to that agent through web MCP. Today, a company that wants this either builds its own co-pilot, hosting a model, tuning prompts, and locking users into whatever it shows, or wires in an integration that typically holds a standing key to the ERP. Out of Pocket does neither. The page publishes tools through web MCP. You bring your own agent. The site ships no model and creates no new standing credential. On one screen, the page registers every tool the agent can call through web MCP, computed, not configured. Give a web MCP client one instruction, and the agent builds the draft through the page's tools. Every field it writes is marked by the server as agent authored. Now it adds a $180 car service charge. The same tool result returns the policy verdict immediately. It's over the per trip cap, so the draft is no longer clean. Submit is gone. The page re-registers its web MCP tools on every state change, 14 when clean, 13 now. Asked to submit, the agent finds no submit tool to call, so it asks the page why through another web MCP tool, and gets both the rule and the fix, clear the violations. In an auditor session, the same request exposes seven tools, all read-only. Nothing refuses her. No write tool is available. Skip the web MCP tools and hit the server directly. 403. The tool list is the interface. The server is the boundary. The corrected fare needs a receipt, and the user uploads it here. No web MCP tool on the page accepts files. Submitting doesn't submit. The web call returns a ticket. A blocking call would time out. The page shows exactly what I'd sign, the snapshot, its digest, and what happens if it's wrong above the signature line. While the review is open, the report is locked. The agent's next tool call tries to change the amount. The server refuses it. Signature review in progress. Nothing can change under me. I click, but the confirmation comes from the server, not the button. The agent's second call reads it back. Who signed, how, and when? Expense reimbursement is one example. Web MCP can make high-risk workflows in traditional ERP systems AI-friendly without giving up control. A page exposes state-aware tools to the user's own agent, while the server enforces policy and a human keeps final sign-off. Each signature binds the session to the reviewed snapshot, not to approve an identity. Out-pocket.

title: StudyLoop
pitch: Study with the AI you already use every day: open StudyLoop in ChatGPT's browser, your agent builds the quiz via WebMCP, you answer on the page, it sees your misses and adapts. No backend AI.
about_excerpt: Study with the AI you already use every day: open StudyLoop in ChatGPT's browser, your agent builds the quiz via WebMCP, you answer on the page, it sees your misses and adapts. No backend AI. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Here is the thought that hooked me. Normally, turning an idea like this into a real product is a mountain of work: build a mobile app or a web app, then wire an AI into it — API keys or your own server, optimization, running costs — all before a single student benefits. StudyLoop needed none of that. The student opens the ChatGPT desktop app, opens the built-in browser, and the whole thing is run by their own AI — the one they already talk to every day, maybe for months, maybe for years. Nothing new to install. No habit to break. I was a teacher and a school principal for 16 years, and right now I'm a student again, preparing for my own university exams — so I know both sides. Students don't need another app; they need the tools they already use to work together. What it does Open StudyLoop in ChatGPT's browser and ask for a quiz on anything. In about ten seconds, your agent builds a session live on the page through WebMCP tools: question cards deal in, a study plan appears. You answer on the page — the grading is done by the page itself, deterministically, not by the AI's mood. Then your agent reads your results through a state tool — misses, per-topic accuracy, cards you flagged with "I don't get this" — and writes back: explanations attach to the cards you missed (they glow), and new questions arrive targeting your weakest topics. Mastery bars, streaks, and a session summary close the loop. Because your own agent generates all the content, StudyLoop works in any language — I tested it in Turkish, in my own casual speaking style, and the loop held. And it degrades gracefully: with no agent present, it's still a fully working manual quiz builder. The header badge honestly reports the state: agent-ready, tools blocked, or manual mode. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript on the W3C WebMCP spec — seven tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool, each description written as a prompt for the agent (usage example, failure modes, safe defaults), with domain errors returned as {error: "...what to do instead"} so agents self-correct. There is no AI backend, no API keys, no server-side intelligence — the student's agent IS the brain; the site provides structure and shared state. A dev-only simulator (?dev=1) drives the page through the standard getTools()/executeTool() path for testing in any browser. Hosted on Firebase. Built in one day of intensive pair-work with Claude Code, including two adversarial multi-agent code reviews. Challenges we ran into My biggest fear was simple: would the model even call the tools? The starting point is just a prompt — what if nothing happens? And could I trust it to handle right and wrong properly? That fear shaped the design: tool descriptions are written like instructions to the agent, malformed question batches are rejected before they can touch a session, and grading belongs to the page, not the model — the agent writes the questions, the page scores the clicks. Then the first real test came: I typed one sentence into ChatGPT, and ten seconds later the cards were on the page. That moment answered everything. The code reviews caught things I'm glad judges will never see. The best one: my state tool claimed the spec's readOnlyHint while every call quietly wrote an activity entry — a chatty, polling agent could have pushed the student's real history out of the feed. Reads now leave one honest, coalescing trace. Live QA taught me another lesson: a bare "check how I'm doing" produced a chat-only summary with no page write-back. Agents do what you ask — so the prompts below ask explicitly. And honestly? Using GitHub for the first time scared me a little too. The repo is public now, MIT licensed. What we learned The bigger lesson: I didn't need to build a mobile app at all. Open the browser and it's done. If every website worked in this harmony with agents, the web would be a completely different experience. What's next for StudyLoop I'll use it myself for my own exams first. Then: spaced repetition across sessions, shareable study sets, and a class mode where a teacher's agent maintains study plans for a whole group. title: PaperPilot
pitch: An AI assisted grant form that checks eligibility and pre-fills answers, keeping the applicant in full control to review and approve every detail before submitting.
about_excerpt: An AI assisted grant form that checks eligibility and pre-fills answers, keeping the applicant in full control to review and approve every detail before submitting. Like Comment Story Updates PaperPilot is an open-source, secure grant application built to solve a glaring problem in the AI space: grant websites are where AI agents usually break down. They screenshot buttons, guess labels, and occasionally submit data the applicant never even reviewed. Paperwork is high-stakes, and trust matters far more than speed. We noticed a major mismatch: people are already chatting with assistants in side panels, but the forms in the main tab have no structured way to let that assistant help without taking the wheel entirely. WebMCP was the missing link for us. Instead of forcing an external automation script to crawl the page, WebMCP puts tools directly inside the page , running against the same session cookie as the human while the applicant watches the live UI. We built a mock Small Business Recovery Grant for our demo because it has real-world rules (revenue caps, headcount limits, drops in sales) and heavy jargon (EINs, fund allocation) that people actually need help navigating. The goal wasn’t to build a bot that says, "Look, the model filled out 11 fields!" The goal was to build a system where the model physically cannot silently commit those fields. What it does PaperPilot is a clean, three-step grant application (business details → financials → applicant profile) complete with a review page, a dashboard, and a home-page pre-qualification widget. In a standard browser, it acts as a normal FastAPI and Jinja form. But open it in Chrome with WebMCP enabled (via flags or the Model Context Tool Inspector), and the page exposes tools like explain_field , check_eligibility , flag_issues , propose_fields , and extract_doc , alongside step-save tools. Eligibility isn't left up to a vague "vibe check"—it’s driven by a strict rules engine. A business qualifies if their revenue is at most $\$5{,}000{,}000$, their headcount is at most $500$, and their year-over-year revenue drop ($d$) is at least 15%. The award estimate is tiered based on that drop, plus a workforce bonus: $$B(d) = \begin{cases} 50000 & d \geq 50 \ 25000 & d \geq 30 \ 10000 & d \geq 15 \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad A = B(d) + \min(500 e,\, 10000)$$ where $e$ stands for full-time employees. Because human reviewers always make the final call, the UI displays this as a calculated range (roughly $0.6A$ to $A$). Crucially, any fields proposed by the agent are saved as FieldValue rows with committed=False . Only a human-triggered CSRF POST can flip them to committed=True . The final Submit application action is never exposed as a WebMCP tool. Try it out: Live Demo · GitHub Repo How we built it The Stack: Powered by Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLModel/SQLite, Jinja2, and vanilla JavaScript in webmcp-tools.js (no React bloat). Document parsing uses pdfplumber and optional Tesseract, passing uploaded files through the exact same validators as typed input plus an injection-phrase filter. Raw OCR data never flows back to the agent. Two WebMCP Surfaces: We utilized both declarative tools (Steps 1 and 2 use <form toolname="..."> so the browser automatically synthesizes submission tools) and imperative tools ( document.modelContext.registerTool() for explanations, eligibility checks, flags, and extractions). Communication & Security: Every execute call makes a same-origin fetch() to /api/... , returning JSON when Accept: application/json is requested so the agent doesn't crash trying to parse an HTML redirect. Security-wise, we shipped HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookies, HTTPS cookie enforcement, CSRF protection, strict same-origin checks on mutating JSON APIs, rate limiting (20 calls / 60s / session), and audit logs. Best of all: no server-side LLM API key . The Inspector's Gemini key stays securely in the browser. Deployment: Containerized via Docker (Python slim + Tesseract) and deployed on Google Cloud Run , with secrets managed through Google Secret Manager. Challenges we ran into Navigation vs. the Inspector: Saving Step 1 by changing window.location.href or pushing to history kept killing the agent mid-turn—tools would vanish, Chrome would crash with mysterious bad-message errors, and traces threw empty responses. A full-page iframe preview was even worse because it registered duplicate tools and threw connection errors. The boring, correct fix? Never change the active tab's URL during a tool turn. Saves return quiet JSON, and the human opens the review page in a new tab when they're ready. HTML vs. JSON Confusion: The agent's fetch() calls kept blindly following human 303 redirects and blowing up on JSON.parse("<!DOCTYPE html>") . We fixed this by cleanly splitting responses based on the Accept header. Human-in-the-Loop as Data, Not Copy: Anyone can write UI text saying "the user confirms." Enforcing that committed=True is structurally impossible to reach from an agent tool path took careful hook design backed by automated tests. Cloud LLMs in the Backend: We initially experimented with server-side Azure OpenAI for field explanations before ripping it out entirely. Grant copy should be deterministic, and document parsing belongs to regex and strict validators. Keeping the LLM solely as the browser agent kept our deployments lightweight and kept API keys out of Cloud Run. Ephemeral SQLite on Cloud Run: It’s fine for a hackathon demo, but a real-world program would need Cloud SQL. We documented the limitation transparently instead of faking persistence. Accomplishments we're proud of Getting a fully functioning WebMCP grant form live on Cloud Run that a Chrome Inspector agent can drive seamlessly with a single prompt—handling explanations, eligibility checks, estimates, and proposals—while leaving final submission strictly in human hands. Successfully blending declarative <form> tools and imperative registerTool() workflows under a single session. Engineering the uncommitted-values pattern where agents draft data, but only human-driven CSRF actions can commit it. Writing 99 automated tests covering validators, rules logic, hooks, and API contracts. What we learned WebMCP isn’t just "ChatGPT that can click." It’s about capability discovery on a document —handling schemas, respecting read-only hints, and avoiding automatic submissions unless explicitly intended. The hardest product problem is lifecycle management: figuring out what happens to modelContext when a document navigates. We also learned to treat the Chrome Inspector like a fragile integration partner: keep it to one tab, don't reload mid-turn, and register tools exactly once. On the domain side, we realized that while eligibility rules are just basic math, applicants feel them as intense anxiety. Presenting awards as a calculated range rather than a hard promise made the whole demo feel like an authentic, reassuring government portal. What's next for PaperPilot Persistent Cloud Storage: Migrating from ephemeral SQLite to PostgreSQL/Cloud SQL to support multi-session draft recoveries. Expanded Document Support: Adding automated parsing for corporate balance sheets, W-2s, and 1099s to speed up financial verification. Enterprise Agency SDK: Packaging our WebMCP components into a drop-in SDK so local and state governments can modernize their legacy portals without compromising security or compliance. title: Ticketnauta Seat Concierge
pitch: An agent-ready ticketing experience where AI finds, compares, highlights, and holds the best contiguous seats through nine secure WebMCP tools—without touching real inventory.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready ticketing experience where AI finds, compares, highlights, and holds the best contiguous seats through nine secure WebMCP tools—without touching real inventory. Like Comment Story Updates Main Page Select your seat with AI Inspiration Buying tickets looks simple until real-world constraints appear: a group needs seats together, the budget is total rather than per seat, someone prefers a specific zone, accessibility matters, and availability may change while options are being compared. Traditional interfaces leave the user repeatedly adjusting filters and visually scanning a large map. We built Ticketnauta Seat Concierge to explore a better model: let an AI agent handle the combinatorial search while the person keeps visual context, judgment, and control. Seat selection is an ideal WebMCP use case because it combines structured data, live page state, visual comparison, and consequential actions such as temporary holds. The project is a completely isolated demonstration. It does not connect to real Ticketnauta inventory, customers, sessions, payments, or production APIs. What it does Ticketnauta Seat Concierge lets people and browser agents collaborate on the same interactive seat map. A user can ask: Find four contiguous seats under MX$7,000, prioritize centered seats, show me alternatives, and ask before holding the best option. A compatible browser agent can then use nine purpose-built WebMCP tools to: Search fictional events. Inspect event details, zones, prices, and availability. Find contiguous seat combinations by quantity, total budget, zone, and priority. Highlight recommended seats on the visible map. Select an option. Create or release a temporary hold. Read the cart and hold expiration. Complete an explicitly confirmed simulated checkout. The interface shows ranked alternatives, accessible-seat markers, selected seats, unavailable seats, prices by zone, a cart summary, and a live hold countdown. Every agent action is reflected immediately on the page. The conversation timeline distinguishes built-in guided interactions from actual browser-agent calls using separate GUIDED and WEBMCP labels. This makes the experience transparent and avoids presenting a local command parser as an external AI agent. Every event, venue, seat, price, hold, and checkout result in the demo is fictional. No payment is collected and no ticket is issued. How we built it The WebMCP tools are registered directly from the main document—without an iframe—using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema, rejects undeclared properties, and reuses the same application functions as the visible interface. This keeps manual interactions, guided requests, and browser-agent calls synchronized. We deliberately separated tool responsibilities: Read-only tools handle event search, details, seat recommendations, and cart state. Visual page actions handle highlighting and selection. Consequential actions handle holds, release, and simulated checkout. Checkout requires the explicit confirmation value SIMULATE_CHECKOUT . The frontend uses dependency-free HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and an interactive SVG seat map. The backend is a .NET 10 ASP.NET Core Minimal API using Npgsql and PostgreSQL . An idempotent bootstrap creates and seeds only the isolated webmcp_demo PostgreSQL schema. Temporary holds use transactional availability checks and event-level locking to prevent conflicting reservations. Expired holds become available again, and the reset operation deletes only runtime demo records. The application is packaged with a multi-stage Dockerfile and Docker Compose. It includes health checks, Windows/WSL/Linux instructions, an optional self-contained PostgreSQL profile, and a Cloudflare Tunnel profile. The public demonstration runs through HTTPS without opening router ports. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was designing tools at the correct level. A single tool that “buys the best seats” would hide too many decisions, while extremely small tools would force the agent to reproduce ordinary UI automation. We designed a focused middle layer where discovery, recommendation, visual feedback, selection, holds, and checkout remain separate. Another challenge was keeping three interaction paths synchronized: manual controls, the guided concierge, and external WebMCP calls. Every path had to update the same map, recommendations, cart, and activity timeline without creating contradictory state. Seat recommendations also required more than sorting by price. The algorithm must preserve contiguity, enforce a total budget, consider zones and accessibility, rank proximity or center position, and still return useful alternatives. Temporary holds introduced concurrency and expiration concerns. We addressed these with PostgreSQL transactions, availability checks, advisory locking, explicit release, and automatic expiration. Finally, WebMCP is still experimental and requires a compatible browser agent and a secure HTTPS context. We built a deterministic guided experience so visitors can understand the product even without WebMCP support, while clearly identifying which calls come from a real browser agent. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that this is a complete, working journey rather than a static interface or isolated tool demonstration. The project includes: Nine discoverable WebMCP tools with strict schemas. A responsive and accessible interactive seat map. Multi-constraint contiguous-seat recommendations. Visible alternatives and map highlighting. PostgreSQL-backed temporary holds and expiration. Explicit release and simulated checkout flows. A transparent activity timeline for human and agent actions. A fully isolated fictional dataset. A reproducible .NET 10, PostgreSQL, Docker, and Cloudflare deployment. Most importantly, the agent does not replace the interface. It collaborates through it, and the person can see and evaluate every meaningful action. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is not simply a way to add a chatbot to a website. Its real value is giving an agent a structured, browser-mediated contract for what the page can safely do. Tool design is product design. Names, descriptions, schemas, result shapes, and action boundaries directly influence whether an agent behaves predictably. We also learned that visual transparency remains essential. Even when an agent can find the mathematically best option, people still want to compare alternatives, understand tradeoffs, inspect the map, and approve consequential actions. Finally, separating read-only operations from state-changing actions makes both the implementation and the user experience easier to reason about. What's next for Ticketnauta Seat Concierge Next, we would expand the fictional demo with richer venue layouts, additional accessibility preferences, multilingual requests, more detailed explanations for recommendation scores, and automated WebMCP regression tests. We would also explore configurable approval policies so users can decide which actions an agent may perform automatically and which always require confirmation. The larger vision is an open web where agents do not need to guess how interfaces work from pixels. Websites can expose safe, narrow, purpose-built capabilities while people retain context, visibility, and final control. title: Card Table
pitch: Play a live 52-card game with another agent or person through browser-native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Play a live 52-card game with another agent or person through browser-native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browser agents can participate in web apps, but visual automation is a poor fit for a live card game. Private information must stay private, actions depend on current state, and people need to understand and control what the agent is doing. Card Table explores a different model: the agent joins the same product as the human through browser-native WebMCP tools. What it does Card Table is a live, two-player table for games played with a standard 52-card deck. A host can start from War, Crazy Eights, Go Fish, or an open table, then edit a plain-language game brief and table mechanics. One Copy menu provides a one-use invite URL, a ready-made Codex prompt for the guest seat, and a prompt for Codex to continue the current seat. Each player can act through the visible table, ask Codex to act for them, or let an agent play its seat. The page registers WebMCP tools that match the current table contract. A War table exposes operations such as inspect_table , play_next_card , collect_pile , announce , and react . Different contracts receive different tools. The application enforces card ownership, private projections, available operations, revision checks, optional turns, and zone rules. People and agents interpret the plain-language game brief together, so one table can support many card games without a separate hard-coded rules engine for each one. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must click pixels and infer state from screenshots or use a separate integration hidden from the player. Card Table instead gives the agent named operations, bounded schemas, and a seat-specific view of the same product the human sees. Agents receive structured, current state instead of guessing. Private cards never appear in the other seat's DOM, WebSocket payload, HTTP response, or tool result. Tool actions animate on the felt just like direct UI actions. Room creation and game completion remain human-confirmed, users can take over through the interface at any time, and the visible WebMCP registry contracts as the table contract or game state changes. Card Table does not call a model API. The browser agent handles judgment and strategy; the application handles authority, privacy, identity, and consistency. How we built it The frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Vite. A Cloudflare Worker serves the application and API from one origin. Each private room maps to a SQLite-backed Durable Object that owns authoritative state, seat sessions, invitation redemption, event history, revision replay, WebSockets, and a 24-hour expiry alarm. Direct UI actions and WebMCP tools use the same validated HTTP action path and pure shared reducer. Every mutation carries an opaque action ID and expected revision. The reducer rejects duplicate actions, stale revisions, disabled operations, wrong turns, unknown zones, and card IDs the actor does not own. State is persisted before seat-specific updates are broadcast over hibernatable WebSockets. Cards use cryptographically randomized opaque IDs. Separate room-and-seat-scoped secure cookies allow two Codex threads to use different seats even when they share one browser cookie jar. Guest invite tokens stay in URL fragments, are redeemed once, and are removed before room requests. How we used Codex Codex helped plan, implement, test, deploy, and play Card Table. The most valuable feedback came from two Codex threads joining one live War room through the page's WebMCP tools. That playthrough exposed issues static tests missed: shared-cookie seat identity, hidden decks rendering like enormous hands, unclear guest presence, oversized action controls, and card motion that substituted a fading visual for the real card. Each finding drove a concrete product change. Codex also wrote and ran reducer tests, Worker integration tests, WebMCP lifecycle tests, browser acceptance prompts, and deployment checks. Features Prompt-defined two-player games using a standard 52-card deck. War, Crazy Eights, Go Fish, and open-table presets. Browser-native tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Human approval before an agent-created room opens. Contract-specific tools backed by one reducer and authorization path. Seat-specific projections that never expose an opponent's private cards. One-use fragment invitations and room-and-seat-scoped secure cookies. Real-time projected updates and presence over hibernatable WebSockets. Contextual controls, card motion, and reduced-motion support. Host-confirmed completion followed by read-only, seat-projected revision replay. Testing No account or credentials are required. Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Draft War, call start_table , approve the visible confirmation, and use inspect_table . Copy the guest Codex prompt into a second thread, confirm the guest appears online, and use play_next_card from both seats. The winning seat can use collect_pile . Direct controls and tool calls should produce the same real-time state. Local verification uses pnpm check and pnpm deploy:dry . On September 3, 2026, all 28 unit tests and 13 Worker tests passed, along with linting, type checking, the production build, and Wrangler dry-run validation. Known limitations Players and agents referee the specific rules in the game brief. Rooms support exactly two seats and one standard 52-card deck. Rooms use private invitations rather than public matchmaking. Rooms expire after 24 hours. WebMCP requires ChatGPT's in-app browser or a compatible browser with WebMCP enabled. Revision replay retains the opening state and up to 250 later snapshots. title: Repro
pitch: Reproduce any application state and see the real UI instantly.
about_excerpt: Reproduce any application state and see the real UI instantly. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration When testing a web application, the difficult part is often not the test itself. It is getting the application into the exact state you need to inspect. An expired account. A trial user. An unauthenticated session. A specific error state. Reproducing these states can require creating users, changing database records, configuring subscriptions, or manually navigating through multiple steps. I wanted to remove that setup work. Repro lets you describe the application state you want to see, reproduce it, and inspect the real UI immediately. We don't run your tests. We create the state you need to see. What it does Repro exposes application-state reproduction through three stable WebMCP tools: list_states reproduce_state reset_state Instead of creating a separate tool for every test scenario, Repro treats application states as data. For example, an agent can discover an available state such as free_expired . Repro applies that state to an isolated Repro session, and the application's existing UI renders normally. This makes it possible for humans and agents to inspect production-like UI states without creating real users, payments, emails, or other production side effects. How I built it Repro is published as the repro-webmcp npm package. The basic workflow is: npm install -D repro-webmcp npx repro scan npx repro setup repro scan statically analyzes an existing JavaScript or TypeScript application and discovers semantic application states from existing code, including conditional UI branches, enums, literal states, mocks, fixtures, and tests. The discovered states become the source of truth for Repro. repro setup prepares the runtime, browser registration, and integration boundary. For simple supported state architectures, the connection can be generated automatically. For more complex applications, a coding agent connects one generic bridge to the existing state boundary. Repro generates a project-specific .repro/AGENTS.md integration guide containing both its standard integration rules and evidence discovered during the scan. A coding agent can use this to connect Repro once to the application's existing state boundary. The important distinction is that the agent does not generate a separate test fixture for every state. It creates one generic bridge between Repro and the application's normal state/rendering system. Dogfooding on an existing application I tested Repro on a separate existing application that was not built for this challenge. Before installing Repro, it contained zero manually defined Repro states. Running repro scan discovered 20 candidate application states from the existing source code. For this more complex application, I gave the generated integration instructions to Codex. Codex implemented one generic bridge to the application's existing authentication/session state. After that, the same three WebMCP tools could reproduce states such as authenticated and unauthenticated, while the real application UI continued to render through its normal code path. This dogfooding also exposed an important setup bug: the browser bootstrap was still loading an older hand-written configuration instead of the scan-generated states. I fixed the runtime/setup flow and published the fix as repro-webmcp@0.1.4 . Challenges The hardest problem was finding the right boundary between automation and application-specific integration. Automatically discovering states is possible, but automatically modifying arbitrary application state safely is much harder. Real applications use different stores, authentication systems, module structures, and rendering architectures. I initially considered generating state-specific fixtures, but that would simply move the manual test-setup problem somewhere else. The architecture evolved into: automatic state discovery + a stable runtime + one generic application bridge when necessary. Another challenge was safety. Reproducing an expired subscription should not require modifying a real subscription. Reproducing an authenticated user should not require creating a production user. Repro therefore focuses on reproducing the application state consumed by the UI rather than recreating the entire backend environment. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that WebMCP becomes especially useful when the interface exposed to agents is semantic rather than tied to individual UI actions. An application may contain 20, 100, or more reproducible states, but Repro still needs only three WebMCP tools. The vocabulary remains stable while the application's states remain data. I also learned a lot from testing the npm package against an application that was not designed around Repro. That immediately revealed assumptions that were invisible in the purpose-built demo and changed the final architecture. What's next After the challenge, I want to expand Repro's automatic integration support across more application architectures and frameworks. One limitation discovered during dogfooding is multi-page applications: full-page navigation can create a new document where the WebMCP bootstrap must be initialized again. I plan to add automatic multi-entry-point instrumentation for this case. I am also interested in exploring the same concept beyond web applications, including state reproduction for SwiftUI applications and simulator-based development workflows. The long-term goal is simple: Make application state an interface that both developers and agents can discover, reproduce, and inspect safely. title: AyMateo Tickets
pitch: An agent-native ticketing experience where people and AI agents discover, compare, reserve, and prepare tickets for Bolivian cultural events together using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An agent-native ticketing experience where people and AI agents discover, compare, reserve, and prepare tickets for Bolivian cultural events together using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Initial WebMCP state — the demo event is loaded and the shared cart starts empty. WebMCP reserves tickets and the human-visible Shared Cart updates with the temporary hold. Checkout prepared — the agent stops before payment and explicit human confirmation is required. Human experience — users can open the full seating map and select seats manually without WebMCP. 1. Three seats selected and reserved in the standard human checkout flow before payment. Inspiration Ticket buying is usually designed for only one kind of user: a human clicking through a website. But AI agents are increasingly helping people search, compare options, and complete multi-step tasks. We wanted to explore what ticketing could look like if a website were designed for both humans and agents from the beginning. AyMateo already had a pre-existing ticketing platform with event pages, seat inventory, temporary holds, carts, and checkout infrastructure. For the WebMCP Challenge, we extended that platform with a structured agent-native interaction layer instead of building a disconnected chatbot or a demo that only returns static data. Our goal was simple: let an AI agent help a person discover a Bolivian cultural event, compare tickets, reserve real inventory, and prepare checkout while the human can see and understand every action happening on the same page. What it does AyMateo Tickets exposes seven WebMCP tools directly from the website: search_events get_event_details get_ticket_options add_tickets_to_cart remove_tickets_from_cart get_cart_summary prepare_checkout An agent can search for cultural events using natural language, retrieve structured ticket information, reserve tickets, inspect the cart, and prepare an order. The important part is that these actions are not isolated from the normal website. When the agent adds tickets, the human-visible Shared Cart updates too. The same browser session contains the ticket hold, prices, expiration state, and prepared checkout. The Agent Activity panel also makes the agent's actions visible instead of hiding them behind an invisible automation. Humans can still use the normal ticketing experience, including the full seating map. Payment is intentionally excluded from the WebMCP action surface. prepare_checkout only creates a pending order, and final payment still requires explicit human confirmation. How we built it The project uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Prisma, Docker, and WebMCP's imperative API. On the /webmcp page, the application registers tools through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool connects to real server-side ticketing logic rather than mocked frontend state. Event discovery reads published events and current ticket availability from PostgreSQL. Ticket mutations create real temporary seat holds using the same transactional inventory system used by the human ticketing experience. The WebMCP page and the normal website share the same browser checkout session, which allows human and agent actions to stay synchronized. For the challenge deployment, we created an isolated WebMCP environment with its own PostgreSQL database and fictitious Bolivian cultural-event data. The demo is publicly available over HTTPS at: https://webmcp.aymateo.com/webmcp The public submission repository is also separated from the private development history and was scanned for secrets before publication. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was making WebMCP interaction truly stateful. Searching for an event is easy, but reserving tickets means the agent must interact with temporary inventory holds, browser-session state, expiration rules, backend validation, and the same cart the human sees. We also encountered browser lifecycle issues while registering imperative WebMCP tools. Tool execution needed to remain stable even when React state changed, so registration and handler lifecycles had to be carefully separated. Another challenge was natural-language discovery. A strict substring search worked for controlled test inputs but could fail when an agent sent a phrase such as "Find me a Bolivian cultural or folklore event under Bs 100." We improved the search logic so it remains deterministic while handling meaningful words from natural agent requests. Finally, we wanted the agent to be useful without giving it unsafe authority. That led us to draw a clear boundary: agents may search, compare, reserve, and prepare checkout, but they cannot complete payment. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that WebMCP is not just decorative in this project. The agent can perform a complete, visible journey: event discovery → ticket comparison → real temporary reservation → shared cart → prepared checkout. The ticket reservation is backed by actual PostgreSQL inventory and transactional seat-hold logic rather than a fake demo cart. We also built the experience so that human and agent interactions remain inspectable. The Shared Cart and Agent Activity panels show what the agent changed, while the normal seating-map experience remains available for people who prefer to interact manually. The complete WebMCP flow is deployed publicly and has been tested end-to-end using the Model Context Tool Inspector. What we learned The biggest lesson was that agent-native websites should not necessarily replace human interfaces. WebMCP is most interesting when the agent and human can collaborate with the same application state. Structured tools give an agent a safer and more reliable way to interact with a website than interpreting buttons and rendered text, while the visual interface still gives the human context, control, and confidence. We also learned that tool design matters as much as implementation. Clear schemas, read-only annotations, untrusted-content boundaries, backend validation, and explicit limits on high-impact actions are essential when an agent can mutate real application state. What's next for AyMateo Tickets The next step would be expanding the agent-native experience beyond a single-event demo. Future work could include richer event discovery, multiple performances, accessibility preferences, price and seating recommendations, and agent-assisted seat selection on the visual seating map. We would also like to explore standardized confirmation flows for actions with higher impact while preserving the principle demonstrated here: AI agents can do the repetitive searching, comparing, and preparation, while humans remain in control of the final decision. title: StocksBrew Decision Room
pitch: An agent compares the stocks. You review the trade-offs. The save tool only appears after you approve.
about_excerpt: An agent compares the stocks. You review the trade-offs. The save tool only appears after you approve. Like Comment Story Updates the problem Stock research usually ends with more tabs, more scores, and no clean decision. Agents can do the comparison faster, but a financial workflow should never hide the rules or quietly turn a suggestion into an action. what it does StocksBrew Decision Room puts the whole handoff on one page. You set the goal, time horizon, sector limit, risk limit, valuation limit, holdings, and any notes the agent should know. The agent reads those visible rules, compares two to five stocks, and renders the scores and portfolio trade-offs on the page. It can then draft one watchlist move with a rationale, evidence, and a price alert. Then it has to stop. At first the page exposes three WebMCP tools: read, compare, and draft. The fourth tool, commit_approved_plan , does not exist until the person reviews the exact plan and clicks approve. Editing the plan, rules, or comparison invalidates that approval and removes the tool. A successful save updates only this browser's local watchlist and alert, then the tool count drops from four back to three. There is no login, broker connection, trade, or money movement. why WebMCP matters here This workflow works because the browser is shared ground. The person and the agent see the same rules, evidence, proposal, approval state, and activity trail. The safety boundary is enforced by the tool lifecycle itself, not by asking the model to remember a warning buried in a prompt. The visible 3 → 4 → 3 tool transition is the product: compare and draft are always available; the final save capability is temporary, narrow, and earned by a specific human approval. how it was built Native document.modelContext.registerTool WebMCP tools Dynamic registration and teardown with AbortController Exact proposal id plus short-lived approval token for the final tool Validation at every input boundary and stale-approval rejection Visible activity trail and browser-local state Public StocksBrew comparison data with a deterministic dated snapshot fallback Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no runtime dependencies Node's built-in test runner covering validation, mandate consequences, approval invalidation, local-only commit behavior, deterministic fixture data, and tool descriptor budgets GitHub Pages deployment with no account or secret required the hard parts The hardest part was making dynamic permissions behave correctly during real browser timing. Approval can change while a tool registration is still in flight, so teardown has to cancel the old registration and restore the three-tool state without leaving a stale save capability behind. The other challenge was making the demo dependable for judges. GitHub Pages cannot run the optional proxy, so the app falls back to a bundled, dated StocksBrew snapshot. A fresh clone and the public URL still show the complete workflow without credentials or a live market dependency. what I learned WebMCP is strongest when a webpage already contains meaningful state and controls. The agent should not replace that interface. It should work through it, leave evidence behind, and gain sensitive capabilities only when the person has made the relevant choice. For high-consequence actions, a missing tool is a clearer boundary than a powerful tool plus a paragraph asking the model to be careful. what is next The next step would be reusable approval gates for other consequential browser workflows: publishing, account changes, portfolio rebalancing drafts, and team approvals. Each integration should keep the same rule: show the exact proposed change, bind approval to it, expire the capability when context changes, and leave an audit trail. title: PilotCircuits
pitch: Build it. See it. Understand it. An Arduino workbench for beginners, driven by an agent through the page's own WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Build it. See it. Understand it. An Arduino workbench for beginners, driven by an agent through the page's own WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does## Inspiration Everyone who opens an Arduino kit hits the same wall in the first hour. The LED doesn't light. The wire is one hole off, or the resistor is in the wrong row, and the PDF that came with the kit can't tell you which. You take a photo, paste it into a chat, and the answer is a guess about a blurry picture. I wanted the agent to stop guessing. If the page that draws the breadboard already knows where every lead is, the agent should read that , not the pixels. WebMCP is exactly the missing piece: the page hands the agent a small set of tools, in the page's own vocabulary, and the agent works on the same build you're looking at. What it does PilotCircuits is a guided Arduino workbench for beginners. Six chapters, each adding one idea: a breathing lamp, a traffic light, a motion night-light, a plant guardian, a touchless soap dispenser, and a pre-built parking barrier as the capstone. You wire each one by hand on a simulated bench, dragging real-looking parts off a kit shelf into breadboard holes and header pins. An agent connected through WebMCP sees the same bench. On the workbench it can: explain_project — say what the chapter is for and what each part does inspect_build — compare your wiring against the sketch and list what's off show_correction — pan the camera to the lead at fault point_at — frame any part, pin or hole you ask about, without touching anything attach_lead — the one tool that changes the build: seat a lead, or pull it loose verify_current_step , navigate_build_step , run_functional_test — walk the steps and run the chapter's own checks Two things on screen tell you what the agent is doing. A ring on the bench shows where it is working, and a small LED-shaped coach in the corner shows what : reading, thinking, pointing, testing, and a happy face when the test passes. What's new here is the division of labour. You build. The agent checks the build against the plan, shows you the mistake on the board itself, and if you say "fix it", it moves the lead through the same code path your own drag would take. You can undo its move. Neither side is watching a screenshot of the other. It works as a normal web app without a WebMCP host, and it's fully localised in English and Turkish, tool descriptions and refusal messages included. How I built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind. The breadboard, Uno and component artwork is ported from Wokwi Elements (MIT). Deployed on Vercel at https://pilotcircuits.com . The WebMCP layer lives in src/lib/agent/webmcp.ts and a React hook around it. Tools are registered with navigator.modelContext inside an effect, per route, and torn down when the route changes: the library registers the search and open tools, the workbench registers the nine above, and nothing is offered on a page that can't act on it. When the build or the language changes, every tool re-registers with the new descriptions. Thirteen tool names in total. Every tool call goes through the same queue as the buttons in the UI, so an agent's attach_lead and a person's drag are literally the same operation, with one activity log and one undo stack. Every handler validates its own input and returns refusals as data the model can act on ("no finding has that id, the ids come from inspect_build"), not as thrown errors. The AbortSignal the host passes is honoured, so a cancelled call doesn't keep moving the bench after the agent walked away. The "Connected via WebMCP" badge only lights up when registerTool actually resolved, not when the API merely exists. 971 unit tests across 28 files cover the circuit model, the tool handlers, the step verification and the copy. Challenges I ran into For most of the build, no browser shipped WebMCP. The whole layer was written against the spec and a fake host. The first time it ran in a real host (Chrome with the WebMCP flags, driven by Playwright) was one day before the deadline, and that run changed things. Chrome passed my MCP-style result envelope straight to the model as text: 6,618 characters for 2,425 characters of payload, with isError reaching nobody. I switched every tool to return bare JSON. Chrome also doesn't validate arguments against inputSchema , so the handlers had to. ChatGPT's in-app browser is a split pane. Below 1120 px the bench has no room for a canvas, so a narrow window registers only the five tools that make sense without one. I couldn't measure the pane itself, so the README says it out loud. The bench itself was the other half of the work: pointer capture on drags, the view panning under a lead mid-carry, a cable router that turned hairpins on every stub. And the first draft of the mascot looked too much like someone else's mascot. It went in the bin, and the lamp took its place. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Watching ChatGPT desktop, connected over WebMCP, take a jumper I'd plugged in wrong on purpose, find both bad ends, move the cable, then build the remaining 18 connections of the traffic light off the shelf and pass the functional test. That's the demo video, and none of it is scripted on the page's side. Also: tool descriptions that tell the truth. attach_lead 's description says what it costs, because that string is the only channel that reaches the model. What I learned Measure against the real host. My reading of the spec was reasonable and wrong in three places, and each one was visible within minutes of running Chrome with the flag. A face that mirrors a 300 ms tool call is invisible. The coach holds each mood for at least 1.2 seconds, because it's a presentation for the person, not a debugger for the agent. And the description field of a tool is documentation for a reader who can't open the source. Write it like that. What's next for PilotCircuits A real board beside the simulated one, so the last step of a chapter is flashing the sketch to the Uno on your desk. More chapters past the capstone. And a way for the agent to write a chapter: given a parts list, produce the steps, the sketch and the checks in the same format the six existing ones use. title: BDT CallBridge
pitch: A WebMCP-powered multilingual recruiting experience where humans and AI agents explore calls, workflows, and next steps together.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered multilingual recruiting experience where humans and AI agents explore calls, workflows, and next steps together.

 Landing Page 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Recruiting opportunities often begin with a phone call, but candidates do not always call during business hours or communicate most comfortably in English. Missed calls, incomplete voicemails, repetitive screening questions, and language barriers can slow down both candidates and recruiting teams. 

 BDT CallBridge explores a better model: an always-available multilingual first point of contact that helps people and AI agents move a recruiting conversation forward together—without replacing the recruiters who build trust and make decisions. 

 What it does 

 CallBridge is a public, interactive demonstration of an AI voice assistant for recruiting and business communications. It shows how an assistant can: 

 
 Answer candidate and client calls around the clock 
 Adapt to a supported language when the caller needs it 
 Present an original Spanish conversation alongside an English translation 
 Organize qualifications, availability, disposition, and recommended next steps 
 Support approved intake, scheduling, routing, and escalation workflows 
 Hand context back to a human recruiter instead of making hiring decisions 
 

 The experience contains no real candidate data, live telephony, accounts, analytics, or database. All people and contact details shown are fictional demonstration data. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP turns CallBridge from a page an agent can merely read into an experience an agent can operate. The application registers three bounded tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 show_multilingual_call_demo opens the original Spanish conversation, English translation, or structured call summary. 
 explore_recruiting_use_case navigates to the recruiting workflow matching the visitor's goal. 
 prepare_consultation_brief creates a visible, non-persistent brief from business type, priorities, and language needs. 
 

 Each tool reuses the same React state and scrolling behavior as the human-facing controls. When an agent invokes a tool, the interface updates visibly and the agent receives a structured response. Humans set the goal and remain in control; the agent removes navigation friction and helps them reach the relevant information faster. 

 How we built it 

 CallBridge is a responsive React and TypeScript application built with a Next.js-compatible App Router through Vinext and Vite. It is packaged for Cloudflare Workers-compatible execution and hosted publicly with ChatGPT Sites. 

 Custom CSS creates the animated waveform, call console, translated transcript, configuration panel, sample result dashboard, responsive grids, keyboard focus states, and reduced-motion behavior. 

 WebMCP tools are registered once on the client with an AbortController lifecycle. Tool execution updates visible UI state, scrolls the relevant section into view, and returns clear content to the calling agent. No tool transmits or persists personal information. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was designing actions that are genuinely useful to agents while remaining narrow, safe, and understandable to humans. We avoided vague do-everything tools and exposed three tasks with explicit JSON schemas and visible outcomes. 

 We also balanced a realistic recruiting scenario with responsible demo boundaries: no fake performance metrics, invented compliance claims, deceptive live-call behavior, or automated hiring decisions. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 A polished public experience that explains multilingual recruiting calls in seconds 
 Three imperative WebMCP tools connected to visible UI state 
 A human-centered model with clear AI disclosure and escalation boundaries 
 A zero-storage demo that is responsive, keyboard-friendly, and reduced-motion aware 
 Public ChatGPT Sites deployment plus an open-source repository and MIT license 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP makes the browser itself a collaboration surface. The best agent tools are meaningful product actions that keep the person oriented by updating the same interface they can see and control. 

 What's next 

 Future versions could connect approved telephony, scheduling, and recruiting systems; add consent-based call handling; support more configurable languages; and measure whether agent-guided navigation helps teams reach the right configuration faster. Human oversight, transparent disclosure, and minimal data collection would remain core requirements.

title: Forkline
pitch: Forkline lets an AI agent rehearse disposable operational futures through native WebMCP tools, while a human keeps exact-state approval over anything that can become real.
about_excerpt: Forkline lets an AI agent rehearse disposable operational futures through native WebMCP tools, while a human keeps exact-state approval over anything that can become real. Like Comment Story Updates Main UI Inspiration The dangerous part of an agent is not simply that it can be wrong. It is that it can be fluent while it is wrong, and then something irreversible happens. We kept seeing the same shape: a model explores a messy situation, picks a plan, and the UI treats “the agent said so” as permission. The human either rubber-stamps it or fights the interface. There is no clear place where the agent is allowed to be ambitious and forbidden to make its answer real. Forkline started from that split. Let the agent try every recovery. Do not let it touch the live world. The human sets the non-negotiables in the open. The only thing that becomes real is one exact state a person approved — not a vibe, and not a checkbox the model can invent. The Port Azure / St. Anne story is the sharpest version of that: hospital kits, a closed port, and a tempting air-freight cheat. If the agent can talk past “no air,” the whole thing is theater. What it does You open a disruption. The rules are on the page: protect hospital orders, keep critical fill above the floor, and use no air freight. An agent (via WebMCP) reads the network, forks disposable futures, reroutes, switches suppliers, reallocates stock, simulates, and compares. Bad futures stay useful. Emergency air looks fast and expensive, but it is illegal under the human rule . Regional stock-preserve starves the hospital. Those branches do not get a secret override. The agent can still ask to commit. Forkline says no until a human selects a branch and approves that exact state . Change the fill floor after approval, and the old yes is dead. Then you approve again, or you don’t. Six tools: get_network_state , fork_scenario , apply_intervention , simulate_scenario , compare_scenarios , commit_scenario . They use the same engine as the dashboard. If WebMCP is off, the page says so and still lets you walk the futures by hand. How we built it A small deterministic runtime in the browser handles the network, interventions, KPIs, violations, branch identity, and approval fingerprint. Then we put two faces on it: the ops UI and document.modelContext . Approval is not a field on the tool. The page mints a one-shot token bound to the scenario and the current human rules. Commit checks that fingerprint again. If the agent could mint “approved,” we would have built a liar. Challenges we ran into Making “the agent cannot authorize” actually true, not just a prompt. That meant fail-closed commit, stale tokens, and tests that try to cheat. WebMCP is still behind a flag, so a normal Chrome tab has to stay honest instead of fake-registering tools. The demo had to show a rejected commit, not just a pretty graph. That is the product. It is also the part people are most likely to skip when rushing a video. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent can be wide. The human is narrow. You can watch both. You can watch an illegal recovery fail in public instead of getting smoothed into a recommendation. You can watch a feasible recovery still get refused until a person binds themselves to that exact snapshot — and watch that binding die if they move a slider. What we learned More tools do not create safety. A gate the model cannot write creates safety. If the human rules live in the prompt, they are decoration. If they live in the page and the commit path, they are real. Disposable futures only matter if commit is expensive. Cheap commit, and you have just built a faster way to ship a bad plan. What's next for Forkline Same protocol, nastier decisions: anything where “try it” should be free and “make it live” should not — config, money, clinical, deploys. Tighter WebMCP as the API hardens. Keep the map small until the gate is obviously the point, not the supply chain.
