title: Aeroficiency
pitch: A web-based workspace for exploring preliminary wing designs, aerodynamic loads, structural response, and efficiency with AI agents.
about_excerpt: A web-based workspace for exploring preliminary wing designs, aerodynamic loads, structural response, and efficiency with AI agents. Like 1 Comment Story Updates First Look Aero Loads - Result 2D Section - Result Efficiency - Result Structure - Result Inspiration It all started a few months ago, during my first year aeronautics project at my university. I was working on a two-bladed HAWT (Horizontal Axis Wind Turbine) designed to produce around 100W and I was in charge of designing the wind turbine blade. The process required testing many different combinations of aerofoils in the blade, approximately 3 million different candidates to find different values, such as pressure coefficient, drag coefficient and find a candidate that maximizes lift while minimizing drag as we want to achieve the highest L/D (Lift to Drag Ratio) possible. Evaluating every combination in detail was simply impractical. But I quickly realised just how computationally heavy the process was. It was really time consuming to run full aerodynamic analysis on all three million candidates, and it was simply not feasible with the computing resources, especially within the limited time I had to complete the project. I needed to figure out a faster way to filter out unsuitable candidates before committing time and computational power to more detailed aerodynamic analysis. This challenge ultimately led me to create Aeroficiency, a tool to quickly narrow down a large number of aerofoil candidates and identify the ones that best suits the user's aerodynamic requirements. What it does Aeroficiency is a browser-based aerofoil design and analysis workspace that allows users to create multiple aerofoil candidates, visualise their geometry, configure them, and run a solver to evaluate and compare aerodynamic and structural performance. Users can explore a 2D section view to visualise streamlines and pressure-coefficient distributions around individual aerofoil sections, while the solver estimates aerodynamic quantities such as lift and drag. Aeroficiency also provides structural results such as wing-tip deflection and yield margin, helping users know whether a design remains structurally suitable. Aeroficiency is not intended to replace high-fidelity CFD. Instead, it provides a fast and approximate way to evaluate the aerodynamic and structural performance of many wing and blade candidates, compare the results side by side, and identify the most promising designs before committing to more computationally expensive analysis. By reducing the number of candidates that require high-fidelity analysis, Aeroficiency can reduce both time and computational cost, making early-stage wing and blade design more accessible to individuals, students, and small teams working with limited budgets. Why WebMCP fits my use case Creating a new wing candidate, changing its geometry, running a new analysis, checking aerodynamic and structural results, and comparing it against existing candidates normally involves many separate steps. With WebMCP, the user can simply describe the design goal and constraints to an AI agent, and the agent can use Aeroficiency’s WebMCP tools to carry out those steps directly inside the application. The user don't manually have to create candidates, change individual parameters, run analyses, check different result sections, and compare each design one by one, the AI agent can handle much of this workflow really quickly while still operating within the same structured engineering state and constraints as the human interface. This creates a useful collaboration between the engineer and the AI agent. The engineer decides what they want to achieve, defines the design requirements and constraints, and reviews the final engineering results, while the agent handles the repetitive design exploration, analysis, and comparison process through WebMCP. How I built it I built Aeroficiency as a browser-based engineering workspace using React and TypeScript. The application uses vinext as a Vite-compatible Next runtime and build layer, with Vite for development and bundling. React Three Fiber and Three.js power the interactive 3D wing visualisation, Zustand manages the in-memory workspace state, and Zod validates structured Site Tool and agent inputs. The engineering analysis runs locally in a Web Worker, and the application is configured and deployed through ChatGPT Sites. I also used OpenAI Codex and Google Antigravity throughout development to help prototype new features, debug issues, review the engineering logic, and test the application's WebMCP tools. Finally, I integrated WebMCP directly into the engineering workflow. I created ten Site Tools that allow compatible AI agents to read the current design state, create candidates, modify geometry, run analyses, and compare results across different candidates. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge I faced was finding the right balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Since Aeroficiency is designed to run directly in a browser, I could not rely on computationally expensive methods such as high-fidelity CFD. I had to simplify the aerodynamic and structural models enough to keep the analyses fast, while still producing results that were useful for preliminary design and comparison. To find this balance, I used MATLAB as a testing environment to run many aerodynamic calculations and compare different modelling approaches before implementing them in Aeroficiency. I also experimented with aerofoil polar data to better represent changes in lift and drag across different operating conditions without introducing the computational cost of higher-fidelity methods. This helped me refine a model that was lightweight enough for repeated browser-based analysis while still providing meaningful results for early-stage design decisions. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that Aeroficiency brings several parts of the preliminary design process into one place, including aerodynamic analysis, structural calculations, interactive visualisation and AI interaction through WebMCP, all within a browser and without requiring heavy computational resources. Because of this, Aeroficiency is not limited to high-performance computers and can also be accessed from devices such as tablets and phones. But what I am most proud of is turning the aeronautical and computing knowledge I had gained from university, alongside what I had taught myself through tutorials and online resources, into a complete, functional web application. Instead of only learning these concepts theoretically, I was able to apply them to a real engineering problem and build a tool that can generate, analyse and compare wing and blade candidates. I am especially proud that I took the initiative to turn what I had learned into something practical and took a meaningful step towards the kind of engineering work I want to pursue. What I learned Before this project, I had only heard of WebMCP and had never actually used it or written any code with it. I assumed AI agents mainly interacted with websites visually by reading screenshots, estimating coordinates, and clicking elements on the screen. Building Aeroficiency showed me that WebMCP allows an agent to interact through clearly defined tools, so it can directly read design data, modify candidates, run analyses, and compare results without relying on screenshots, coordinate estimation, and repeated visual interactions. At the same time, developing Aeroficiency pushed me much deeper into the aerodynamics and structural analysis I had studied during my first year. Turning those theories into a working tool helped me better understand not only how the calculations work, but also their assumptions, limitations, and where more advanced methods are required. What's next for Aeroficiency Aeroficiency is still at an early stage, and there are many areas I want to develop further. One of my main goals is to extend the aerodynamic analysis to higher angles of attack and better represent what happens as the flow begins to separate. I want users to be able to visualise in 3D where and how flow separation develops across the wing or blade. I also want to improve the accuracy of the calculations by making greater use of polar data across different angles of attack and Reynolds numbers, rather than relying primarily on simplified attached-flow approximations. Future development would focus on improving estimates of lift, drag and stall behaviour while still keeping the analysis fast and computationally efficient. Lastly, I want to maximise the efficiency of AI-driven autonomous design using WebMCP. Currently, users still need to create candidates and provide much of the aerofoil and polar data themselves. In the future, I want a user to simply describe what they need, for example, a wind turbine blade designed for a particular wind speed, power requirement and set of structural constraints. title: Forecast Ledger
pitch: A WebMCP dashboard where analysts and AI agents audit the same power-market forecasts and supporting evidence.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP dashboard where analysts and AI agents audit the same power-market forecasts and supporting evidence. Like Comment Story Updates Successful codex audit - Codex’s completed answer alongside the dashboard reordered to the five weakest days. Track-record overview The dashboard at the top with “6 site tools ready,” the running evidence and visible evaluation boundary Protocol and provenance The Information availability view showing sources, cutoff rules and integrity evidence. Protocol and provenance The Information availability view showing sources, cutoff rules and integrity evidence. Inspiration The original reason I started this work was quite personal. I am planning to reapply to Cobblestone Energy, a proprietary trading firm in European energy markets for the job role of a junior data scientist, in November after interviewing with them in May. I wanted to use the time beforehand to build something directly related to power markets. I did not want to make another project that only produced a good-looking model score. I wanted to show that I could produce forecasts before the outcomes were known and be honest about the result, even if it did not work. That became a project forecasting hourly electricity prices in Germany’s day-ahead market, where electricity for the following day is bought and sold through an auction. Each forecast has to be saved and timestamped before that auction closes, meaning the actual prices cannot influence the prediction. Once those prices are published, the score is added without changing the original forecast. If the forecasting process fails on a particular day, that day remains recorded as missed rather than being filled in later. I also decided the evaluation rules in advance. These safeguards reduce the risk of accidentally using future information or only presenting the days when the model worked. Without them, a forecasting chart can look convincing without showing whether the result could really have been achieved at the time. When I saw the WebMCP Challenge, it seemed like a natural extension of what I was already building. The evidence was there, but it was spread across files, tables and charts. A person could investigate it, while an agent would still have to scrape the page and guess what everything meant. Forecast Ledger was my attempt to let both of them inspect the same record and use the same dashboard, without adding a chatbot or changing the forecasting model itself. What it does The site is split into three main views. The track record shows the results collected so far and explains why the final assessment against the pre-agreed rules is still pending. The forecast ledger keeps every scored and missed day visible, while the protocol page explains the tests, data sources and deadlines for when information was allowed to enter each forecast. I added six WebMCP tools that Codex can discover directly from the page. It can audit the complete record, inspect missed runs, rank the weakest days, open a particular forecast date and check the research protocol. It can also compare the model with two simple benchmarks: using the price from the same hour one week earlier or the same hour one day earlier. These comparisons help show whether the forecasting model adds anything beyond assuming that recent price patterns will continue. The main feature is that a tool call also changes what the person using the site can see. In my demo, one prompt asks Codex to audit the record, inspect the misses and rank the five weakest days. The ledger then reorders itself and opens the weakest day. Codex and the person watching are therefore looking at the same evidence rather than separate versions of the analysis. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets a website give an AI agent a set of clearly defined tools that it can call. Without WebMCP, an agent can read parts of the page, but it has to work out for itself which dates, benchmarks and information checks belong together. It may be able to describe a chart, but it does not reliably understand how the different parts of the research record are connected. With WebMCP, the site tells Codex what it can do and what information each tool needs. Codex receives the evidence in a structured form, while I still have the visual dashboard and can check the result for myself. How I built it The existing Python project creates and timestamps the forecasts, then adds their scores to a public record once the actual prices are known. For the challenge, I built an exporter that matches each fixed forecast with its later outcome and writes a checked copy of the record for the browser app. I built the interface with React, Vite and Recharts, then registered the six tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The tools reuse the dashboard’s existing filters, sorting and selections instead of creating a separate interface for Codex. Each tool defines the information it accepts through a JSON schema and checks dates and allowed options before running. I also made each tool wait for the dashboard to reach the requested view before returning. This helps ensure that the answer Codex gives matches the evidence visible on the screen. I added tests covering the calculations, tool registration, valid and invalid inputs, interface changes and the static deployment. There is no OpenAI API backend. The AI in this project is Codex using the WebMCP tools supplied by the page. Challenges The first challenge was keeping the WebMCP work separate from the forecasting project that was already running. I did not want the new interface to interfere with the live record, so I preserved the Git history, marked where the challenge work began and switched off the copied automatic forecast jobs. The original repository still handles the forecasts and scoring, while the challenge version only displays a checked snapshot. The second challenge was getting to grips with WebMCP. I had heard of MCP and understood the general idea, but registering tools inside a website I had built and then getting Codex to run them against the live page was new to me. Understanding how the structured inputs, tool results and visible dashboard state needed to work together was a real learning curve. The final challenge was presenting the project clearly in a two-minute video. I had to work out when to move between sections, how far to scroll and how quickly I could speak without rushing. The Codex audit also takes close to a minute, so I had to show that it was genuinely running while speeding up the waiting section enough to keep the whole video within the limit. What I learned The main thing I learned is that WebMCP works best when the tools use the same actions already available to a person using the site. Reusing the dashboard’s real filters, sorting and selections meant that Codex and the person watching were always looking at the same evidence. I also learned the difference between changing the evidence and changing how it is displayed. The research record itself is read-only: Codex cannot alter the forecasts, scores or rules. It can still move between tabs, filter the ledger, change its order and select a day to help the person using the site investigate the record. Boundaries Forecast Ledger is for auditing forecasting research, not making trades. It does not calculate profit and loss. Its benchmarks are simple historical comparisons rather than a test against the market’s own expectations. Missed runs cannot be repaired later, and the project will not decide whether the model passed its pre-agreed tests until the evaluation period ends. The current result may look encouraging, but the final evaluation could still find no meaningful improvement. title: CashLatch
pitch: Manage your money with ChatGPT- while CashLatch protects your limits and keeps you in control.
about_excerpt: Manage your money with ChatGPT- while CashLatch protects your limits and keeps you in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Managing money often means checking balances, remembering bills, tracking savings goals and doing the same calculations repeatedly. ChatGPT can help compare options, but a normal conversation does not automatically know what is currently saved in a financial tool. It may also continue using an old recommendation after the balance or bills have changed. I built CashLatch to connect these two parts. ChatGPT helps the user understand their options, while CashLatch keeps the current information, checks the user’s limits and requires approval before recording a recommendation. What CashLatch does CashLatch is a browser-based money workspace where users can: Track their current balance, expected income and expenses. Add monthly bills with amounts and due dates. Create savings goals and monitor their progress. Choose the minimum balance they want to keep. Limit how much one recommendation can put toward goals. See how their balance may change over 30, 60 and 90 days. Use different currencies and separate money workspaces. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can read the money workspace currently open in CashLatch. It can calculate what the goals need, estimate future balances, compare different funding options and prepare a recommendation on the webpage. The user can review the exact amount, where it will go and how much money may remain. ChatGPT cannot approve the recommendation for them. After the user approves it, ChatGPT can apply only that exact recommendation, and only once. If the balance, bills, goals or limits change, CashLatch cancels the old approval. ChatGPT must read the updated information and prepare a new recommendation. CashLatch is a planning workspace. Applying a recommendation updates its local records; it does not transfer real bank funds. How I built it CashLatch is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript modules. The interface is responsive and includes money workspaces, currency selection, monthly bills, savings goals, transactions, balance estimates, safety limits and recent activity. The app uses the WebMCP imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool . It provides tools that let ChatGPT: Read the open money workspace. Add or update savings goals. Add or update monthly bills. Record income and expenses. Estimate future balances. Calculate how much each goal needs. Check different ways to fund goals. Prepare a recommendation for review. Propose safety-limit changes without applying them. A recommendation cannot be applied immediately. When the user approves an exact recommendation on the webpage, CashLatch temporarily creates a one-time apply tool for it. Before applying, CashLatch checks the latest balance, bills and safety limits again. The approval expires after five minutes, disappears after one use and is cancelled by any financial change. A SHA-256 fingerprint helps CashLatch detect whether the information used for approval has changed. Money-workspace data is stored in the browser using localStorage . CashLatch does not require an external financial database or an OpenAI API key. Challenges I faced The biggest challenge was making WebMCP useful instead of simply adding chat controls to a webpage. The important difference is not that ChatGPT can calculate a recommendation. It is that ChatGPT can work with the information currently open in CashLatch, while the website independently checks the result and keeps the user in control. Another challenge was designing the approval flow. The first version used technical terms such as staging, allocation, authorization and stale state. These were difficult for normal users to understand. I replaced them with clearer terms such as recommendation, money added to goals, approve, apply once and needs an update. I also worked through browser permissions, dynamic tool registration, local persistence, responsive navigation, form contrast, graph readability and clear monthly-bill presentation. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is most useful when the website remains responsible for its own data and rules. ChatGPT is good at understanding a request and comparing options. CashLatch is responsible for checking the numbers, showing the exact result and requiring user approval. I also learned that approval should depend on current information. If the user’s money changes after approval, continuing with the old recommendation may no longer be appropriate. Finally, I learned that a technically correct workflow is not enough. The interface and tool responses must use language that non-technical users can understand. What I am proud of CashLatch demonstrates a complete WebMCP workflow: ChatGPT reads the open money workspace. It compares multiple ways to fund a goal. CashLatch checks the recommendation against monthly bills and safety limits. The user reviews and approves the exact recommendation. A financial change cancels that approval. ChatGPT prepares a new recommendation using the latest information. The newly approved recommendation can be applied once. The balance, goal progress, confirmation and recent activity are updated. This gives ChatGPT useful access without giving it unlimited control. What’s next The next steps are broader browser testing, improved accessibility and clearer first-time guidance. Future versions could also support optional encrypted cross-device sync and connections to external financial services. These would require proper authentication, consent and additional security controls. title: StayWelll with Proof
pitch: StayWell is a premium hotel web app. Proof is the verified agent-assistance layer inside StayWell.
about_excerpt: StayWell is a premium hotel web app. Proof is the verified agent-assistance layer inside StayWell. Like Comment Story Updates Title StayWell, with Proof: a hotel where your agent's work is checked. What we built StayWell is a hotel booking experience with real room collections, live availability, demand-aware pricing, bookings, and a guest itinerary. A person can use it normally: choose dates, compare Garden Kings, Terrace Studios, River Suites, and Penthouse Residences, then make and manage a reservation — with a demo checkout, nothing real is charged. Proof is the part of StayWell that helps when a reservation change matters. A guest can ask an agent: "Move my stay to Friday for two nights, under $300." The agent reads the live reservation and availability, compares options, and prepares a change. The guest approves it. StayWell then re-reads its own final state and checks whether the room, date, price, and every other condition actually match the request. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Hotels are full of consequential, changing details: dates, inventory, room types, cancellation rules, and prices. An agent can remove a lot of manual work, but a guest should never have to take its word that a booking changed correctly. WebMCP gives an agent structured access to the same StayWell reservation the guest sees. It can read a reservation, search availability, quote a change, set conditions, stage a proposal, find recovery options, and verify after a change. The tool set changes with the live task: verify_result does not exist before a change is applied, and recovery tools appear only after a mismatch. What agents cannot do is just as important: they have no approval, commit, exception-acceptance, or "mark complete" tool. Those are structurally absent. Approval belongs to the guest, and completion belongs to StayWell's deterministic checker. What people and agents can do together that was not possible before Before something like WebMCP, delegation was all-or-nothing: either you did the booking yourself, or you handed your session to an agent and hoped. StayWell shows a third thing: an agent that works on your behalf through a tool surface that is expressive enough to be useful and narrow enough to be safe. The agent can genuinely change your stay — and can never be the one to call it done, because the tools that finalize and verify are not on its menu. A guest and an agent can negotiate a real, priced change together, in one thread, with the site itself as referee. The memorable moment On the demo seed, the agent quotes $294. Competing demand lands between the quote and the guest's approval. When StayWell applies the change, the real total is $319. Instead of saying "done," Proof catches the mismatch, explains the failed price condition, and offers choices — and this time there is a way forward that breaks nothing: another room at $247 that still checks in Friday for two nights. The guest approves it; every condition now passes; the receipt is green. The whole arc — promise, caught difference, honest recovery, verified result — runs in under a minute, live, with no API keys and no video tricks. (A "Reset demo" control restores the canonical world on demand.) How we implemented WebMCP The site is a WebMCP server on document.modelContext : 13 tools registered natively when the browser supports it (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome 149+ behind a flag), with a labelled polyfill fallback elsewhere — /agent-check shows which mode you are in and lets you exercise the tools yourself. Registration is derived from live task state, so tools genuinely appear and disappear as the task moves; the withheld set (approve, commit, mark-verified, edit-constraints) is enforced by a boundary test that fails the build if any WebMCP-reachable code path can reach a commit or approval route. The built-in chat agent is deliberately not privileged: it drives the same HTTP routes over the same cookies and meets the same 403s. Results The reproducible evaluation suite covers 59 deterministic scenarios: 0 false completions, 8/8 unauthorised approvals rejected, 8/8 agent commit attempts rejected, and 2/2 stale plans refused, alongside 208 passing unit and boundary tests. Run pnpm evals and pnpm test to reproduce. Built with Next.js App Router, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, document.modelContext WebMCP, and an engine-agnostic verification domain. The repository is Apache-2.0 licensed. title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: TALK FAST
pitch: Your blind spot has a voice. One human, one AI agent, one manual — through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Your blind spot has a voice. One human, one AI agent, one manual — through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates What it is TALK FAST is an asymmetric co-op arcade game for one human operator and one AI agent reader. The human sees a physical 3D console and presses every control. The agent agrees not to inspect the screen and instead holds the manual through WebMCP tools registered by the page. Neither can win alone: ten minutes, three strikes, five acts. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Most agent demos have the agent do the task for you. TALK FAST uses the WebMCP boundary as the wall between two players. Information asymmetry—the central game mechanic—runs through the API surface. The agent receives structured, typed access to only the information a reader should have: procedures, charts, codebooks, the clock, and the operator’s text channel. Each act registers its own scoped tools with an AbortSignal and removes them when it ends, so the agent’s live tool list becomes part of the game state. Honest caveat: the page cannot technically prevent an agent from looking at the screen. The tools make fair play the obvious typed path, and the client-captured interaction record makes the intended collaboration inspectable. How it creates a better experience Without WebMCP, the reader would have to scrape a DOM it is not supposed to see, while the operator would have to paste manual pages into chat. With WebMCP, the agent can call narrow tools, reason over the correct manual, ask for clarification, and place one decisive instruction on the operator’s teleprompter. Consequential actions stay visibly bounded. Every normal control press belongs to the human; the sealed override is marked consequential and requires confirmation; and one act gives the reader exactly one physical action of its own. Strikes are attributed to the reader or operator, making communication failures legible. The result is both a game and a compact practice arena for human-agent delegation: describe state precisely, ask useful questions, verify instructions, and keep consequential actions explicit. It is not presented as validated training; the mechanics simply make those collaboration habits immediate and measurable. What humans and agents can now do together TALK FAST creates a task neither participant can finish alone. The human has eyes and hands but no manual. The agent has the manual but no sanctioned access to the visual answer and almost no control over the console. Winning requires a fast, precise, two-way conversation. A completed run can be signed into a chronological public Operations Log. The server independently replays the input log against the same seeded engine before storing its score, while the replay page preserves the client-captured WebMCP interaction record. Reader identity and native-WebMCP status remain explicitly self-reported, so this is evidence of a collaboration rather than a model benchmark. How WebMCP is implemented The bridge in src/lib/webmcp.ts feature-detects document.modelContext , registers every tool natively with an AbortController per scope, and tracks registration promises and failures for an on-screen Evidence panel. It passes execute(input, { signal }) through so reader_wait_for_operator is genuinely cancellable, listens for tool lifecycle events, and dispatches the in-page console through the browser’s own getTools() / executeTool() path when available. Global tools cover briefing, status, manual search, teleprompter output, the operator channel, log signing, and replay history. Act-scoped tools cover glyph lookup, chart queries, and the reader’s timed key action. The same tool objects are mirrored into an explicitly labelled simulator so the game remains testable in browsers without native WebMCP; the UI never disguises that fallback as native execution. The application uses Next.js App Router, TypeScript, React, three.js / React Three Fiber, Drizzle ORM, and PostgreSQL. The 3D operations room responds to live tool traffic, strikes, time pressure, and act changes. Runs use server-issued sessions, one-time submission, deterministic replay, and server-computed scoring. title: What Can I Click?
pitch: What Can I Click gives teams a way to validate ClickHouse architecture choices before they build by visualizing how data, schemas, and query paths behave, so you can pick what’s correct.
about_excerpt:
What Can I Click gives teams a way to validate ClickHouse architecture choices before they build by visualizing how data, schemas, and query paths behave, so you can pick what’s correct.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Choosing the right architecture 

 ClickHouse can make enormous datasets feel instant, but getting there requires decisions whose consequences are difficult to see. A tiny insert creates another immutable part. A high-cardinality partition key creates isolated merge pools. A convenient sorting key can force queries to scan far more data than expected. 

 These choices often look harmless in configuration files and only become obvious when a production system begins falling behind. 

 I faced this recently, and I knew many companies had faced it too. From Zepto to Trigger.dev , teams have had to refine their ClickHouse architectures repeatedly as their data and workloads grew. 

 Just paste it into the agent? 

 That convinced me there was a real problem to solve. Giving an agent one ClickHouse article to read or blindly asking it would not be enough - which is what most people would do inadvertently when they run out of time. 

 Real systems need custom architectures, and translating general advice into workload-specific decisions is often where things go wrong. 

 The WebMCP Part 

 WebMCP felt like an exciting way to approach this. I wanted an agent to understand each visitor’s requirements, ask the right follow-up questions, retrieve relevant evidence, and display personalized recommendations directly inside the same interactive experience. 

 Inspiration for the 3D part merge visualization 

 OpenAI’s Cubecade demo inspired the project’s visual direction. It made me want to use React Three Fiber and Three.js to turn abstract ClickHouse behavior into something people could see, explore, and understand. 

 The result is What Can I Click? —an interactive ClickHouse architecture guide where humans and agents can explore the same system together. 

 Try it for yourself 

 Try the live experience or view the source . 

 It felt like a genuinely useful application of this new technology. I’d love to hear what you think!

title: doA2A
pitch: A WebMCP prototype where agents prepare bounded work and people authorize exact consequential actions.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP prototype where agents prepare bounded work and people authorize exact consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates 1 doA2Ai - Human-authorized execution for WebMCP Inspiration Agents should be able to do useful housekeeping tasks on your browser without acting like they own the mortgage, and without requiring the user's banking credentials to do it (unless of course, you give it explicit permission!). An agent can be helpful without being given a giant blob of access, but only if the boundary stays visible; doA2Ai explores a practical version of that idea: give an agent the tools needed for the current task, keep consequential decisions with the person, and verify that the result still matches what the person authorized. The goal is not less agent capability; it is more precise capability and user support through agency. Why WebMCP WebMCP gives the model an easy way to expose structured tools for the task that exists. Instead of making an agent reverse-engineer buttons and visual state, the browser can present a page-scoped capability surface that can be inspected and constrained - like a www dot paint by number for agents. doA2Ai adds an authority boundary around that surface; the extension identifies the current HTTPS origin and tool definitions, applies local policy, and keeps human-only values and decisions out of the agent's authority. The capability surface and the review path change as the task changes, and the user is given the option to allow or deny certain permissions. What people and agents can do together The agent can inspect the current target's available WebMCP tools and prepare a bounded request. The person keeps the parts that are actually theirs: policy, human-only values, exact review, and the final decision. The result is an explicit set of outcomes: - an allowed action within delegated authority; - an exact action held for human review; or - a policy-blocked action that is not executed. Receipts record the proposal, decision, execution status, and verification state. If the candidate changes between authorization and execution, doA2Ai blocks the action and requires reauthorization instead of treating the change as close enough. How it was built The installable Chrome extension owns rules, task state, decisions, connection state, and receipt history locally. A deployable HTTPS service and read-only control center provide proof-of-possession device pairing, replay-resistant signed requests, short-lived device and task-scoped connection credentials, and terminal receipt-digest binding. The service is a broker and control center, not an agent and not a WebMCP target. The real target remains a separate HTTPS page. The public repository contains the extension, service source, product contract, and owner/judge runbook: https://github.com/kaileahmarin/doA2Ai I used ChatGPT through Chrome for WebMCP protocol invocation and Gemini for additional testing. The project was built and tested with OpenAI Codex. Testing and limitations The intended judge path uses Chrome with WebMCP enabled, the official WebMCP Coffee Store target, and a compatible browser-integrated agent. The runbook covers an allowed path, an exact human-review path, a blocked path, and receipt verification using harmless test data. This is a V1 hackathon candidate, not a production authorization service. Mediation is cooperative: a client that bypasses the protected tool path can still call an ordinary page-owned WebMCP tool. OAuth protected-resource discovery, production tenant isolation, account recovery, and independent attestation of arbitrary page-owned effects are intentionally outside this slice. What we learned The hardest part was deciding exactly how to invoke user input when the candidate changes. Capability, authority, and outcome have to stay aligned. Human-only values cannot quietly leak into agent schemas or receipts. Authorization has to bind to an exact proposal, and uncertainty has to remain visible instead of being silently retried. That is the core idea behind doA2Ai: agents can do more without being given everything, while people keep authority over consequential actions. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Blindspot
pitch: A five-minute bomb-defusal game where a human sees the bomb, an AI agent gets seven WebMCP tools, and neither can win alone.
about_excerpt: A five-minute bomb-defusal game where a human sees the bomb, an AI agent gets seven WebMCP tools, and neither can win alone. Like Comment Story Updates The bomb has a blind spot Blindspot is a five-minute cooperative bomb-defusal game built around a capability split. The human can see the bomb: its wire colours, keypad symbols, button markings, casing, and the coloured strip that appears during a hold. The AI agent gets the manual and seven WebMCP tools: two read tools for rules and progress, plus five narrowly scoped actions. Neither side has the complete answer in the intended tool-only run, so they must talk before the timer reaches zero. Why WebMCP is the mechanic, not a checkbox Most agent demos try to expose as much page state as possible. Blindspot asks the opposite question: what should a good tool contract deliberately withhold? get_bomb_status reports the countdown, strikes, module types, and progress, then explicitly lists the visual facts it refuses to return. The action tools can cut, press, hold, and release, but they never reveal the bomb's appearance. This makes least-privilege interface design playable. If one tool leaks a wire colour or keypad symbol, the co-op game collapses because the agent no longer needs its human partner. This is a tool-contract demonstration, not a claim that WebMCP is a browser sandbox. An agent separately granted vision or DOM access could inspect the rendered page. The mission prompt therefore asks the agent to use only Blindspot's WebMCP tools, making the seven contracts the complete interface for the run. The human-agent experience The agent calls get_bomb_status and get_manual . It asks the human for only the visual facts required by a rule. It acts through typed WebMCP calls while both participants watch every call and result appear live. On the button module, the agent holds the button, a strip lights up only in the human view, the human reports its colour, and the agent schedules the correct release digit. A successful run ends in a mission report with time left, strikes, and tool-call count. The page includes a physical bomb-console interface, responsive human and agent views, an enlarged handoff state, opt-in synthesized sound, accessible redundant colour labels, and a replayable deterministic judge seed. Implementation Blindspot is intentionally small: vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no runtime dependencies or build step. src/tools.js declares the seven real contracts and registers each one with document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext , including name , description , JSON inputSchema , annotations, and execute . The same instrumented handlers update the live call feed. A fallback console is generated from those schemas only when native WebMCP is unavailable. Native sessions keep the executable controls with the connected agent. The public repo includes an MIT license, complete run instructions, a deterministic judge walkthrough, and 26 headless checks. The suite covers rules, clock throttling, all seven registration descriptors, partial registration reporting, hostile call-feed input, audio opt-in, schema-driven fallback accessibility, and bomb-appearance leak probes across fresh seeded games. GitHub Actions runs the suite and syntax checks on every push. Verified live I tested the production deployment in ChatGPT's in-app browser. It registered all seven tools from the production origin, completed the deterministic bomb through native WebMCP, and ended DEFUSED with zero strikes. title: Interactive Star Lab
pitch: A WebMCP-powered stargazing guide that helps you discover what is visible from your location, plan observations, and turn what you see into a simple observation report.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered stargazing guide that helps you discover what is visible from your location, plan observations, and turn what you see into a simple observation report. Like Comment Story Updates Interactive Star Lab — A WebMCP-Powered Stargazing Guide WebMCP Tools Let an Agent Configure the Sky and Operate the Observation Workflow Review Observation Targets and Fixed Visibility Predictions Before Going Outside A Printable Observation Guide with Targets, Directions, Predictions, and a Sky Map Compare the Mission’s Predictions with What the Observer Actually Saw Manual Controls Remain Available for Location, Time, Direction, and Visibility Settings A What-If Comparison Reveals Stars That Are Present but Hidden by Daylight The Agent Plans, the Human Observes, and the Application Records and Compares the Results Interactive Star Lab Try the WebMCP Experience Open the live application in a WebMCP-enabled browser. Ask your Agent: Set the viewer to New York City at 9 PM on September 3, 2026 local time and open the Sky view. The Agent calls configure_sky_view , and the location, time zone, local time, and Sky view are configured in one operation. The Friction Before Stargazing There is a gap between being interested in the night sky and actually going outside to observe it. Someone might think: I want to see the stars tonight. I wonder what I can see while traveling. I want to go stargazing with my kids. But turning that interest into an actual observation requires several decisions. Beginners need to figure out: What is visible from their location When to observe Which direction to look Which stars are easy to find How twilight and city lights affect visibility What to record during the observation Surveys of the general public in Japan show a noticeable drop-off between people who consciously look at the Moon and stars and those who go on to use telescopes or attend stargazing events. The problem is not simply a lack of interest in astronomy. There is friction between curiosity and action. Interactive Star Lab turns “I want to see the stars” into an actionable observation plan. A Different Approach from Smartphone Star Maps Modern smartphone astronomy apps are already very good at answering: What is that star above me? Using GPS, cameras, orientation sensors, and AR, they can help users identify objects in the sky with very little setup. Interactive Star Lab is not intended to replace that experience. It focuses on an earlier question: I want to observe the sky soon. What should I look for, and how should I prepare? Astronomy software can expose precise controls for latitude, longitude, date, time, azimuth, altitude, field of view, magnitude, light pollution, and other conditions. That flexibility is useful for experienced users. A beginner who says, “I want to spend 30 minutes stargazing in Hakata at 8 PM tomorrow,” however, probably does not want to translate that goal into a set of astronomical parameters. Interactive Star Lab takes a different approach. It runs in a web browser and does not depend on AR or a particular set of device sensors. Instead of adding more controls, it tries to reduce the number of decisions a user has to make before starting an observation. Turning Intent into Settings with WebMCP WebMCP connects a user's intent to the astronomy application. For example, a user can ask an Agent: I want to stargaze in Hakata for about 30 minutes at 8 PM tomorrow. Pick a few stars that are easy for a beginner to find and create an observation plan. The user does not need to look up Hakata's latitude and longitude. The Agent can interpret “Hakata,” resolve it to geographic coordinates, and pass those values to Interactive Star Lab through WebMCP. The same approach works for places that are not built into the application as presets, such as: Near Osaka Castle Around the Fukuoka City Science Museum Near a hotel while traveling The application therefore does not need a predefined list of every possible observing location. The LLM handles human expressions and incomplete intent. Interactive Star Lab handles deterministic astronomical calculations from location and time. AI can handle the ambiguity. The astronomy engine handles the precision. Instead of asking the user to decompose a goal into configuration fields, WebMCP lets the Agent translate that goal into application operations. From an Observation Plan to the Real Sky Interactive Star Lab calculates the sky for a specified location and time and supports the workflow from planning to observation. Sky Simulation The application displays the sky for a selected location, date, time, and viewing direction. It can show stars, star names, constellation lines, and constellation names. When the location or time changes, the star positions are recalculated. Visibility Simulation A star being above the horizon does not necessarily mean that a person can see it. Interactive Star Lab estimates visibility using conditions such as: Solar altitude Twilight Stellar magnitude Light pollution Users can also compare day and night at the same location to distinguish between stars that are physically present in that direction and stars that are likely to be visible at that moment. Observation Mission The Agent or the user can select observation targets and create an Observation Mission . A Mission stores: Observation location Date and time Target stars Pre-observation visibility predictions Keeping the prediction made before the observation allows it to be compared later with what the observer actually saw. Observation Guide An Observation Guide can be generated from a Mission. It includes information such as the observation time, location, targets, viewing direction, visibility predictions, and Sky Snapshot so it can be used during the real-world observation. Human and Agent Roles Interactive Star Lab does not ask the Agent to perform the observation itself. The Agent handles preparation: Plan → Configure → Predict → Prepare The human then performs the real-world part: Look → Observe → Judge For each target, the observer can record: Visible Not Visible Unsure A star predicted to be visible may still be difficult or impossible to see. Clouds, streetlights, buildings, local sky brightness, eyesight, and other conditions may differ from what the simulation can represent. Those differences are part of the observation rather than errors to be hidden. The workflow therefore does not end when AI explains what should be in the sky. The Agent prepares a prediction, and the human tests that prediction against the real world. Learning Through Observation Education and independent research projects are natural use cases for this workflow. Learning astronomy involves more than memorizing constellation names. Observation requires choosing a location and direction, recording the time, observing again later, and comparing how the sky changes. Interactive Star Lab supports this as a simple cycle: Predict → Observe → Record → Compare The application is not limited to education. It can also support: Beginners trying stargazing for the first time Parents observing with children Travelers exploring the night sky at a destination Students working on independent research Casual stargazers who want help planning an observation These users share the same problem: turning curiosity about the sky into a concrete observation. WebMCP Implementation Interactive Star Lab exposes WebMCP tools that cover the complete observation workflow. An Agent can use these tools to: Configure observation conditions Query the simulated sky Create an Observation Mission Open the Sky view Save a Sky Snapshot Retrieve and compare observation results Generate an Observation Guide and PDF Under the hood: The application registers 21 typed tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . configure_sky_view reduces location setup, local-time configuration, and Sky navigation from three tool calls to one. UI and WebMCP operations share the same React state and astronomical calculation logic. Mission predictions are fixed at creation time and are never recalculated afterward. PNG data is kept out of Agent responses; the tools return metadata and, when cloud persistence is enabled, short-lived signed URLs instead. Write tools use strict input validation and never infer or fabricate observation results. The Agent does not rely on a separate astronomy engine or a parallel application backend. Actions performed through the Web UI and WebMCP use the same domain logic and update the same application state. As a result, a Sky view or Mission prepared by the Agent can be inspected immediately by the human in the browser and used for the real-world observation. How We Built It The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite and deployed on Vercel . Celestial positions are calculated with Astronomy Engine , and the sky is rendered with HTML5 Canvas . Supabase is used to persist Missions, observation results, and Sky Snapshots. The application can

title: Triangulate
pitch: Where researchers and their AI agents triangulate real DBS research evidence together.
about_excerpt: Where researchers and their AI agents triangulate real DBS research evidence together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Deep brain stimulation programming has no standard method — patients average 6.9 clinic visits in the first year alone just to get their settings right, for a device that stays implanted for a decade or more. The research trying to fix that is real and published, but it's scattered: an image-guided algorithm out of Berlin, sweet-spot mapping out of Bern, sensor-guided approaches, a foundational protocol from Toronto that's still the baseline everyone measures against. Nobody had put it in one place a researcher could actually search. That gap, and the WebMCP Challenge's push toward tools that agents can use as first-class citizens instead of scraping a UI, was the whole starting point. What it does Triangulate is a workbench, not a chatbot. A researcher — or their AI agent, through the exact same tools — can search a curated set of 14 verified DBS programming studies, compare methods side by side, ask for a research plan built from a question and a set of studies, save that plan, and export it as a cited brief. A sixth tool reaches live into Europe PMC for anything the curated set doesn't cover, clearly marked unreviewed so it's never confused with the vetted evidence. Six document.modelContext.registerTool() calls, all wired to the same functions the on-page buttons call. That's the actual fit with WebMCP: a generic chatbot answering "find me DBS studies" gives back unstructured prose that's gone once the chat scrolls. Triangulate instead exposes real, schema-constrained tools, so results stay structured and persistent in a shared workspace instead of trapped in a transcript, and tools chain reliably — search_studies into compare_protocols into build_research_plan — because each one's output is real data, not re-parsed guesses. That's also what's newly possible: because each tool's output is exactly the input the next one expects — a study id from search_studies is exactly what compare_protocols and build_research_plan take — an agent can chain a request like 'compare the Bayesian and sweet-spot studies, then draft a plan for tremor patients' into real, structured tool calls instead of hallucinating a summary of research it never structurally engaged with. I verified every tool individually, end to end, including the exact chain of ids each one expects from the last. How I built it React, TypeScript, and Vite, in a GitHub Codespace. I started with a five-study placeholder just to prove document.modelContext.registerTool() actually worked end to end, then went and pulled real citations — Charité Berlin's StimFit trial, Bern's ARTORG sweet-spot papers, the original Toronto Western algorithms, an industry-sponsored adaptive DBS trial — and built the dataset out to 14, each with a real, checkable link. The tools were built one at a time and tested in the WebMCP Inspector before moving to the next: search first, then compare, then the plan builder, then persistence, then the brief, then live search once we confirmed Europe PMC allows direct browser requests with no backend needed. The UI went through more than one real redesign once it became clear a wall of scrolling cards wasn't going to cut it for a 3-minute demo. Challenges I ran into The biggest one: document.modelContext.registerTool() throwing InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name under React's StrictMode double-invoke in dev. Fixing it properly meant switching every registration to the current WebMCP draft's AbortSignal -based cleanup instead of trying to manually unregister — unregisterTool() was actually dropped from the spec in April 2026 in favor of that pattern. Separately, I hit a real crash: two research plans saved to localStorage before a schema change didn't have a field the newer code expected, and reading .length on undefined took the whole page down. The fix was a small normalizePlan() function that backfills missing fields on load, which is now just standard practice for anything read back out of storage. I also had a longer stretch of the research-question text not actually influencing the plan output — it was stored but not used — which I caught by testing the same three studies with two different questions and noticing the output didn't change. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Fourteen real, independently checkable citations, not filler. Six tools that all survived direct testing, not just a demo run. A working live literature search against Europe PMC with zero backend, confirmed via a real CORS test rather than assumed. And a research-plan builder that actually reads the question — mentioning "tremor" in a question the selected studies don't cover surfaces that gap by name, first, before the generic ones. What I learned The most useful distinction I learned: document.modelContext is the production registration API; navigator.modelContextTesting is a separate, narrower API that only debugging tools like the WebMCP Inspector depend on. A tool can be fully registered and working for a real agent while a specific inspector extension still shows zero — which is exactly what happened to me, and cost real time to pin down with actual console checks instead of assumptions. I also came away with a firm rule for anything touching browser storage: never trust that old saved data matches your current schema, normalize on read. What's next for Triangulate Letting a researcher promote a live, unreviewed search result into the curated tier with one click after actually reading it — a lightweight path to growing the dataset without needing accounts or moderation infrastructure. Accounts themselves, so a saved workspace follows a researcher across devices instead of living in one browser's local storage. And growing the curated set past 14 as the literature does. title: Marginalia
pitch: Marginalia is an agent-driven epistemological margin for the web: it knows what you know, ingests what you read, and bridges them — connections, meaning, citations, assistance, integrated knowledge.
about_excerpt: Marginalia is an agent-driven epistemological margin for the web: it knows what you know, ingests what you read, and bridges them — connections, meaning, citations, assistance, integrated knowledge. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every AI reading tool today is a chat box beside the text: ask, get a smooth answer, move on. That smoothness is the enemy of understanding — and it never knows what you already know. Two of my own projects had already designed the fix twice without a surface for it: an expand-and-annotate reader in an open-source LaTeX research environment, and "annotated reading versions" of papers in a learning system I'm building around evidence-gated mastery. The missing piece was a way for an agent to work inside the reading, live, while I read. WebMCP is exactly that piece. The name is a homage to the oldest form of this idea: marginalia — commentary written in the margins of a text, never in the text. What it does Marginalia is a reader where a human and their agent work on the same page. The page holds the document, your marks, and your own notes; the agent brings what it knows about you; WebMCP tools are where the two meet. No tool can write to the source. The agent lives in the margin. Open a paper, an article, or a docs page. Tell your agent what you already know — it records that as proposed knowledge you confirm with a tap — and the document reshapes around you: sections you've mastered fold to a stub with a reason , sections you haven't get expansions, glosses, [figures,] and connections to your own notes. Density isn't a global dial; it's a function of what you know about the concepts in each section. An expert in one domain and a novice in another is the normal case. Three layers, never merged, each toggleable: source (immutable), you (your marks), agent (its artifacts — attributed, reasoned, removable, with one button to remove them all). Switch the agent layer off and you are looking at the untouched text. The demo reads across a century: Rutherford's 1911 scattering paper (public domain), a 2025 Curious Kids essay from The Conversation on where atoms come from (CC BY-ND — and the layer rule is ND-compliance by construction: the text is byte-identical, everything else is margin), and Chrome's own WebMCP documentation (CC BY 4.0), which the agent annotates using the very tools registered on the page it's reading. How we built it Vanilla ES modules, no build step, one static page deployed on Netlify. Page state is a single frozen-source / mutable-margin store; every WebMCP tool validates its input and then calls the store, so the rules are enforced in code, not in a prompt. Tools registered via the WebMCP imperative API: get_reading_state , get_section_text , get_knowledge , upsert_knowledge , set_section_depth , annotate , search_notes , insert_figure [adjust to what shipped]. Every tool returns structured errors with a next_step written in coach voice for the agent to relay ("hiding a section requires a confirmed knowledge entry — ask the reader to confirm first"). [Your notes never leave the browser: drop a folder of Markdown and the agent queries a client-side index through search_notes .] [Math renders with KaTeX in both source and margin.] [SVG figures pass a sanitizer before rendering.] Two rules do most of the work: the layer rule (there is no write-to-source tool — enforcement by absence) and the pending-reshape rule (the agent never reshapes the section you are currently reading; changes land as pending and apply when you arrive). The document never moves under you. Why WebMCP and not an MCP server: the state that matters — the document, the click you just made, your notes, the artifacts already in the margin — is page state you are editing live. A server can't see it; the page can, and hands it to the agent on the next call. And the layer rule is only enforceable where the tools live: a page can simply not register a write tool. A prompt can be argued out of; a missing function cannot. Challenges we ran into Building against a protocol that is a week old, in a few hours, with a team of one human orchestrating several coding agents in parallel: one file per lane, an integrator merging, "tested" meaning a screenshot in the PR. [Getting tools visible in the ChatGPT in-app browser vs. the Chrome inspector extension — the API surface is still moving, so we register on both names and log which one took.] Licensing was its own design problem: the demo content had to be legally copyable into a public repo and shown on video, which is how a 1911 paper, a CC BY-ND essay and CC BY docs ended up sharing a stage. Accomplishments that we're proud of A document that visibly reshapes as you say what you know — with a reason under every fold. An ethical constraint (AI never writes into human text) that is also a technical guarantee and, incidentally, what makes CC BY-ND content legal to read this way. Honest states everywhere: refusals explain themselves, "no notes loaded" is a state, not an error. What we learned The interesting WebMCP apps aren't the ones where the agent fills in forms. They're the ones where the page holds something the agent can't have — here, the reader's live behaviour and their own archive — and the tool schema encodes a relationship: the agent proposes, the page referees, the human decides. What's next for Marginalia Integration with knowledge bases, memory systems and testing.
