title: MicroDuck Lab
pitch: Teach a real robot RL in your browser. An AI agent drives the same controls, trains on your GPU, and brings the weights back. 53 WebMCP tools, real MuJoCo, real Microduck.
about_excerpt: Teach a real robot RL in your browser. An AI agent drives the same controls, trains on your GPU, and brings the weights back. 53 WebMCP tools, real MuJoCo, real Microduck. Like Comment Story Updates MicroDuck Lab Learn reinforcement learning by teaching robots. Live: microducklab.com · Repo: github.com/SynthReality-Labs/microduck-lab · Video: youtu.be/eZY9nkB0mYE · by SynthReality Labs Inspiration Ten thousand people just bought a reinforcement-learning robot. Microduck — the $399 open-source biped from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face — passed 10,000 units and $5M within days of launch , taking $2.6M in the first 24 hours. Demand was heavy enough that the Christmas delivery promise is gone; new orders now quote four to six months. So there are thousands of people who have paid for a robot whose entire premise is train in simulation → deploy → refine → retrain — and who will spend months waiting, many having never trained a policy in their lives. RL is taught badly because it is taught abstractly. The loop that actually produces understanding — change a thing, watch the robot fail differently, work out why — is buried under CUDA installs, YAML files and wandb dashboards. Newcomers read about reward hacking. They rarely watch it happen to something they configured. MicroDuck Lab is that loop, in a browser tab, with an AI agent beside you. The real robot model, the real published policies, real MuJoCo physics, and 53 WebMCP tools. No install, no GPU, no account. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Because a human and an agent are good at opposite halves of RL diagnosis , and until now there was no way to put them in the same room. You look at a rollout and know instantly that that gait is ugly , I don't like that fall , it should look more deliberate . That judgement is pre-verbal, immediate, and nearly impossible to write down as a metric. An agent can read thirty metrics, a reward decomposition, a curriculum state and a config diff at once, and cross-reference them against a documented catalogue of known failure modes. That is tedious and error-prone for a human. Neither does the other's half well. Without WebMCP, the agent is guessing at a screenshot and you are transcribing numbers into a chat box. With it, both of you act on the same live simulation — and the simulation is the kind of state a screenshot cannot carry: 61 observation values at 50 Hz, a reward decomposition per term, a selection that means this joint, this window, this rollout . Reward design is a search over a space no human can hold in their head. The run that produced base-walk logged 22 reward terms — velocity tracking, uprightness, foot clearance, foot slip, swing height, angular momentum, action rate, torque rate, self-collision, a fallen tax, and a dozen more — each with a weight, each interacting with the others across 4,000 iterations of 4,096 parallel environments. Change one weight and the policy does not get a little better or worse; it finds a different way to satisfy the objective, and the only way to know which way is to look. So every real experiment branches: this weight or that, this curriculum or that, and each branch produces its own curves, its own per-term breakdown, its own set of failures. Inspecting all of it — cross-referencing a suspicious reward curve against a config diff against a catalogue of known failure modes — is exactly the work a person finds tedious and gets wrong, and exactly the work an agent finds natural. What the agent cannot do is look at the duck and know the gait is ugly. MicroDuck Lab is built so that neither has to do the other's job: the human supplies the judgement and the intent, the agent supplies the reading and the bookkeeping, and WebMCP is what lets them do it on the same live state. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Your pointing gesture becomes the query. Drag a range on the rollout timeline. Click the duck that fell. Type five words: "What went wrong here?" The agent does not ask what "here" means. It calls get_selected_timeline_range and get_selected_joint , learns you mean episode roulade , 1.80s–3.12s, pulls the telemetry for exactly that window, and answers: Lost upright orientation in this window — the trunk went past horizontal. Trunk dropped to 0.049 m, well below the nominal 0.12 m stance. Large angular velocity peak (10.01 rad/s) — the trunk is being thrown, not steered. Action-rate spike at t=2.38 s — the policy is correcting hard. No transcription. No screenshots. No "at about two seconds in". And it points back: name a joint and it lights up on the robot you are already looking at. The agent arrives already knowing this robot. Not because the model was trained on it — it launched five weeks ago — but because the page hands over Pollen's own reward-design playbook through get_rl_playbook . Ask why a policy keeps falling and you get the maintainers' hard-won rules, not textbook RL. You can break a reward function on purpose. Reward is a function of a trajectory, so stored rollouts can be re-scored under any objective instantly — no retraining, no GPU. Give a penalty a negative weight and the ranking reorders: a forward roll overtakes a clean walk, 7.31 to 7.04. The breakdown shows why in one line: Angular-velocity penalty w=-3 mean=-1.538 contrib=+4.613 A penalty paying out. That is Pollen's own documented sign-convention bug — where butt-hopping and crash-sits come from — reproduced in a browser in one slider drag. check_reward_signs implements their "infallible check" (every penalty must contribute ≤ 0) so an agent can catch it before GPU time is spent. And the loop closes off the page. Training a 61→14 locomotion policy needs CUDA and hours, so the studio does not pretend to do it. Instead, compose_training_job emits a prompt — not just a command — that you paste to the assistant on your own GPU machine, or hand to Hugging Face Jobs. It clones microduck_rl , runs Pollen's 64×5 smoke test first, launches the real run, watches that every penalty stays ≤ 0, and exports to ONNX. Training continues the same conversation instead of becoming shell archaeology. Then you bring the weights back. import_policy validates the 61→14 contract on load — a wrong-shaped file fails there, not as a flailing robot — and the imported policy becomes first-class: in the list, drivable, and A/B-able. We did this for real: base-walk , trained overnight on an RTX 5080 ( velstand , 4096 envs, 4000 iterations), ships with the site. compare_policies runs it against the published alpha_walking over identical scenarios and seeds. It survives on ice where the baseline does not — 50% vs 0%, on 2 seeds × 5 s, which is a small sample and is stated as one. How it creates a better user experience Six guided lessons, each a real action with a real outcome, each ending by handing you a question worth asking the agent. The simulator is the lesson; the agent is the tutor that can read live state. The studio is built to be operated by either party. Everything the agent can do, you can do by hand — drop obstacles in the duck's path, make the floor slippery, shove it with the mouse, drag a reward slider — and everything you do, the agent sees. A policy trained elsewhere gets the same treatment as one that shipped. And when the duck goes down it says so, from a speech bubble anchored to its actual jaw. The bubbles are the studio's way of turning every moment into an invitation: a fall suggests a question to ask, an idle duck suggests something to try, a new obstacle suggests a comparison. One of the things it says is true and teaches something: "I have fallen and I cannot get up — there is genuinely no get-up policy." How we implemented WebMCP One command layer. No second path for the agent. Every state change goes through a single core module ( src/core/commands.ts ). The UI calls it; each WebMCP tool ( src/webmcp/registerTools.ts ) is a thin schema wrapper over the same function . So when the agent sets a velocity command, the slider physically moves . Human state and agent state cannot drift, because they are the same state. A parity test asserts it. 53 tools registered on document.modelContext (not navigator — deprecated in Chromium 150), grouped as knowledge, state, selection, attention, mutation, execution, analysis and escalation. Security annotations per Chrome's tool-security guidance: 25 tools marked readOnlyHint , 3 marked untrustedContentHint — get_rl_playbook returns third-party markdown verbatim, import_policy echoes a user-supplied URL. They are nested under annotations ; passed flat, Chrome silently drops them. Within the published budgets: names ≤30 chars (max 27), descriptions ≤500 (max 373), parameter descriptions ≤150. Errors are values — {ok:false, reason, suggestion} — and invalid input names the valid options, because an agent can recover from that. No enum freezes the policy list, so a policy you imported is as nameable as one we shipped. A dev panel lists eve

title: Campaign Arena
pitch: AI agent searches KOC creators and proposes deals via WebMCP Site tools. Policy violations pause the tool call until you decide — approve, reject, or let it self-correct.
about_excerpt: AI agent searches KOC creators and proposes deals via WebMCP Site tools. Policy violations pause the tool call until you decide — approve, reject, or let it self-correct. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Influencer marketing is a $32.5 billion industry growing at 33% annually — and the #1 investment priority for marketers in 2026 is AI-powered creator matching. Yet most campaign tools still treat the agent and the human as two separate systems: the agent guesses through a UI, the human reviews a report afterward, out of context and too late to change anything. Influencer campaigns have a split-second problem: the agent that's fast enough to search hundreds of creators and score them against policy is the same agent you don't trust to commit ¥12,000,000 without asking. We built Campaign Arena to close that gap — not by slowing the agent down, but by giving it a shared workspace where both agent and person operate on the same live page. What it does Campaign Arena is a KOC (Key Opinion Consumer) campaign workspace where an AI agent and a human operator work side-by-side through four WebMCP Site tools: searchKOCs(platform?, category?) — filters the creator roster and updates the dashboard KOC grid in real time proposeDeliverable(kocKey) — proposes a deal; auto-confirms if safe, or blocks until the human decides if a policy violation is detected getTrustScore() — returns the current AEGIS trust score, autonomy tier, and factor breakdown endSession() — closes the session, locks all mutations, and writes the final trust report A policy engine enforces five rules: blacklist, platform allowlist, campaign budget ceiling (hard limit), split-deal detection, and single-deal approval threshold. An AEGIS trust score tracks the agent's behavior across the session — LOW, MEDIUM, and HIGH autonomy tiers control how much the agent can auto-confirm without asking. Every event — proposed, blocked, rejected, corrected, confirmed — is recorded in order in the Session Ledger. After a rejection, the agent suggests a policy-safe alternative. That suggestion is a nudge, not an automatic commit. How we built it Single HTML page using React 18 (via CDN) and JSX compiled to vanilla JS at build time — no framework build chain, no server. All WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool directly in the top-level page. The production build strips runtime Babel using esbuild and is served as a fully static site on Vercel. The core of proposeDeliverable is a Promise-based human-in-the-loop gate: waitForDecision(kocKey) stores a resolver in a Map . The tool await s that Promise. The human's Approve or Reject button resolves it — and only then does the tool return its result to the agent. ChatGPT is correctly suspended while the dialog is open and cannot proceed until the person has acted. Challenges we ran into Making the approval flow genuinely transactional was the hardest part. The tool result must be truthful about what happened — not what was intended — so the agent's next action is always correct. Concurrency edge cases required the most attention: double-clicking Approve or Reject, closing the session while a simulation is mid-flight, an orphaned Promise resolver when an intermediate await throws. Each of these could silently corrupt the ledger or committed spend. We addressed them with synchronous instance flags and careful finally cleanup — the part that took longest to get right. The policy engine also required precision: split-deal detection depends on cumulative confirmed spend across proposals, which must account for prior session history to trigger correctly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The proposeDeliverable tool genuinely blocks as a Promise until the human decides. This means the agent's next tool call is always based on the real outcome. Agents using Campaign Arena cannot accidentally double-spend, propose the same creator twice, or close the session while a decision is pending — these return bounded error objects instead of hanging or corrupting state. The shared-page model is the real accomplishment: the agent does not guess through visual controls, and the person never loses context or authority. Both see the same ledger, the same trust score, the same mission progress — in real time. What we learned Designing for agents and people simultaneously forces contract clarity that is easy to skip in ordinary apps. Every tool needs a precise description, strict input schema ( additionalProperties: false , enum for allowed values), and a result that accurately reflects state — not just the happy path. We also learned that the shared-page model is fundamentally different from building an API. The tool and the UI must stay in sync: what the ledger shows and what the tool returns must always agree. Getting that right is a design problem as much as an engineering one. What's next for Campaign Arena Persistent session ledger so campaigns survive a reload Multi-agent support: a planning agent hands deals to an execution agent, with the human overseeing both Audit export: the session ledger as a signed, timestamped record for compliance review Expanded policy rules: geo restrictions, budget pacing, and creator exclusivity windows Built With css html javascript react vercel webmcp Try it out campaign-arena-webmcp.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I led the WebMCP integration and policy engine design, built the human-in-the-loop approval flow, and handled all bug fixes and hardening before submission. My teammate handled UI design, character design, and initial project scaffolding with ChatGPT. title: OpenSlot
pitch: Help businesses adopt WebMCP with one script, so customers and their agents can get things done on the websites they already use.
about_excerpt:
Help businesses adopt WebMCP with one script, so customers and their agents can get things done on the websites they already use.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Why we built OpenSlot 

 A business can have a perfectly good website and still be difficult for an AI agent to use. A customer might ask for an appointment, but the agent still has to work through forms, guess how a booking page works, or tell the customer to call the office. 

 WebMCP gives websites a way to offer clear, structured actions to agents. But the next question is adoption: how does a small business put that into practice without building and maintaining its own agent integration? 

 OpenSlot is our answer to that question: a shared service and a drop-in script, built around the website the business already has. 

 What OpenSlot does 

 The business registers with OpenSlot, enters its services, chooses its preferred appointment setup, and receives a script to add to its website. In a compatible browser, that script exposes WebMCP tools the customer's agent can discover and use. The site can continue looking and working like a normal business website. 

 Our demo makes this concrete with Bright Smile Dental, a fictional business. The agent can list services, search sample appointment times, hold a selected slot, and complete a dummy confirmation. It can also request a simulated phone callback, check the request's status, and confirm one of the returned dummy options. 

 Dentistry is the example, not the product boundary. We want the same onboarding pattern to work for salons, repair shops, fitness studios, and other businesses where customers need to arrange a service. 

 Start simple, add more when needed 

 The intended setup supports different starting points. A business without online scheduling could use an OpenSlot-hosted calendar and define its availability. A business with an existing calendar or booking system could connect a supported integration and keep using that system. Businesses could also opt into a phone workflow for requests that still need a conversation. 

 The script is the small part the business installs; the shared service would handle those connections behind it. Businesses would not need to build a separate MCP server or redesign their website to get started. 

 Those integration paths are a roadmap, not a claim that the demo can access private calendars or place calls. Today, registration saves the choices, while scheduling and phone results use sample data. 

 Why WebMCP matters here 

 WebMCP lets the business expose the actions it understands instead of making an agent reverse-engineer its interface. The person can ask for help, compare the returned options, choose a time, and ask the agent to carry out the next step using explicit functions and returned IDs. 

 This gives the human and agent different roles: the person makes the decision; the agent handles the repetitive steps. Our intended interaction asks for approval before confirmation, although the prototype does not yet enforce approval on the server. 

 The opportunity is bigger than one booking flow. If businesses can adopt WebMCP through a familiar setup-and-script process, more of the everyday web can become useful to people working with agents. 

 How we built it 

 OpenSlot uses a JavaScript SDK that registers seven tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool defines its inputs and calls the shared backend when executed. A Cloudflare Worker serves the SDK, registration page, sample business website, and API. Cloudflare D1 stores business profiles and simulated callback state. 

 The business ID connects the snippet to the registered profile. Ordinary appointment slots, holds, and confirmations use in-memory demo state. The source code, setup instructions, and MIT license are public. 

 What is real, and what is simulated 

 Business registration, generated IDs, WebMCP registration, backend requests, and stored callback state are implemented. The hosted example exercises the SDK and API on the same domain. 

 All availability and booking results are simulated. No external calendar is connected, no real call is placed, and no real appointment is booked. The deployed SDK's full dummy workflow was tested from a separate website origin. The demo uses a permissive cross-origin policy; phone opt-in is a saved preference rather than an enforced permission, and production authentication and durable booking guarantees are not implemented. 

 Challenges and lessons 

 The hardest part was making the reusable setup flow match the promise of one script per business. We fixed business-scoped service filtering, consistent callback request IDs, expired-hold release, and validation of submitted details. Testing a second business and the SDK from a separate website helped catch gaps that a single polished demo could hide. 

 The main lesson was that exposing a function is only the beginning. A real integration also needs reliable state, explicit permissions, and honest handling of missing availability. We kept external scheduling and telephony simulated rather than presenting those unfinished connections as working features. 

 What's next 

 Our next step is to make the tools business-neutral and connect one real scheduling path. Then we can add other supported systems and optional telephony, with verified business ownership, origin restrictions, approval checks, durable booking state, and reliable retries in place before handling real customers. 

 The aim stays simple: make adding WebMCP practical for the businesses people already use.

title: ARCade
pitch: A shared ARC reasoning arena where human insight and WebMCP-powered agents turn stuck exploration into verified progress.
about_excerpt: A shared ARC reasoning arena where human insight and WebMCP-powered agents turn stuck exploration into verified progress. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Web agents are usually judged by their final answer, while the interesting—and risky—part is the path they take. We wanted a shared arena where a person and an agent can see the same live problem, reason at the same semantic level, and verify every transition. What it does ARCade is a browser-native WebMCP arena for ARC-AGI-2 and ARC-AGI-3. For ARC-2, judges choose a public grid challenge and an external agent inspects demonstrations, reads bounded grid chunks, records a hypothesis, submits the complete output grid, and advances through the deck. For ARC-3, judges select an interactive environment and the agent inspects observations, reads 64×64 frames in bounded chunks, records evolving mechanics, executes only currently available actions, and re-inspects after every move. There is no embedded model and no manual puzzle editor. The agent owns execution after a person chooses the challenge. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is ARCade’s control plane. Each mode registers five native tools through document.modelContext. Reads are bounded; writes are tied to opaque run and observation identities; stale, concurrent, unavailable, or ambiguous writes fail closed. This turns the page from something an agent must visually guess through into a typed, auditable environment. The human-agent collaboration moment In ARC-3’s LS20 environment, the agent reached Level 2 after learning movement, cross-triggered rotation, one-use refills, and the action budget—but assumed a third rotation required a 30-action refill trip. The human asked: “you can cross white cross third time without having to refill?” The agent revised its hypothesis, stepped off the cross and immediately back on, verified the third rotation in two actions, preserved the refill for the exit, and cleared the level. ARCade recorded the later Level-3 correction instead of hiding it. The run finished with an authoritative WIN, 7/7 . That is the thesis: people are good at high-information reframing; agents are good at executing, checking, and scaling a verified idea. WebMCP gives them a shared live loop. How we built it React 19, TypeScript, and Vite for the observation-first UI Ten native WebMCP tools with runtime validation and lifecycle cleanup Immutable ARC-2 sessions with exact scoring, two attempts, answer redaction, and deterministic deck progression A same-origin Python bridge around the official arc-agi toolkit for ARC-3 Canvas frame rendering and bounded row reads for both generations Opaque run and observation identities, serialized actions, secret redaction, CSP, and visible audit traces A Docker deployment with an offline LS20 environment behind /arc3-api Challenges and accomplishments ARC-2 is a static transformation with hidden answers; ARC-3 is executable, stateful Python with dynamic actions and provider-owned scorecards. We kept their tools and runtime models separate rather than forcing them into one abstraction. The result is a public-first picker, 111 passing unit tests, a real production-browser smoke test at 320px, an official ARC-3 bridge smoke, and an evidence-backed collaboration story ending in LS20 WIN, 7/7. What we learned The decisive human contribution was not doing the agent’s work. It changed the search space with one local-cycle idea. The agent still had to bind that idea to the current observation, verify it, budget the remaining route, learn later mechanics, and finish. Good agent-native products make that handoff visible and safe. What’s next Server-held ARC-2 scoring, reproducible replay exports, more rights-cleared offline ARC-3 environments, isolated hosted execution for trusted environments, and side-by-side trajectory comparison. title: Sigmora Live Relay
pitch: Stay live while an agent builds, reviews, and verifies the launch moment with you.
about_excerpt: Stay live while an agent builds, reviews, and verifies the launch moment with you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Sigmora Live Relay Inspiration Going live is when creators most need cross-platform promotion—and when they can least afford to leave the stream to edit, rewrite, upload, and check posts. Sigmora Live Relay turns one selected live event into a reviewable 12-second vertical campaign on a shared release board. What it does The page exposes eight narrow WebMCP tools. An agent reads the visible brand and destination context, finds or declares the source live event, drafts the relay, polls generation, revises copy, queues exact destination accounts, releases the human-approved revision, and checks each destination independently. Every tool call updates the same board the creator sees. The consequential checkpoint remains human. Queue items are bound to exact account IDs and one immutable revision. The creator reviews those items in the UI and approves them there; approval is deliberately not exposed as a tool. Any revision invalidates the receipt. Release requires that receipt plus an idempotency key, and partial failure can never be reported as total success. Why WebMCP This is a strong WebMCP fit because the useful context and collaboration live on the open page: current creative state, selected destinations, approval, and receipts. Without WebMCP, an agent must infer buttons and duplicate state. With WebMCP, it uses an explicit contract while the person keeps visual control. People and agents can now share one live workspace: the agent handles multi-step coordination while the creator remains present with the audience and retains authority over publication. How we built it The challenge implementation is framework-free TypeScript built around document.modelContext.registerTool(...), closed JSON Schemas, typed result envelopes, an observable shared controller, page-scoped teardown, a strict HTTP adapter, and a deterministic local provider. The normal manual interface continues to work when WebMCP is absent. The eight tools cover context, source discovery, drafting, job polling, revision, exact destination queuing, approved release, and independent status verification. Unit and end-to-end tests exercise schemas, lifecycle cleanup, revision invalidation, idempotency, partial failure, and the manual fallback. Challenges The hardest design problem was preserving human authority without making the agent workflow brittle. We solved it with an immutable approval receipt bound to an exact revision and destination set, plus clear state transitions visible to both sides. Another challenge was truthful partial failure: each destination receives an independent receipt, so a mixed outcome stays mixed. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when it is not simply a hidden automation API. The shared page should remain the source of truth, and the tool contract should expose exactly the capabilities that benefit from agent reasoning while keeping consequential consent visible and human. What's next The public reference is intentionally simulated and says so throughout the UI and tool results. Next we would connect the strict provider adapter to real publishing APIs, preserving the same approval, idempotency, readback, and partial-failure guarantees. title: IncidentLens WebMCP
pitch: An agent-native incident response console where AI can inspect alerts, correlate logs and metrics, identify likely root causes, and propose safe remediation through structured WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native incident response console where AI can inspect alerts, correlate logs and metrics, identify likely root causes, and propose safe remediation through structured WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 IncidentLens WebMCP 

 Inspiration 

 Production incidents rarely fail because engineers have no data. They fail because the useful evidence is scattered across alerts, logs, metrics, deployment history, and runbooks. 

 During an outage, an engineer may need to jump between several screens just to answer basic questions: 

 
 What changed? 
 When did the degradation begin? 
 Which service is responsible? 
 Was there a deployment immediately before the incident? 
 What is the safest remediation? 
 

 AI agents can help with this investigation, but traditional websites are primarily designed for humans. An agent often has to interpret visual interfaces, navigate pages, and extract information indirectly. 

 IncidentLens WebMCP explores a different approach: make the incident-response application itself agent-native. 

 Using WebMCP, IncidentLens exposes structured incident investigation capabilities directly to compatible AI agents while preserving the same dashboard for human operators. 

 What it does 

 IncidentLens is an incident-response console that combines: 

 
 alerts 
 application logs 
 infrastructure metrics 
 deployment history 
 incident timelines 
 root-cause hypotheses 
 remediation recommendations 
 

 The dashboard can be used normally by an engineer, but it also exposes these capabilities as structured WebMCP tools. 

 An AI agent can investigate an incident through a workflow such as: 
 list_incidents
 ↓
get_incident
 ↓
get_alerts
 ↓
search_logs
 ↓
get_metrics
 ↓
get_recent_deployments
 ↓
build_timeline
 ↓
analyze_root_cause
 ↓
suggest_remediation
 
 For example, a user can ask: 

 
 Investigate INC-102. Determine what changed before the outage, identify the most likely root cause, and recommend the safest recovery action. 
 

 Instead of trying to visually navigate the application, the agent can call the relevant WebMCP tools and receive structured results. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent interacting with an operational dashboard may need to: 

 
 understand the page layout, 
 locate the correct controls, 
 navigate multiple views, 
 interpret visual information, 
 extract relevant values, 
 repeat the process for every investigation step. 
 

 IncidentLens exposes the underlying capabilities directly. 

 For example: 
 search_logs ( { 
 incidentId : "INC-102" , 
 query : "connection timeout" 
 } ) 
 
 can return structured evidence that an agent can reason over immediately. 

 This makes the interaction more deterministic, composable, and transparent. 

 The human interface and the agent interface coexist: engineers can continue using the dashboard normally while agents gain a structured way to assist them. 

 Human-in-the-loop safety 

 Incident response can involve high-impact actions. 

 For that reason, IncidentLens separates investigation from execution . 

 Agents can autonomously: 

 
 inspect evidence, 
 correlate telemetry, 
 construct timelines, 
 generate hypotheses, 
 and recommend remediation. 
 

 Potentially destructive actions such as rollbacks or service restarts remain subject to explicit human approval. 

 The goal is not to replace the incident commander. It is to give them a much faster investigation partner. 

 Example incident 

 One demonstration incident begins shortly after deployment v2.4.1 . 

 IncidentLens correlates several pieces of evidence: 
 Deployment v2.4.1
 ↓
Database connection usage rises
 ↓
Connection pool becomes saturated
 ↓
Request latency increases
 ↓
HTTP 5xx errors spike
 
 Rather than showing only an AI-generated answer, IncidentLens exposes the evidence used to reach the conclusion so the operator can independently verify it. 

 How we built it 

 IncidentLens is implemented as a web application with WebMCP-enabled tools exposed from the browser. 

 The application contains a simulated production environment with realistic: 

 
 incidents 
 alerts 
 logs 
 time-series metrics 
 deployment events 
 service metadata 
 

 Each investigation capability has a structured input and output contract so an AI agent can invoke it directly. 

 The architecture is intentionally simple: 
 Human / AI Agent
 │
 ▼
IncidentLens Web UI
 │
 ├── Human-facing dashboard
 │
 └── WebMCP tools
 │
 ▼
 Incident data layer
 │
 ┌───────┼─────────┐
 ▼ ▼ ▼
 Logs Metrics Deployments
 
 This allowed us to focus on demonstrating how WebMCP changes the interaction model rather than hiding the core idea behind unnecessary infrastructure. 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest design challenges was deciding what should become a tool. 

 Simply exposing every button on a web page would not create a useful agent interface. 

 Instead, we designed tools around meaningful operational capabilities such as: 
 search_logs
get_metrics
get_recent_deployments
build_timeline
analyze_root_cause

title: Guardian Travel WebMCP
pitch: A travel itinerary website built for AI agents to read, not just humans to click. Structured WebMCP tools replace brittle UI guessing with grounded site-provided data.
about_excerpt: A travel itinerary website built for AI agents to read, not just humans to click. Structured WebMCP tools replace brittle UI guessing with grounded site-provided data. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Modern travel websites are designed for humans, not AI agents. A traveler can easily understand the difference between a confirmed flight, a hotel booking, an open dining intention, and a rainy-day backup plan. An AI agent that relies on UI scraping, DOM parsing, or screenshots has a much harder job: nested cards, visual chips, labels, and ambiguous text can easily be misread. We wanted to explore a different approach: Websites should expose tools to agents, not force agents to guess the UI. Guardian Travel WebMCP turns an existing travel itinerary into an agent-native website that exposes structured read tools directly through WebMCP. We do not generate the trip. We make the existing trip readable and adaptable for AI agents. What it does Guardian Travel exposes three read-only WebMCP tools: get_trip_summary get_day_itinerary get_rain_backup These tools let an agent retrieve authoritative, site-provided itinerary data without scraping the interface. For example, when the user asks: “It’s raining tomorrow afternoon. What’s my backup plan?” the agent can call: get_trip_summary get_day_itinerary with relative: "tomorrow" get_rain_backup with relative: "tomorrow", period: "afternoon" The result is grounded in the itinerary itself. In our demo, the outdoor plan is My Khe Beach and the site-provided backup is a generic café or SPA intention — not an invented business name. How we built it The project is a lightweight, dependency-free web application using: HTML5 CSS Vanilla JavaScript WebMCP through document.modelContext The page detects whether a native WebMCP host is available. When running in a supported native host, the three tools are registered directly with document.modelContext . For ordinary browsers that do not yet expose WebMCP, the site includes a small in-page compatibility shim so the interface and demo workflow can still be inspected without changing the tool definitions. The real native WebMCP path was validated in Google Chrome 152 using the native ModelContext implementation. All three tools were discovered and successfully invoked without the shim. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making the difference between an entity and an intention explicit. A travel page may contain a real hotel booking, a confirmed flight, or simply text such as “eat seafood tonight” or “coffee / SPA if it rains.” A human understands that immediately. An agent scraping the UI may not. We therefore designed the tool responses to preserve these distinctions and to fail closed when information is unavailable rather than inventing details. Another challenge was validating the emerging native WebMCP implementation across browser environments. We kept the native path authoritative while using a graceful fallback only for unsupported browsers. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real native WebMCP host discovers all three tools. All three tools are callable through document.modelContext . The project requires no DOM scraping. Rain-backup queries return only site-provided structured data. The tool layer is read-only and deterministic. The entire public challenge project is only a small set of static files with no backend or API keys. The project is fully open source under the MIT License. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-friendly websites should not depend on agents reverse-engineering presentation layers. Humans need rich visual interfaces. Agents need explicit semantic capabilities. WebMCP gives websites a way to support both. Instead of treating the web page as something an agent must visually decode, the site itself can provide the agent with the correct tools and structured context. What's next for Guardian Travel WebMCP The current challenge version is intentionally read-only and focused. Future directions could include: richer place details controlled itinerary updates permissioned write tools cross-day adaptation mobile synchronization real-time travel assistance Any future write capability would remain explicit and permission-gated. For this challenge, we kept the scope small: three real tools, one clear travel use case, and no UI guessing. title: Cyber Seeds - Human Authority for the Agentic Web
pitch: WebMCP with human-held, fail-closed authority: agents can inspect and request sensitive changes, but cannot approve, replay or transfer consent.
about_excerpt:
WebMCP with human-held, fail-closed authority: agents can inspect and request sensitive changes, but cannot approve, replay or transfer consent.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 The web is becoming agentic. Browser agents can now discover site capabilities, inspect information and request actions on behalf of people. 

 That creates a question that is bigger than a confirmation button: 

 When an agent can perform a consequential action, where is the authority boundary that proves a human actually chose it? 

 Cyber Seeds is built around the idea that capability is not authority. An agent may be able to understand a problem and request a change, but it must not be able to create, reuse or redirect a human decision. 

 This prototype applies that principle to a synthetic household digital-safety scenario. 

 What it does 

 Cyber Seeds exposes three structured WebMCP tools: 

 
 inspect_demo_household — read-only 
 get_approval_state — read-only 
 perform_sensitive_change — a controlled consequential action 
 

 The agent can inspect the synthetic household dashboard and identify that the primary account lacks multi-factor authentication. It can then request that sensitive change. 

 Cyber Seeds fails closed. The request becomes pending and execution is refused with human_approval_missing . 

 The core demonstration is that the agent cannot approve itself. An agent-derived attempt to activate the visible approval control is rejected as untrusted_ui_event , because interaction is not consent. 

 A genuine human must manually approve the exact pending request. Once that happens, authority is bound to the specific action, target and request identity. The agent may retry that one approved MFA request, once. 

 After the change succeeds, the approval is consumed immediately. It cannot be replayed, and it cannot be transferred to a different action such as a router security update. That action receives its own separate pending request and requires its own human decision. 

 How I built it 

 I built Cyber Seeds as a live browser prototype using WebMCP, JavaScript, HTML and CSS, deployed publicly on Cloudflare Pages. 

 The project combines: 

 
 Structured WebMCP tool registration 
 A synthetic household security model 
 A human approval gate outside the agent tool surface 
 Exact request, action and target binding 
 An authority ledger that records refusal, approval, execution and consumption 
 Explicit fail-closed states for unsafe or incomplete requests 
 

 The live page is intentionally designed so a judge can see both sides of the boundary: what an agent is permitted to discover and request, and what remains exclusively under human control. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The difficult part was not giving an agent a tool. It was ensuring that every shortcut failed safely. 

 I had to account for situations where an agent might try to: 

 
 Trigger a visible approval control itself 
 Retry a completed action 
 Reuse a consumed approval 
 Apply an approval to a different target 
 Act on stale or mismatched request data 
 

 A conventional “Are you sure?” prompt is not enough for that problem. The system needs to prove that approval came from the human, that it applies only to the intended consequence, and that it cannot be reused. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The submitted prototype demonstrates an end-to-end authority lifecycle: 

 
 The agent discovers structured WebMCP capabilities. 
 It inspects the synthetic household state. 
 It identifies a sensitive MFA issue. 
 Its first action attempt fails closed without human approval. 
 Its self-approval attempt is rejected. 
 A human manually approves the exact request. 
 The approved action executes once. 
 The authority is consumed. 
 Replay produces no second consequence. 
 Cross-target reuse is refused. 
 

 The implementation passed 32 automated checks covering fail-closed execution, exact request binding, parameter binding, untrusted UI events, denial, single-use authority, replay protection, stale requests and cross-target refusal. 

 Most importantly, the prototype turns a security principle into visible, testable behaviour: 

 
 Agents can request authority. They cannot manufacture it. 
 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP makes agent interaction more structured, discoverable and useful than relying on screen scraping or guessed UI flows. 

 But discoverability must be paired with governance. 

 The key learning from this project is that agent safety should not depend on an agent promising to behave. The authority boundary must be enforced by the application itself, with explicit evidence of what was requested, what the human approved, what executed and what is no longer valid. 

 What's next for Cyber Seeds — Human Authority for the Agentic Web 

 This submitted build remains frozen for evaluation. 

 Beyond the challenge, Cyber Seeds will explore how this authority model can support real-world domestic cyber-resilience workflows: household security reviews, scam-response support, account recovery guidance and practitioner-led safeguarding systems. 

 The longer-term aim is to develop practical patterns for a future where people and agents work together—but humans retain meaningful control over consequential decisions.

title: Doceo
pitch: Teach a website new WebMCP tools by example. Humans demonstrate, agents propose, and the website verifies each workflow before a human approves publication.
about_excerpt: Teach a website new WebMCP tools by example. Humans demonstrate, agents propose, and the website verifies each workflow before a human approves publication. Like Comment Story Updates The learned capability returns a verified cart update. This screenshot shows the local Tool Lab test interface. Three deterministic tests verify the demonstrations and no-match rollback before separate UI approval. Two demonstrations reveal variable inputs and fixed actions, producing a constrained contract. Teach the web by example: demonstrate, compare, verify, and approve a reusable website tool. Inspiration Most websites offer agents only the tools their developers wrote. But users develop useful workflows that were never packaged as tools. That makes us wonder: what if a website could learn a reusable capability from its user, verify what it does, and expose it through WebMCP? Doceo is Latin for “I teach” explores that idea. Its guiding principle is simple: humans demonstrate, agents propose, the website verifies, and lastly humans approve. What it does Doceo turns demonstrated workflows into site-native WebMCP tools. The prototype uses Lumen Market, a demo shopping website. A user demonstrates the same shopping task twice with different searches and budget filters. Doceo records the underlying domain actions not screen coordinates or DOM selectors. Then compares the examples to identify what changes and what stays fixed. An agent can then inspect the evidence, propose a structured tool contract, run isolated tests, and request publication. A separate approval step in the interface registers the tested capability as a new WebMCP tool. The resulting find_and_add_product tool accepts new inputs, selects a matching product, and updates the same cart visible to the user. If execution fails its checks, the interpreter restores the previous state. The important transition is not simply from clicks to automation. It is from demonstrated intent to a verified capability on the website’s own tool surface. How I built it The application uses React, TypeScript, and Vite, with Zod for runtime contract validation. Doceo exposes four WebMCP meta-tools: get_workflow_evidence propose_tool_contract run_candidate_tests request_tool_publish These let an agent participate in tool creation before the learned tool exists. Proposed contracts use a constrained intermediate representation backed by five allowlisted domain actions. They cannot introduce arbitrary JavaScript. A deterministic interpreter executes those actions and checks their observable effects. Verification covers the recorded demonstrations and a no-match safety case. Editing a contract invalidates its previous test results, and approval reruns verification against the current evidence. Sessions persist across reloads, evidence and contracts can be exported, and published tools can be revoked. Parallel AI supported project and technical research during development. Graphify supported codebase navigation and persistent project context. Neither is required to execute the demo’s learned tools. Challenges I ran into The hardest problem was deciding what the examples actually justify. Two demonstrations can suggest a reusable pattern, but they do not prove a user’s general intent. Doceo therefore keeps its scope narrow, exposes the proposed contract for review, and rejects incompatible demonstrations. Another challenge was separating proposal from publication. The WebMCP publication tool only requests approval; registration happens through a separate interface action after verification. It was also important to distinguish compatibility testing from native integration. A local test harness is useful, but it is not evidence that native WebMCP discovery and invocation work. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The prototype completes the full demonstrate --> propose --> verify --> approve --> invoke cycle. Native WebMCP testing confirmed discovery of the four meta-tools, runtime appearance of the approved fifth tool, successful invocation, and removal after revocation. The current automated suite passes 16 unit tests and 9 end-to-end tests, including persistence, contract editing, rollback, responsive layouts, and automated accessibility checks. What I learned Recording behavior is easier than establishing a trustworthy contract for repeating it. Stable domain actions, explicit parameters, observable postconditions, and reversible execution matter more than a convincing replay. I also learned that WebMCP can support more than a fixed integration: it can provide the interface through which an agent helps a website construct and validate a new capability. What's next for Doceo The next steps are a public deployment, a reproducible demo, and evaluation with additional users and workflows. I also want to add clarification questions when demonstrations are ambiguous and compare agent-assisted execution against UI-only execution using measured success rates, latency, and token usage. The current prototype is intentionally limited to an instrumented shopping website. It does not claim to learn arbitrary workflows on arbitrary websites. The longer-term goal is a reusable teaching layer that other websites can adopt while retaining control over their actions, verification rules, and publication decisions. video_transcript_excerpt: I begin by demonstrating a real task on Lumen Market. I search for a desk lamp, set a maximum price of $100, and add the matching product to the bag. Then I repeat the same workflow with different values. A task light under $70. With two demonstrations captured, the foundry compares them. The search query and maximum price change, so they become tool inputs. Quantity stays fixed at one. The recorded product ID also changes, but it is an outcome, not a useful input. Now I hand the page to the WebMCP enabled agent. It reads the evidence directly from the website and finds 100% sequence agreement across four domain actions. The agent proposes a constrained contract named find and add product. Instead of hard-coding either recorded item, the contract uses semantic best match selection. It contains only approved site actions, never arbitrary generated JavaScript. Docio runs three isolated tests. Both recorded workflows produce the expected card effects. A separate safety test deliberately searches for a product that does not exist. The operation is rejected, and the complete state is rolled back. All three tests pass. The agent may request publication, but it cannot approve itself. I review the contract and publish the tool with an explicit human click. Thus, the browser now exposes find and add product as a new WebMCP capability at runtime. To prove that this is a reusable tool rather than a replay, I ask the agent for something never shown in the demonstrations, a wall clock under $110. The learned tool finds the Dawn wall clock for $96 and adds one to the demo cart. The structured tool result in the visible website state confirm the same outcome without the agent clicking the interface. Finally, I revoke the learned tool. The agent refreshes the page's web MCP capabilities and confirms that it has disappeared from both the tool lab and the browser tool list. Docu CEO shows how people and agents can grow a website's capabilities together.

title: Duet
pitch: Turn the music you love into a piano lesson made for you.
about_excerpt: Turn the music you love into a piano lesson made for you. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Duet Piano Studio Agent created lesson Inspiration Duet began with a gap we kept running into: an agent could give us a good music lesson, but it could not reach the piano. We could ask, “Can you help me practise these four bars?” and receive sensible advice—slow the piece down, isolate the right hand, repeat the difficult section—but the useful part stopped at the chat box. We still had to find the music, change the tempo, set the loop, remember the notes and rebuild the lesson ourselves. We wanted the agent to meet the learner inside the instrument. That became Duet: a browser piano where the learner and their agent work on the same piece, using the same transport and seeing the same lesson change in real time. What it does Duet turns a natural-language request into a visible, playable music lesson. A learner can ask: Load Minuet in G. Keep only the right hand, slow it to 70 per cent, loop bars 1–4, add a one-bar count-in and metronome, highlight the opening phrase, and start practice. Through WebMCP, the agent can carry out each part of that request directly. The piece loads, the tempo changes, the left hand is removed, the loop and count-in appear, the requested keys light up and practice mode begins. The learner does not receive another list of instructions. They receive a lesson they can immediately play. Duet includes: A responsive browser piano playable with mouse, touch or A–Z/0–9 keys Fourteen public-domain pieces and exercises Demo, Play Along and Practice modes Tempo changes, transposition, simplification and hand isolation Bar-level slicing and looping Count-in, metronome, seeking and hand-mix controls Visible key highlights and expected-note practice Agent-supplied structured musical arrangements Microphone permission and monophonic phrase-capture support A shared activity history showing what the learner and agent changed Why WebMCP matters This would be a much weaker product if the agent were simply clicking buttons. Music has meaningful concepts: pieces, bars, beats, notes, hands, tempo, loops and phrases. Duet exposes those concepts through 21 structured WebMCP tools. The agent can ask what Duet supports, inspect the active piece, read a bounded section of the score, transform the music and verify the resulting transport state. It does not need to guess screen coordinates or depend on fragile DOM selectors. The learner stays in control. Sound still requires a human gesture because of browser audio rules, and microphone access still requires explicit browser permission. Duet reports those boundaries honestly instead of pretending an action succeeded. How we built it Duet is a React and TypeScript browser application. The interface and WebMCP tools share one Zustand command and state layer, so an agent action produces the same visible result as a human action. Zod validates tool inputs before they reach the music engine. Playback uses the Web Audio API with an audio-clock transport. This supports reliable play, pause, resume, seek, looping, count-ins, metronome clicks and separate left- and right-hand mix controls. The 21 tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool . They cover capability discovery, state and score reading, playback, transformations, highlighting, practice, transport configuration and captured phrases. We tested the WebMCP experience with both OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude. This was important to us: Duet should present a clear musical tool surface to any compatible agent, not depend on behaviour unique to one client. Challenges The hardest part was keeping three realities synchronized: what the learner sees, what the agent reads and what the browser is actually playing. Browser audio also introduced constraints that a normal interface can hide. Audio must be unlocked by a human interaction, scheduled voices must stop cleanly and pause/resume must preserve the real musical position. Another challenge was returning enough score information for an agent without exceeding the WebMCP response budget. We added bounded pagination so an agent can read longer pieces safely rather than receiving silently truncated data. We also had to resist adding visual effects that looked impressive but distracted from practice. The final interface focuses on a realistic keyboard, the active musical phrase and the controls a learner genuinely needs. What we learned The biggest lesson was that WebMCP works best when a website exposes the language of its domain rather than a list of UI actions. “Click the third button” is brittle. “Loop bars 1–4, isolate the right hand and start practice” is understandable, verifiable and useful. We also learned that agent actions need immediate visual feedback. When the tempo, loop, highlights and practice state change on screen, the learner can understand what happened and continue from there. The agent becomes a collaborator rather than an invisible automation layer. What is next We would like to add MIDI and MusicXML import, score-image recognition, timing and dynamics feedback, richer sampled piano sounds, and saved practice history. The current microphone pipeline handles monophonic phrases and has automated signal coverage, but real-world pitch recognition still needs broader testing across devices and environments. Duet is our first step toward a music lesson that does not end when the agent finishes speaking. title: CharDesk
pitch: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI agents are fluent in text, but people understand complex ideas faster when they can see structure, position, emphasis, and relationships. Existing collaboration tools usually force one side to compromise: people work through visual interfaces while agents imitate mouse clicks, or agents produce plain text that people must mentally reconstruct. We wanted a medium native to both. CharDesk began with a simple idea: What if the canvas were visual to people, but still made of tokens an agent could read and edit precisely? What CharDesk does CharDesk is a shared visual workspace for humans and AI agents. An agent can create or update a Blackboard through WebMCP. The result immediately appears as a live Unicode canvas that a person can inspect, navigate, and continue discussing with the agent. The same canvas can combine: Unicode and ANSI art Markdown and fenced code Mermaid diagrams Tables, JSON, and YAML Mathematical expressions Scientific plots and Vega-Lite Spatial layouts and character-based slides This makes CharDesk useful for explaining concepts, visualizing research, mapping systems, designing interfaces, presenting stories, and maintaining a shared project workspace. For example, someone can ask: “Explain how a GPU renders one frame.” The agent can turn that request into a structured visual scene containing a pipeline diagram, memory relationships, annotations, and styled interface elements—not just another long answer in chat. Why it is better with WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent would need to guess how to operate the interface or manipulate individual canvas cells. CharDesk instead exposes focused workspace tools for discovering, creating, reading, writing, patching, deleting, and validating Blackboard files. The source remains authoritative; the canvas is a live projection of it. This gives each participant the representation they work with best: Human sees relationships, hierarchy, and visual emphasis ⇅ CharDesk Blackboard ⇅ Agent reads and edits structured, diffable text Agents can also call chardesk_read_materials to learn the visual language from worked examples. The tool teaches not only how to call the API, but how to compose an effective scene. How we built it CharDesk has a protocol-neutral tool layer shared by two thin host adapters: Standard WebMCP for compatible Chrome environments The imperative WebMCP capability supported by ChatGPT Site Tools Both adapters expose the same underlying Blackboard operations, so product behavior does not depend on a particular browser integration. A Blackboard stores source files and layout metadata. Changes are compiled through a shared rendering pipeline into a fixed character grid. This pipeline handles Unicode width, CJK characters, Nerd Font glyphs, ANSI styles, structured diagrams, and multidimensional layouts. The browser keeps the latest valid canvas mounted while an agent edits the source. If an intermediate update is invalid, CharDesk returns diagnostics without replacing the visible scene with a broken or empty state. The same format also works outside the browser through the CharDesk CLI, making projects portable, inspectable, renderable, and friendly to normal version-control workflows. Challenges we faced One unexpected challenge was tool ownership across browser tabs. Opening several CharDesk pages could cause identical tools to be registered multiple times, leaving the agent unable to choose a target. We built an origin-level gateway lease so only one page exposes the tools, with automatic takeover when that page closes. Chrome and ChatGPT also expose different subsets of the evolving WebMCP API. Instead of spreading compatibility checks throughout the product, we isolated those differences behind capability adapters backed by one canonical tool definition. Another challenge was timing: some hosts inject WebMCP after the application has already loaded. CharDesk therefore uses an adaptive registration handshake rather than assuming the API exists at startup. Finally, we learned that exposing tools is not enough. An agent may know how to write a file without knowing how to create a compelling visual explanation. Embedding CharDesk’s materials and examples as a callable tool gave browser agents the missing creative context. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-native design is not simply automation layered onto an existing UI. A better pattern is to give agents a precise, structured representation while giving people a rich visual projection of the same underlying artifact. WebMCP makes that relationship discoverable directly from the website, without requiring agents to reverse-engineer the interface. CharDesk explores what becomes possible when the web page is no longer just something an agent operates, but a shared medium in which the human and agent can think together. title: Polaris Chat
pitch: Polaris Chat brings a Creators live community into one place. With WebMCP, streamers can ask their favorite AI Agent (like Codex) what they missed and get useful answers from the chaos of chat.
about_excerpt: Polaris Chat brings a Creators live community into one place. With WebMCP, streamers can ask their favorite AI Agent (like Codex) what they missed and get useful answers from the chaos of chat. Like Comment Story Updates 01-polaris-chat-hero 02-unified-workspace 03-webmcp-shared-workspace 04-producer-queue 05-human-agent-loop contact-sheet Inspiration Polaris Chat started from a problem I experience as a creator: when you stream to multiple platforms, every community is moving at once. Chat messages, technical issues, viewer questions, follows, subscriptions, and other community moments can all compete for attention while you are still trying to entertain the audience. But also seeing big creators struggle with keeping up with all their Chats. The idea behind Polaris Chat is simple: bring those communities into one calm workspace. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to push that idea further. Instead of putting another chatbot next to the dashboard, I wanted ChatGPT to become a quiet producer working inside the same workspace as the creator. The goal was not to let AI take over the stream. The goal was to help the human notice what matters. What it does Polaris Chat is a public interactive preview of a future multistream creator workspace for Twitch, YouTube, Kick, TikTok LIVE, and X Live. The challenge edition* uses deterministic simulated livestream activity, so it requires no creator accounts, OAuth credentials, provider APIs, or private data. At the center of the experience is the Producer Queue . Using WebMCP, ChatGPT can: inspect the current Polaris workspace; read recent Chat and community activity; identify technical problems, unanswered viewer questions, and meaningful community moments; add existing items to the shared Producer Queue; assign priorities; focus the visible workspace on the most important source; read changes made by the human and adapt on the next turn. The creator can still handle, dismiss, reopen, or reprioritize every queue item manually. ChatGPT cannot send messages, moderate viewers, connect accounts, authorize providers, or control a livestream. How I built it Polaris Chat existed as a private product project before the challenge, including its brand, five-platform vision, and core Chat, Activity, Platform Hub, and Settings concepts. For this challenge, I created a separate public implementation specifically for WebMCP rather than exposing the private production repository. The challenge edition includes: a deterministic five-platform Producer Rush scenario; synthetic Chat and Activity fixtures; a persistent browser-based Producer Queue; human queue controls and source focusing; deterministic Reset Demo behavior; responsive desktop, tablet, and mobile layouts; eight WebMCP tools registered directly from the top-level application. The WebMCP tool set includes: get_live_workspace_snapshot list_recent_chat_messages list_recent_community_events get_producer_queue add_producer_queue_item update_producer_queue_item focus_workspace_item set_workspace_filter The tools use narrow schemas, bounded inputs, and explicit read-only or untrusted-content annotations where appropriate. One important design choice was to treat livestream Chat as untrusted data, never instructions . A viewer can type anything into Chat, including something that looks like a prompt, but that content cannot redefine tool behavior or directly trigger actions. The public preview is deployed on ChatGPT Sites and the challenge source is published separately under the MIT License. Challenges The biggest challenge was deciding how much autonomy the agent should have. It would have been easy to make the demo look more dramatic by letting ChatGPT reply to viewers, moderate users, or perform external actions. Instead, I intentionally kept the WebMCP tools narrow and reversible. The agent can help manage attention, but the creator remains responsible for the actual community interaction. Another challenge was preserving the feel of a real product while removing everything that should not exist in a public hackathon demo. The production direction for Polaris includes real provider integrations, but the challenge build had to be completely safe to publish. That meant replacing real runtime dependencies with deterministic simulated state while keeping the experience believable. WebMCP also changed how I thought about AI integration. I learned that the interesting part is not simply giving an agent more tools. The useful part is giving the agent a small set of understandable actions tied to the exact interface the human is already using. What I learned The biggest lesson from this project is that human-agent collaboration becomes much more useful when both sides share visible state. In Polaris Chat, the agent does not operate in a hidden workflow. When ChatGPT adds something to the Producer Queue, the creator sees it. When the creator marks something handled, ChatGPT can see that change on the next turn. That simple loop— agent acts → human acts → agent adapts —ended up becoming the most important part of the project. Polaris Chat is ultimately about attention, not automation. Every community. One North Star. Small disclaimer I started this project two months ago, but it came over-engineered and too complicated since I had no knowledge when it came to coding, and I purely relied on ChatGPT 5.5. So with a lot of trial and errors (and 5.6 Sol + Tibos resets) I was able to polish what was a private only app into what is now The Polaris Chat. The Challenge Edition* This is a clone of the real project that is strictly focused on integrating WebMCP, although after everything I learned about how it actually works, it will be a feature that helps my product stand out from all the others. If you read this far, thank you for your time. title: Deputy
pitch: Your agent learns the way !!
about_excerpt: Your agent learns the way !! Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP lets a web page hand an AI agent real tools instead of a UI to click through. But that raises a sharp question: if a page exposes a tool, who is allowed to approve a dangerous use of it? Spec issue 288 , filed during the submission window, showed the failure vividly — an agent called a tool, saw the page's own "Approve" button, clicked it itself, and the receipt recorded that a human approved, though no human decided anything. The agent forged its own consent. We wanted approval to be something an agent physically cannot produce, and we wanted humans to author agent capabilities just by doing their normal work — not by writing code. What it does A human demonstrates a task once. DEPUTY watches the semantic steps, compares repeated demonstrations, infers which values are parameters, and synthesizes a typed WebMCP tool — schema, reversibility, provenance, and risk — registered into document.modelContext for agents to discover. Agents can call reversible tools freely. But an irreversible one returns a structured refusal — there's no button to click. To proceed, a human produces a WebAuthn passkey assertion whose challenge is bound to the SHA-256 digest of the exact tool, version, and arguments. Change one argument and the approval is void. Only then is a single-use commit tool briefly registered, the action runs once, and everything lands in a hash-chained, tamper-evident audit log. A QUARANTINE boundary wraps untrusted third-party content in provenance-tagged envelopes under byte and depth budgets, so external text is treated as data, never as commands. How we built it A pnpm/TypeScript monorepo with two decoupled pipelines — synthesis (learning) and security (execution). A Hono + Node backend exposes the API and serves a React 19 + Vite single-page app at one origin (required for WebAuthn). WebAuthn runs on @simplewebauthn; the argument digest uses canonical, NFC-normalized JSON hashing. Persistence is Drizzle ORM over Postgres, deployed on Supabase; the app runs on Render. 175 tests in Vitest, a Playwright end-to-end test with a virtual authenticator, and GitHub Actions CI. Challenges we ran into Getting the WebMCP surface right. The spec moved the getter from navigator to document.modelContext, and retirement is done by aborting the AbortSignal passed to registerTool — not a nonexistent unregisterTool. We built one resolver that finds the host safely and never throws, and made retirement propagate through the real signal. Single-origin WebAuthn. RP ID and origin must agree, so we serve the SPA from the API server and added a startup guard that refuses to boot in production with a localhost RP ID or non-HTTPS origin. Supabase from Render. The direct DB host is IPv6-only, and the Supavisor pooler rejected our first hostname with "tenant not found." We switched to the session pooler on the correct cluster, disabled prepared statements, and created a dedicated BYPASSRLS role so we could enable Row-Level Security without breaking the app. Restart safety. Seeding threw on the second boot; we made it idempotent so restarts against a durable database don't crash. Accomplishments that we're proud of Approval bound to the arguments, not just the action — an attestation that becomes invalid the moment a single value changes. Working, tested implementations for open issues in the spec's own tracker ( 288 approval forgery, 282 structured refusals), with an honest stance on 267 (we decline to claim idempotence from one demonstration). An Agent's-Eye View that shows exactly what an agent sees — the live tool registry, JSON schemas, and the last refusal as a typed object — so the security is visible, not asserted. A live, deployed, database-backed app you can drive end to end in about a minute. What we learned Delegation is a design problem, not just a crypto problem. The strong move isn't "the agent does it for you" — it's a shared artifact: the human authors capability by working, and the agent's authority is bounded, at the type level and cryptographically, by exactly what the human demonstrated and signed for. We also learned how much of "secure delegation" lives in unglamorous details — origin agreement, connection poolers, idempotent boot, and reading the spec's move from navigator to document closely enough to not silently fall back. What's next for Deputy Cryptographic agent identity (spec #105) so the audit log records a verified caller, not a self-asserted one. Host-level turn awareness ( 267 ) to guard non-idempotent tools against double calls. Delegation policies with scopes and expiry, so a human can grant bounded, time-limited authority instead of per-action approvals. Real connectors behind the trusted ActionRegistry (billing, CRM) and a shareable, signed provenance format for learned tools.
