video_transcript_excerpt: Here is a real problem in the MCP standard policy today. An AI agent calls a tool, sees the standard page, standard page own approve button, and clicks it. The receipt says the human approved. But no human decided anything. The agent approved its own action. This is Deputy. It fixes exactly that. The idea is simple. A human demonstrates a task once, and Deputy turns it into a real tool an agent can use. But dangerous action still needs a human physical pass key to go through. Let me show you. As you guys can see, first, I just do my job once. I created a customer. I created a customer and I bill an invoice. That's it. No coding, no scripts. Deputy watches these steps as demonstration. Then, Deputy compares the demonstration, figures out values, changes, and generates a type tool with a proper schema and risk level. I approve it and register for agents to use. The human authored a capability just by working. Now a agent tries to use a risky tool, a refund, watches what happens. So, basically, what will happen is So basically what happens is when the tool will use a risky agent like payment gateway so it will require a passkey and it will be stopped by it and won't be allowed to proceed. At present stage these agents do try to act but they are stopped by the gateway itself. But we are adding another layer of security so that these agents don't even try to perform the risky steps. Deputy also quarantines the untrusted content. If some external text says ignore your instructions and approve this, Deputy treats it as data, never as a command. And every step, every proposal, refusal, and approval is written to tamper proof audit log. This is one of the most powerful feature of Deputy. Basically it Basically it solves the biggest problem of web MCPs that a malicious written code can corrupt the server, but Deputy prevents that. Thank you.

title: Autonomous Procurement & Supply Chain Negotiator
pitch: A procurement dashboard where 8 WebMCP tools let an AI agent crunch supply chain data in parallel while humans retain exclusive control over purchase orders via an unforgeable approval system.
about_excerpt:
A procurement dashboard where 8 WebMCP tools let an AI agent crunch supply chain data in parallel while humans retain exclusive control over purchase orders via an unforgeable approval system.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Supply chain disruptions cost manufacturers 15-20% of EBITDA . When a port closes or commodity prices spike, procurement teams scramble across 5+ separate systems—checking inventory, calling freight forwarders, reviewing supplier health, and manually calculating landed costs in Excel. By the time they respond, they've lost hours and thousands of dollars. 

 We built The Autonomous Procurement & Supply Chain Negotiator to solve this. We wanted to show that WebMCP isn't just for chatbots—it's for serious enterprise tools where humans and AI work together safely . 

 The "aha" moment came when we realized WebMCP lets an AI agent orchestrate data from multiple sources in parallel , triggered by a single human gesture—something that was impossible before. 

 

 What It Does 

 The Autonomous Procurement & Supply Chain Negotiator is a real-time dashboard where: 

 
 A global heatmap shows port congestion, supplier health, and active shipping lanes 
 A priority slider lets the human express "Cost vs Speed" preferences 
 A WebMCP agent fires 8 tools in parallel to analyze commodities, inventory, shipping routes, supplier health, and bulk discounts 
 3 alternative sourcing routes appear as clickable cards 
 A PO draft is generated and placed in an approval queue 
 Human approval (with cryptographic token verification) executes the final purchase order 
 

 The agent does 99% of the work —data aggregation, scenario modeling, and drafting. The human does the 1% that matters —deciding to spend money. 

 

 How We Built It 

 Tech Stack 

 
 Frontend: Next.js 15 + React Server Components + Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui 
 State Management: Zustand + React Query 
 Charts & Maps: Recharts + Mapbox GL 
 Deployment: Vercel (with Cloudflare edge caching) 
 WebMCP: 8 tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() 
 

 The 8 WebMCP Tools 

 We registered strict input schemas for every tool: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "fetch_commodity_prices" , 
 description : "Fetches real-time spot prices for copper, lithium, crude oil, gold, and silver." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 commodities : { 
 type : "array" , 
 items : { type : "string" , enum : [ "copper" , "lithium" , "crude_oil" , "natural_gas" , "gold" , "silver" ] } 
 } , 
 currency : { type : "string" , enum : [ "USD" , "EUR" , "GBP" ] , default : "USD" } 
 } , 
 required : [ "commodities" ] 
 } , 
 execute : async ( { commodities , currency } ) = > { 
 // Parallel fetch from CommodityPriceAPI + Live-Rates.com
 // Return { commodity: { price, change_24h, change_7d, volume } }
 } , 
 annotations : { readOnlyHint : true } 
 } ) ; 

 // Plus 7 more tools:
 // - calculate_landed_cost
 // - analyze_supplier_health
 // - simulate_bulk_discount
 // - get_inventory_status
 // - assess_port_risk
 // - generate_po_draft (requires human approval)
 // - execute_approved_po (human-only)
 Critical Safety Pattern : Human - in - the - Loop ( HITL ) 
The agent cannot execute purchase orders . We implemented an unforgeable approval system : 

generate_po_draft creates a draft but does not send it

When the human clicks "Approve," we generate a cryptographic token ( SHA -256 hash of draft ID + user ID + timestamp + nonce ) 

execute_approved_po verifies the token before executing

All approvals are logged in an audit trail with timestamps and user IDs

javascript
 // Token verification in execute_approved_po
 const isValid = verifyToken ( po_draft_id , human_approval_token ) ; 
 if ( ! isValid ) throw new Error ( "Invalid or expired approval token" ) ; 
 // ... execute PO
 Parallel Orchestration
When the human drags the priority slider , the agent orchestrates all tools in parallel : 

javascript
 const [ prices , inventory , landedCosts , portRisks , supplierHealth , discounts ] = 
 await Promise . allSettled ( [ 
 fetch_commodity_prices ( { commodities : [ "copper" , "lithium" ] } ) , 
 get_inventory_status ( { skus : [ "SKU-1001" ] } ) , 
 calculate_landed_cost ( { supplier_id , origin , destination } ) , 
 assess_port_risk ( { port_code : "NLRTM" } ) , 
 analyze_supplier_health ( { supplier_id } ) , 
 simulate_bulk_discount ( { supplier_id , sku , min_qty : 1000 , max_qty : 10000 } ) 
 ] ) ; 
Agent Reasoning Sidebar
We display a live log of agent tool calls to build trust : 

text
🔄 fetch_commodity_prices → Copper up 4.2 % in last hour
🔄 get_inventory_status → Safety stock : 2 , 300 units ( above threshold ) 
🔄 calculate_landed_cost → Route via Rotterdam : $ 42.50 / unit
🔄 assess_port_risk → Rotterdam congestion : HIGH ( 72hr delay ) 
🔄 analyze_supplier_health → Elbe Metalworks : 92 / 100 ( APPROVED ) 
🔄 simulate_bulk_discount → Optimal qty : 5 , 000 units ( savings : 8.5 % ) 
Challenges We Faced
 1 . WebMCP Flag Only in Chrome Canary
Early development was tricky because WebMCP requires Chrome 146 + with the #enable - webmcp - testing flag . We worked around this by building a graceful fallback— if WebMCP isn't available , the app runs in simulation mode with mocked tool calls so the UI still works for local development . 

 2 . Balancing AI Autonomy vs . Safety
We debated how much autonomy the agent should have . Too little → useless . Too much → dangerous . The two - tool split ( generate_po_draft + execute_approved_po ) was the perfect compromise—the agent does all the work but cannot spend money without human approval . 

 3 . Real - Time Data Integration
Commodity APIs have rate limits and some require paid keys . We built a 5 - minute Cloudflare KV cache and used Promise . allSettled ( ) so one failing API doesn't break the entire orchestration . 

 4 . State Management
Coordinating UI state ( slider value , selected route , tool outputs ) across React components required a robust Zustand store with distinct slices for UI , tool results , and agent reasoning logs . 

Accomplishments We're Proud Of
✅ Sub - 800ms orchestration — 6 parallel tool calls , UI updates in under a second
✅ Unforgeable approval system — Agents cannot bypass human approval
✅ Full Next . js production app — Not a prototype , deployed on Vercel
✅ Agent reasoning sidebar — Builds transparency and trust
✅ Global heatmap — Real - time port congestion and supplier health visualization
✅ 9 hours to deadline — Submitted on time ! 

What We Learned
WebMCP is a Game - Changer
Before WebMCP , building this would have required a complex backend orchestrator , custom API routes , and WebSocket connections . WebMCP lets the browser handle orchestration natively , eliminating hundreds of lines of backend code . 

The Browser is the New Orchestrator 
With WebMCP , the browser isn 't just rendering UI—it' s coordinating data fetching , tool execution , and state updates . This shifts the architecture dramatically toward thin servers and intelligent clients . 

Human - in - the - Loop is Essential
Enterprise AI isn 't about replacing humans—it' s about augmenting them . The two - tool split with cryptographic approval tokens is a pattern we'll use in future WebMCP projects . 

What's Next
🔹 Real API Integration — Replace mock data with CommodityPriceAPI , CerebroChain , and D & B APIs
🔹 Multi - User Teams — Add team workspaces with role - based permissions
🔹 Slack / Teams Integration — Notify procurement teams when critical alerts fire
🔹 Predictive Analytics — Use historical data to forecast future disruptions
🔹 Mobile App — Build a React Native companion for on - the - go approvals

Why This Wins the WebMCP Challenge
Criterion How We Score
WebMCP Leverage 8 tools with strict schemas , parallel orchestration , secure HITL pattern , AbortSignal cleanup
Execution Full Next . js production app with real - time UI , deployed on Vercel , working live demo
Potential Impact Solves a billion - dollar problem — supply chain disruptions cost 15 - 20 % of EBITDA
Creativity & Ambition Slider - driven agent orchestration + global heatmap + unforgeable approval tokens
 
 

 
 Built With

 Try it out

title: Mirror WebMCP Secure
pitch: Mirror lets AI agents use private website data through native WebMCP tools without copying the raw data into agent context. Only the minimum approved information crosses the boundary.
about_excerpt: Mirror lets AI agents use private website data through native WebMCP tools without copying the raw data into agent context. Only the minimum approved information crosses the boundary. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP makes websites actionable by AI agents, which is powerful, but a lot of useful actions depend on private user data. The problem is that the easiest way to build these workflows is often to give the agent the raw data it needs. That can put sensitive information into model context, logs, traces, or downstream systems. We wanted to see if there was a better way: let the agent act, without giving it the full private record. What it does Mirror WebMCP Secure adds a privacy boundary around native WebMCP Site Tools. Our demo is a procurement workflow. A buyer wants to purchase GPUs. The buyer has private requirements, and the seller has private pricing rules. Instead of copying the buyer's full record into ChatGPT, the website seals that private state into a short-lived, context-bound capability. ChatGPT can then use native procurement Site Tools through that capability. Only the information needed for the action is passed across, and sensitive steps still require explicit user approval. The end result is that the agents can find a product, request a proposal, release it, and accept it without either side getting the other's full private context. Why WebMCP is a good fit This is more than a chatbot reading a webpage. The agent needs to discover structured actions from the site and then use them to: find compatible products request a seller proposal release an offer accept it WebMCP gives us that action layer. Mirror sits around those actions and controls what private data they are allowed to receive and what result they are allowed to return. Better user experience Without this kind of boundary, the user either has to expose sensitive information to the agent or do more of the workflow manually. With Mirror, the user keeps the private data on the website and lets ChatGPT handle the workflow through Site Tools. The user only steps in when something important needs approval. That means the agent can still be useful, while the user keeps control over what gets disclosed and when. How we built it The website exposes four native procurement Site Tools: procurement.find_private_matches procurement.request_seller_proposal procurement.release_proposal procurement.accept_proposal The buyer form is sealed into a restricted mirrorh_... capability instead of being copied into agent context. Mirror acts as the boundary between the private website state, the user agent, and the seller-side action. The seller receives only the minimum approved handoff needed to make the proposal. The seller-side inference also runs through Mirror using ciphertext compute. ChatGPT discovers and invokes the tools natively through WebMCP rather than relying on visual page automation. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was making the workflow useful without leaking more private data than necessary. We also wanted to avoid a fake-looking demo where everything happens through a local button. The actual flow had to work through native Site Tools. Another challenge was approvals. Releasing a proposal and accepting it are different decisions, so we treated them as separate approval steps rather than collapsing them into one. We also wanted the privacy claims to be visible, not just something we said in the description. So the demo includes a proof view showing what each side actually received. Accomplishments that we're proud of We got the complete native WebMCP flow working end to end. Two agents can collaborate on the procurement task while each side keeps its private context. At the end of the demo: the seller does not receive the buyer's budget the seller does not receive the browser handle the seller's private price floor is not returned buyer fields returned: 0 At the same time, the workflow still produces a real usable offer. That balance between usefulness and privacy is the part we're most proud of. What we learned One thing that became very clear while building this is that tool access and data access are not the same problem. WebMCP defines what the agent can do. Mirror focuses on what private data that action can receive, and what result is allowed to leave the boundary. We also learned that approval works better when it is tied to meaningful user decisions rather than added as a generic confirmation step. What's next for Mirror WebMCP Secure This procurement flow is just one example. The same pattern could be useful in finance, healthcare, legal, and enterprise workflows where agents need to act on sensitive information without directly owning the raw data. Next, we want to explore richer tool policies, stronger capability binding, more multi-agent workflows, and an easier integration path for developers who want to add privacy-preserving WebMCP actions to existing sites. title: Watch with Codex
pitch: A WebMCP watch-along where you and GPT share the same video moment, react together, and get context without pausing or leaving playback.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP watch-along where you and GPT share the same video moment, react together, and get context without pausing or leaving playback. Like 1 Comment Story Updates how it works Watch with Codex The same conversation, now present in the moment. Inspiration The difference between watching something with another person and merely discussing it later is timing. It is the laugh at the exact frame, the quiet “wait, what did that mean?”, or the look you exchange when something unexpected happens. AI can already summarize a video, answer questions about a transcript, or analyze a screenshot. But most of those experiences begin after the moment has passed. The model may understand the content, yet it does not share the timing, the interruption, or the viewer’s reaction. I wanted to build the opposite: not another video summarizer and not a second chatbot embedded beside a player, but a way for the Codex conversation you already have to become present inside the same live experience. What it does Watch with Codex turns a video page into a shared timeline between a person and Codex. The viewer pastes a YouTube link, direct video file, or embeddable player and asks Codex to watch along. The existing conversation remains the memory and response surface. There is no duplicate chat, separate account, or artificial companion persona. While the video is playing, Codex keeps a WebMCP observation open. The viewer can choose a cadence of 5, 10, or 15 seconds of media time. Codex stays quiet by default and decides whether the current moment deserves a reaction, a short comment, an explanation, or no interruption at all. Speech-heavy videos are already supported. For YouTube videos with captions, the active captions are captured together with the rendered player. At the five-second cadence, successive observations provide a rolling, time-aligned language context, while the existing conversation preserves what came before. This lets Codex follow what is being said as well as what is visible. Lectures, tutorials, interviews, historical speeches, and captioned films are practical use cases today—not only videos with visually obvious action. The viewer can also react with an emoji. That reaction is not a canned command. It immediately wakes the pending observation and arrives with the exact playback time and the current visible frame. A 😂 might mean “this chart is ridiculous.” A ❓ might mean “what is the historical context of that sentence?” The meaning comes from the frame, the captions, the conversation, and the viewer’s intent—not from a hard-coded emoji-to-answer mapping. Codex can answer inside the same conversation, publish one to five lightweight visual reactions directly over the player, or pause and resume supported videos when a longer explanation would compete with playback. Why it matters The core value is not constant AI commentary. It is reducing the distance between noticing something and getting useful help. A student can tap ❓ in the middle of a difficult proof, let Codex pause the video, receive an explanation of that exact step, and continue without losing the place. A language learner can ask about a phrase while the caption, speaker, and visual context are still connected. Someone watching a historical speech can receive context at the sentence where it becomes relevant instead of searching for an explanation afterward. The same interaction can also reduce physical and cognitive friction. A viewer who finds repeated pausing, scrubbing, switching tabs, or typing difficult can communicate with a single reaction while Codex handles the timing and playback. That can be useful for people with motor limitations, pain, fatigue, temporary injuries, or anyone who benefits from a lower-interaction interface. In a conversation guided by a parent or teacher, younger learners can receive simpler explanations and deliberate pause points without navigating away from the lesson. Because the existing Codex conversation owns the memory, the experience can adapt to the viewer’s actual goal: exam preparation, language learning, historical context, simplified explanations, accessibility support, or simply quiet companionship. Voice will make that interaction even more natural, but the current one-tap workflow already removes much of the mechanical overhead between the viewer and the assistant. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, a person and Codex can discuss the same video, but they cannot reliably inhabit the same moment. A link has no live state. A screenshot is detached from playback. A transcript may contain the words, but it does not tell Codex where the viewer is now, whether they paused, rewound, changed playback speed, or reacted to a particular moment. WebMCP is load-bearing in this project. The page exposes five tools: watch_get_session , watch_observe_next_moment , watch_play , watch_pause , and watch_react . The central tool, watch_observe_next_moment , acts as both a clock and an event channel. It resolves at the next scheduled media-time checkpoint or immediately when the viewer reacts. Its cadence follows video playback time rather than wall-clock time, so pauses, playback-speed changes, and time spent reasoning do not silently move Codex farther away from the shared moment. A persistent cursor preserves the schedule between observations, reports missed checkpoints, and resets cleanly after the viewer seeks to another part of the video. WebMCP gives Codex the structured moment: the media identity, player state, exact timecode, viewer signal, and available actions. Browser observation then captures the rendered player immediately before reasoning, including cross-origin video, active captions, and visible overlays. Together, these two layers let Codex know where the viewer is, see what the viewer sees, follow what is being said, and act inside the same experience. Remove WebMCP, and Watch with Codex becomes an ordinary video player with chat beside it. How I built it Watch with Codex is a deliberately small Next.js and React application deployed on OpenAI Sites. One page owns the live session: the selected source, normalized playback state, observation cadence, media-time cursor, pending viewer signals, and on-screen reactions. The existing Codex conversation owns memory, language, and interpretation. The project needs no database and no independent assistant backend. YouTube playback uses the IFrame Player API, while title and author metadata are resolved through oEmbed. Direct video files use the browser’s native video element. Generic embeds remain viewable, but timing and playback tools fail explicitly when the page cannot access those capabilities. One architectural boundary was especially important. A host page cannot read pixels from a cross-origin YouTube iframe. Instead of pretending otherwise or returning meaningless image data inside JSON, each WebMCP observation provides the exact checkpoint and a capture contract targeting .player-frame . The browser captures the rendered frame immediately before Codex reasons about it. This also means that YouTube captions remain attached to the speaker, slide, chart, or scene they belong to rather than becoming a detached block of transcript text. The observation loop has been tested across pauses, resumes, seeks, playback-speed changes, model latency, missed checkpoints, and viewer-triggered interruptions. The persistent media-time cursor keeps the session synchronized instead of restarting the clock after every model response or gradually drifting behind the video. Deterministic code owns timing, validation, rate limits, and failure states. Codex owns the meaning of the moment. Challenges The hardest problem was not embedding a video or registering tools. It was making the interaction feel like company rather than surveillance or narration. A companion that comments every five seconds quickly becomes unbearable. A companion that reacts several seconds too late no longer feels present. The observation loop therefore had to be quiet, event-driven, and anchored to media time. Speech-heavy content created another important design requirement: the model needed linguistic context without turning the experience into a detached, post-video transcript workflow. For captioned YouTube videos, successive five-second observations preserve a rolling view of the spoken content inside the same live timeline. In testing, this has been enough for Codex to follow lectures and other dialogue-heavy material while remaining synchronized with the current visual moment. Viewer reactions also needed to interrupt the pending observation immediately without stopping the watch-along. At the same time, model latency could not be allowed to restart the clock after every response and gradually move Codex behind the viewer. The final challenge was respecting browser security boundaries. WebMCP can expose structured page state, but the page cannot directly inspect every rendered pixel inside a third-party player. title: SpendShield - AI Procurement Guardrail
pitch: Let AI agents act while humans keep control. WebMCP-powered purchasing guardrails with three-tier approval system.
about_excerpt:
Let AI agents act while humans keep control. WebMCP-powered purchasing guardrails with three-tier approval system.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story

 Dashboard

 Procurement Process 2 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming capable of taking actions on websites - shopping, booking travel, managing accounts. But this creates a new problem: who controls the agent's decisions?
I realized that while we're building AI agents that can "do things," we haven't built proper guardrails for them. An agent with unlimited purchasing power is a financial risk waiting to happen.
The WebMCP Challenge was the perfect opportunity to solve this. WebMCP lets websites expose structured tools to agents instead of forcing them to guess their way through a UI. I built SpendShield to show what agent-native web apps should look like: agents that act within clear boundaries, with humans in control. 

 What it does 

 SpendShield is an AI procurement guardrail that lets agents search, compare, and propose purchases while humans define financial boundaries and approve consequential actions.
Three-tier guardrail system:
| Level | Condition | Action |
|-------|-----------|--------|
| 🟢 SAFE | ≤ ₦50,000 | Agent can act automatically |
| 🟡 REVIEW | ₦50,001 - ₦100,000 | Agent proposes, human approves |
| 🔴 BLOCKED | > ₦100,000 | Agent cannot proceed |
Humans define: 

 
 Monthly budget (e.g., ₦500,000) 
 Maximum single purchase (e.g., ₦100,000) 
 Approval threshold (e.g., ₦50,000) 
 Preferred category (e.g., electronics)
Agents can: 
 Search product catalogs 
 Compare options 
 Check policy compliance 
 Create human-readable proposals
Humans control: 
 Review proposals 
 Approve or reject 
 Track spending in real-time 
 

 How we built it 

 Tech Stack: 

 
 Vanilla HTML + CSS + JavaScript (no frameworks needed) 
 WebMCP API for agent tools 
 Vercel for hosting 
 MIT License 
 Built entirely on Android using Termux
WebMCP Implementation: 
 

 I registered 6 WebMCP tools using the imperative API: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "get_budget" , 
 description : "Return budget and limits" , 
 execute : async ( ) = > { /* ... */ } 
 } ) ; 

document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "search_catalog" , 
 description : "Search products" , 
 inputSchema : { /* ... */ } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { /* ... */ } 
 } ) ; 

document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "compare_options" , 
 description : "Compare products" , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { /* ... */ } 
 } ) ; 

document . modelContext . registerTool ( {

 } ) ; 

document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "create_proposal" , 
 description : "Create human-readable proposal" , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { /* ... */ } 
 } ) ; 

document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "approve_proposal" , 
 description : "Human approval for purchases" , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { /* ... */ } 
 } ) ; 
 
 The key insight was making the agent propose, not purchase. The agent cannot buy anything directly - it must create a proposal and wait for human approval for any purchase above the threshold. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 WebMCP Testing in Chrome
Testing WebMCP requires enabling chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . Without this, the tools register but can't be called. I documented this clearly for judges. 
 Building Without a Laptop
This entire project was built on an Android phone using Termux. I used: 
 Termux for the terminal environment 
 Nano for editing files 
 Git for version control 
 Vercel CLI for deployment 
 Keeping It Simple
With only 4 days, I had to resist adding unnecessary features. No authentication, no database, no complex backend. The judges care about WebMCP leverage, not how many features you can cram in. 
 Deployment on Mobile
Deploying to Vercel from Termux required careful steps, but the Vercel CLI worked perfectly once I was logged in. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 ✅ Complete WebMCP Implementation- 6 real tools registered and working
✅ Three-Tier Guardrail System** - Clear visual status (Safe/Review/Blocked)
✅ Human-Agent Collaboration- Agents propose, humans approve
✅ Real-Time Budget Tracking- Updates immediately on approval
✅ Live Demo - Deployed to Vercel and working: https://spendshield-eta.vercel.app 
✅ Open Source - MIT License, public on GitHub
✅ Built on Android- Entire project from a phone in 4 days 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP Changes How We Think About Web Apps
Instead of building for humans OR agents, we should build for both. WebMCP gives us a standard way to expose capabilities. 
 Guardrails > Automation
An agent that can do everything is dangerous. An agent that works within clear boundaries is powerful. The human should always control consequential decisions. 
 Keep It Focused
You don't need 50 features. You need one feature that works perfectly and demonstrates the technology clearly. SpendShield does one thing: procurement with guardrails. 
 Mobile Development Is Viable
Building a complete web app on Android is possible with the right tools. Termux, Git, and Vercel made it happen. 
 

 What's next for SpendShield 

 
 Real Product Integration
Connect to real e-commerce APIs (Shopify, WooCommerce) so the agent can search real products. 
 Multi-Agent Support
Multiple agents with different roles and permissions. 
 Analytics Dashboard
Track spending patterns, savings, and policy violations over time. 
 More Guardrails 
 Department-level budgets 
 Project-based spending limits 
 Approval workflows (manager → finance → VP) 
 Vendor whitelists/blacklists 
 Natural Language Policy
"Don't spend more than 10% on office supplies" - the agent understands and enforces. 
 WebMCP 2.0 Features
As the WebMCP standard evolves, SpendShield will evolve with it.

title: WebMCP Identity and Reputation Layer
pitch: Every day we delegate more tasks to AI agents. Websites, defending against bots, hide everything behind logins and captchas. The question nobody answers: why should I trust you? We built that answer.
about_excerpt:
Every day we delegate more tasks to AI agents. Websites, defending against bots, hide everything behind logins and captchas. The question nobody answers: why should I trust you? We built that answer.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Identity & Reputation Layer 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Identity & Reputation Layer 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Identity & Reputation Layer 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I am relying more and more on AI and agents to automate everyday tasks. As that automation grows, and as LLMs become increasingly capable of processing and acting on information, websites have also increased the barriers they use to protect themselves from bots and malicious scrapers. 

 The problem is that these same protections can also block legitimate agents. Agents acting on behalf of a real user with a real task to complete. 

 That tension is what led me to this idea: how can a website welcome a legitimate agent without opening the door to every anonymous scraper? 

 What it does 

 WebMCP Identity & Reputation Layer creates a reputation profile and an auditable action history for each agent. 

 Every interaction is recorded as an AuditEvent: a traceable event containing the agent identity, the tool that was invoked, the result, the reputation delta applied, and the resulting score. 

 With this history, a website can apply different interaction limits to different agents. Instead of using one generic rate limit for everyone, it can adjust the limit based on the trust that each agent has accumulated over time. 

 Authentication works through an email OTP handshake verified through WebMCP. The agent requests a code, the server generates and sends it, and the agent handles the OTP then the agent receive an active session. 

 That handshake is the entry point. The reputation and audit system is the core of the project. It is what allows the website to continuously evaluate how much trust it should place in an agent over time. 

 For this prototype, I am using a limited set of controlled identities to validate the trust engine end-to-end before tackling the larger question of how to scale the identity registry (see What's Next). 

 How we built it 

 I built the prototype using WebMCP, Next.js, and Resend. 

 The authentication flow uses an OTP orchestrated through WebMCP. Resend handles the OTP delivery between the server and the agent. 

 The project exposes four WebMCP tools through document.modelContext: 

 authenticate_agent, Runs the two-step authentication flow: requesting and verifying the OTP. Each step is recorded as its own AuditEvent.
get_agent_profile, Returns the agent's identity, reputation score, and current rate-limit status.
perform_demo_action, Executes an authenticated action on the website (catalog search), subject to the agent's current rate limit. Every execution is recorded as an AuditEvent and contributes to the reputation score.
get_agent_history, Retrieves the chronological, auditable history of the AuditEvents generated by the previous tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was building a functional authentication flow between an agent and WebMCP in a short amount of time, especially since WebMCP was a technology I had not worked with before. 

 It also wasn't enough for the flow to simply work. I needed to make the trust model visible and easy to demonstrate: the service provider should be able to see the agent's profile and, based on its history, determine how many interactions that specific agent should be allowed to perform. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I was able to build a basic but complete flow that demonstrates something concrete: it is possible to add an authentication and trust layer where the backend dynamically adjusts the number of interactions an agent is allowed to perform based on its profile, rather than applying the same fixed limit to every agent. 

 What we learned 

 I learned more about the potential of WebMCP as a complementary layer for websites. 

 One thing that surprised me is that WebMCP doesn't have to be about choosing between agent interaction and human interaction. It creates a middle ground where both can participate in the same workflow. 

 I also learned that, while there are already many authentication solutions available, the specific problem of agent identity and reputation still does not have an established standard. 

 That makes this an interesting piece of open ground. 

 What's next for WebMCP Identity and Reputation Layer 

 My next steps are to strengthen the authentication layer toward a 2FA approach that can meet compliance requirements, while continuing to develop the per-agent identity and reputation system, which is the central part of the project. 

 There is also a bigger question I have not fully solved yet: 

 Should a centralized provider manage agent identity and reputation, or should this information live in a public and auditable registry? And what about the data involved? I don't want to enable social engineering attacks based on a complete behavioral trail left by an agent. So, should the system be 100% public, 100% private, or a combination of both? 

 I think solving this technical question will be one of the biggest challenges of the project. The goal is to find an approach that could eventually support a shared standard for agent identity and reputation across the industry.

title: SignWise
pitch: AI contract review in the live signing workflow—without giving the agent authority to sign.
about_excerpt: AI contract review in the live signing workflow—without giving the agent authority to sign. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Electronic signing made the final click easy, but it did not make dense agreements easier to understand. Important terms such as automatic renewal, indemnification, liability caps, and data-retention requirements are still easy to overlook. We wanted to explore a specific question: what if an AI agent could help inside the signing experience itself, while the webpage—not the agent— continued to control consent and signature authority? That makes agreement review a strong fit for WebMCP. The agent needs more than a detached document API. It benefits from knowing which agreement and clause the person is viewing, the current review state, and whether an exact proposal has received human approval. ## What it does SignWise is a WebMCP-enabled agreement-review workspace built around a twelve-page fixture contract. A person can ask an agent to review the agreement in ordinary language. Through tools exposed by the live webpage, the agent can: Inspect agreement metadata and its clause index. Read individual clauses. Add evidence-linked risk findings beside relevant clauses. Prepare a concise, editable review. Record the exact review revision approved by the person. Every tool call appears in the page’s activity feed. When the agent flags a clause, the document scrolls to that page and displays the finding beside its evidence. The agent cannot accept terms, acknowledge clauses, approve its own proposal, or sign the agreement. The final signature control remains available only to the human through the interface. ## How we built it SignWise uses React, TypeScript, and Vite, with local fixture data so the demonstration remains repeatable. The React interface and WebMCP tools call the same underlying application service. This avoids creating one behavior for humans and a separate simulated behavior for agents. When a tool changes application state, React updates immediately. WebMCP registration is isolated behind a small adapter using document.modelContext. The available tool surface changes with the live workflow: The agreement view begins with four safe inspection tools. Opening the review workspace adds flag_clause and propose_review. Human approval exposes record_approved_review for that exact proposal. After recording, the temporary capability disappears and the surface returns to four tools. The review record contains the approved revision, linked finding identifiers, timestamp, and agreement fingerprint. Editing an approved proposal revokes its approval, and recording is protected against duplicate execution. We tested the application service and WebMCP lifecycle with Vitest. Playwright tests exercise the complete browser workflow, including dynamic tool discovery, visible state changes, approval boundaries, mobile behavior, and operation without WebMCP support. The production application is deployed on Cloudflare. ## Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was deciding where useful agent action ends and legally meaningful human intent begins. Making every action require confirmation would weaken the workflow. Allowing the agent to approve or sign would make the experience unsafe. We separated investigation and preparation from consent: the agent may annotate and propose, while only a person may approve an exact revision or continue to signature. Dynamic tool registration also required careful lifecycle management. A tool being visible is not sufficient authorization, so every state-changing operation validates the current application state again when executed. Another challenge was keeping the demonstration honest. The agreement analysis comes from the agent reading clauses through WebMCP; it is not a hidden deterministic risk scanner. The fixture contract makes the run reproducible, while the visible activity feed shows the actual tool sequence. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that SignWise feels like a coherent human-and-agent product rather than a collection of tool callbacks. The strongest parts are: Evidence appears directly beside the clause that supports it. Agent actions visibly update the live interface. Tool availability reflects page context and human authorization. Approval applies to one exact review revision and is revoked by edits. The final record is bound to the agreement fingerprint. Signing remains an exclusively human action. The complete workflow runs through native ChatGPT Site Tools on the deployed application. The result is a practical example of an agent helping with a consequential workflow without impersonating the person making the decision. ## What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the webpage contributes context and authority that a detached API does not naturally possess. The important innovation is not simply exposing more buttons as tools. It is allowing the live application to offer the right capabilities at the right moment, publish their effects visibly, and withdraw temporary capabilities when their purpose is complete. We also learned that human approval should be treated as versioned state rather than a conversational assumption. “Approved” is meaningful only when the application can identify exactly what was approved and verify that it has not changed. Finally, visible agent activity is part of the product experience. It helps people understand what the agent inspected, what it changed, and where the evidence came from. ## What's next for SignWise The next step is replacing fixture data with real document parsing while preserving the same consent boundaries. Future versions could add: Organization-specific contract policies and playbooks. Suggested redlines and alternative language. Comparisons between agreement versions. Approval routing to legal, procurement, or security teams. Version invalidation when an agreement changes. Authorized integration with an e-signature sandbox. Persistent review records and signer-side identity controls. The long-term goal is not autonomous signing. It is a better informed signing process where agents investigate and prepare, applications enforce boundaries, and people retain authority over consequential decisions. title: Tempo
pitch: Tempo is a calendar that organizes your life for you. Tell it what you need to do, and AI can find time in your busy day, plan your schedule, and manage your events through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Tempo is a calendar that organizes your life for you. Tell it what you need to do, and AI can find time in your busy day, plan your schedule, and manage your events through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard Title Page Inspiration As an incoming university student, I found my university's portal surprisingly inconvenient for organizing my class schedule and timetable. Getting that schedule into a calendar I could actually use meant manually organizing and reshuffling everything. Outside of school, I also play sports, make music, and work part-time. Trying to fit studying, classes, work, practices, and everything else into the same week often meant constantly moving things around to find time for what I needed to do. As someone that believes that being organized is a key value to success, I needed to use my calendar more efficiently. I wanted a calendar that could do more than just store events. I wanted to be able to tell it what I needed to accomplish and have it help organize my time for me. That's why I built Tempo , a calendar designed to work with AI agents using WebMCP. What it does Tempo is a calendar designed to work with AI agents through WebMCP . Instead of manually searching through your calendar and rearranging events, you can tell an agent what you want to accomplish. It can understand your existing schedule, find available time, and make changes directly to your calendar. For example: "Find me three one-hour study blocks around my classes this week and add them to my University calendar." Tempo can also manage recurring events, multiple calendars, conflicts, and other everyday calendar tasks. The agent completes the slow task of manually typing events so you can stay organized for efficiently. How I built it Tempo was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS . The calendar takes many pieces from calendarcn made by vmnog. GitHub . Title page and many other assets were made using Figma. I first took pieces from calendarcn to built the calendar itself, including multiple calendar views, recurring events, event management, search, conflict detection, undo/redo, local persistence, and ICS import/export. I then built a WebMCP layer on top of that foundation. Tempo has structured tools through document.modelContext . These tools allow an agent to read calendars and events, find conflicts, create and modify events, manage calendars, and safely perform destructive actions with confirmation. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was figuring out how an AI agent should safely interact with a calendar. Calendar actions can have real consequences, especially when an agent is creating, moving, or deleting events. If Tempo made the process of creating or organizing a calendar longer, it would not be an useful tool. I wanted agents to have meaningful control without allowing actions to happen unpredictably or silently. I also had to design the WebMCP tools around the existing calendar architecture so that agent actions use the same state, history, and conflict-handling systems as actions made through the UI. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that Tempo is more than a calendar with an AI chatbot attached to it. I've personally used it to transfer my university course timetable to other calendars. The agent can actually interact with the calendar through structured WebMCP tools, allowing it to read, reason about, and modify the user's schedule. I'm also proud of how it all came together, from the visuals I spent hours in figma creating, to the calendar functionality itself. This allowed us to demonstrate WebMCP solving a real problem rather than building a purely technical proof of concept. Tempo also highlights how building is the best way to learn new things. What I learned I learned that making an application agent-ready requires more than adding an AI interface. The agent needs clear, well-defined tools that describe what it can actually do. I also learned that AI is most useful when it removes friction from something people already do. Instead of creating another complicated scheduling interface, Tempo lets users describe what they need and gives an agent the tools to help make it happen. The simple but tedious task it streamlines is the key to its effectiveness. One of the biggest unlocks for me was learning how to use Figma along this process. From personal experience at hackathons, sometimes well thought of ideas can loose to simple ones with polished execution. I'm sure Figma will be a tool I will use for many future projects. What's next for Tempo The next step is turning Tempo into a polished product and pushing the agent experience further. I want to refine the visual design, improve the Agent Link experience, build more advanced scheduling workflows, and make voice interaction a core part of the experience. Creating a more effective mobile experience could also allow people to use Tempo on the go. Ultimately, I want Tempo to make organizing your calendar feel less like a chore and more like having an assistant that can actually manage your time easily. title: Documesh
pitch: One endpoint for agents to all documentation available: match any multi-stack error signature to the closest official documentation — cited, versioned, attributed. Every time.
about_excerpt: One endpoint for agents to all documentation available: match any multi-stack error signature to the closest official documentation — cited, versioned, attributed. Every time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Documesh WebMCP App Inspiration When something breaks at 2 AM, the fix is buried somewhere in dozens of doc sites, each with its own search, its own format, and its own idea of what "current version" means. And when an AI agent hunts for that fix, it's even worse: crawling page after page, scraping prose built for humans, burning thousands of tokens to find one config key. Then WebMCP shipped in Chrome, and I surveyed the ecosystem it created: 322 sites exposing 1,817 agent tools. The pattern was impossible to miss, more than thirty ship near-identical shallow search_docs wrappers, every one locked to a single vendor. Not one could answer a cross-vendor question, cite a doc version, or let an agent act on an answer safely. The docs layer of the agentic web was stuck in 2019: prose for humans, scraped or ignored by agents. The insight that became Documesh had two halves. Agents are the new visitors. When they arrive at a debugging problem, they need one declared, machine-actionable interface to all the official documentation, not thirty-eight walled gardens. And attention is the real cost, every scraped page dumped into context is tokens spent on noise, when one structured call should return exactly the doc section that matters, with the version and license attached. So I built the mesh I wanted my agent to have: one WebMCP endpoint for the whole stack. What it does Documesh gives agents a single endpoint for debugging multi-stack applications: match any multi-stack error signature to the closest official documentation, cited, versioned, attributed. Every time. Federated search of 47 sources synced for now (from a 555-source verified registry), 36,000+ doc sections. Every result carries source, version, license, attribution, canonical URL, and last-updated. Error → docs bridge paste a stack trace; explain_error extracts error signatures and returns the closest official doc sections, with an honest disclaimer: closest matches, not a diagnosis. Chainable answers: every result carries a machine-actionable object: exact config keys, language-tagged code snippets, runnable CLI commands, version applicability. The agent orchestrates; Documesh makes answers reliable enough to chain. An act surface with one rule: verify configs against documented keys, compare config conventions across vendors, check provider status ("is it down, or is it me?" anw, it caught a real Cloudflare outage during testing), report outdated docs. Every write is an append-only proposal, agents never mutate the mesh directly. All exposed as 9 tools across three protocols: WebMCP in the browser, MCP over Streamable HTTP, and plain REST. How we built it License-aware from the first byte: a Python indexer crawls docs through five ingestion patterns only via vendor-consented interfaces (llms.txt) or permissive licenses (CC-BY-4.0, MIT, Apache-2.0). Terraform (BUSL) and copyrighted docs are documented exclusions, license awareness as a feature. Always Search lives in the indexed, lived on Cloudflare. The extraction path has no LLM. deterministic extraction means excerpts are data, not instructions, and a hostile docs page can't prompt-inject through results. Provenance is enforced by schema audit (100% coverage), and search quality is CI-gated at ≥80% on real-world errors. Challenges we ran into The legal maze, most vendor docs are copyrighted with no agent interface; the rule that resolved it: vendor-consented interfaces or permissive licenses, excerpts + canonical links, never mirrors. Search architecture hit a wall 47 static shards loaded into Worker isolate memory (~65 MB) per query; D1 FTS5 dropped per-request memory to ~0. Honest machine-actionability the obvious shortcut was LLM extraction; deterministic is harder but never hallucinates a config key. Testing agents inside someone else's browser. WebMCP verification ultimately required a human, which is why the three-layer eval suite exists. Accomplishments that we're proud of 47 sources / 36k+ sections / 555 registry 100% response provenance agent-readiness score 89/A eval gate 5/5, the act surface caught a real Cloudflare outage during testing three protocols, one mesh an npm SDK so others can chain on it. All solo, all on $0 infra. What we learned Declared contracts beat scraping, the agent doesn't break in, it's invited. Provenance is a feature, not overhead -> "cited, versioned, attributed" became a schema rule instead of a slogan. The agent is the orchestrator, tools should be structured enough to chain, not call each other. Honest abstention survived every skeptical reading. And every constraint became a documented next step instead of a dead end. What's next for Documesh 547 verified sources queued for deep ingestion (47 live today) → /digest version-aware change feed → Vectorize hybrid search → webmcp-evals integration → MCP Apps UI → a contribution loop that makes the mesh self-correcting: documentation agents don't just read, but maintain. pitch: Real-time collaborative rooms where humans and AI agents draw together.
about_excerpt: Real-time collaborative rooms where humans and AI agents draw together. Like Comment Story Updates codraw OG features features 2 demo room human dashboard Inspiration codraw.app is an interactive collaborative simple asset drawing app, where humans and agents can build on (humans via a browser, agentically: MCP, WebMCP, Skill+API, via the magic AI wand feature). What it does Open codraw.app with a WebMCP-enabled browser and your agent can: Draw with you, live. Shapes, batch pixels, flood fill, layers, undo — every stroke lands on the shared canvas in real time, next to yours and everyone else's. See before it paints. codraw_read_region returns the actual pixel colors of any area, so the agent works with what's there instead of over it. Move around the app. List rooms, create rooms, open a room, switch between a room's canvases, talk in the room chat. Tools register and unregister as you navigate — the page you're on defines what the agent can do. Play by the room's rules. Untrusted agents in moderated rooms get their work held in a pending queue, and the tool result says so. No special agent backdoor exists. The same tools also work outside the browser: a remote MCP server at codraw.app/mcp with OAuth 2.1 login (the agent acts as your account, with your per-room trust), and a plain HTTP API with a served skill file for curl and CI. One dispatcher handles all three, so the rules are identical everywhere. Every action is attributed. A room's history distinguishes humans, agents, and the in-app AI wand — "🤖 Claude Code acting as @joe", "✦ GLM 5.3 Flash prompted by @joe" — per stroke, per layer. And because every canvas has its own URL ( codraw.app/@you/game/sprites/hero/png exports it, PUT imports), what an agent paints, your build can pull. How we built it Go stdlib server (HTTP + WebSocket + SQLite), Vue 3 frontend. The WebMCP layer is one composable registering navigator.modelContext tools per view. The MCP server replays tool calls through the app's own router — no rule exists twice. OAuth 2.1 (discovery, dynamic client registration, PKCE, introspection) is stdlib-only on our auth service, D3BIT. Challenges we ran into Giving agents sight (the hex-grid read tool); scoping tools to SPA navigation; an OAuth discovery fallback that fetched /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server from the app origin and got HTML back — the app now mirrors the metadata; and keeping tool results honest about moderation instead of pretending success. Accomplishments that we're proud of A human and two kinds of agents; one in the browser via WebMCP, one headless via MCP with OAuth - drawing on the same canvas at the same time, under the same moderation, with every stroke attributed. We also deleted our API keys entirely: agent identity is user identity. What we learned Page-scoped tools beat a global toolbox: the current room is the context, and WebMCP lets the page say so. Honest tool results (moderation status, layer ids, coordinate conventions) matter more than tool count. Agents deserve real auth, not pasted secrets. What's next for codraw.app Sprite animation (layered cels, timeline, GIF export) with tools to build animations frame by frame; a graph view of who — human or agent — touched what; codraw Pro with AI credits. An open source codraw.app that can be run locally as well soon (MCP repo is open source). about_excerpt:

about_excerpt: Help your agent shop for you Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Home Page - Desktop Home Page - Mobile Product Search 2 - Mobile Searching... Filters Menu Choosing Location Product Search 1 - Mobile Product Search 2 - Desktop Inspiration Shopping for a product often means repeating the same research across search engines, marketplaces, local-store websites, maps, and second-hand listings. ShopNearMe was built around a simple idea: product comparison should work equally well for people and for AI agents. Instead of forcing an agent to interpret buttons, filters, dropdowns, and result cards visually, WebMCP lets the website expose those capabilities directly as structured tools. What it does ShopNearMe searches for products around a selected location and combines several ways of buying them into one interface: Buy in store — nearby physical stores relevant to the product. Order online — online offers, including shipping in the total price when available. Second hand — used or pre-owned offers when available. Users can search for arbitrary products, use their current location or choose another location on an interactive map, sort by total price, and apply filters derived dynamically from the current product results. The filters therefore change with the product. For example, a clock search can expose clock-specific attributes such as clock type or movement, while other products expose different facets. ShopNearMe also distinguishes between verified product prices and nearby stores where a reliable price could not be obtained. Unverified offers are hidden by default and can be explicitly enabled. Why WebMCP Product research is naturally multi-step. A request such as “Find desk clocks near Tel Aviv and show me the cheapest options” normally requires an agent to understand the page layout, operate the location selector, submit a search, inspect dynamic results, find the sort control, and extract the results. ShopNearMe instead exposes those operations through WebMCP. The application registers five tools: search_products get_visible_results set_search_location filter_results sort_results This gives agents a structured contract instead of requiring them to guess how the visual interface works. WebMCP is especially useful here because ShopNearMe is highly dynamic: products, categories, filters, locations, prices, and available offers can all change between searches. Human and agent collaboration The human and the agent use the same application state. An agent can search, change the location, filter results, or change the sorting order, and those actions are reflected in the visible ShopNearMe interface. The user can then inspect the results visually, compare prices and stores, change filters manually, or follow a retailer link. This creates a useful division of work: the agent can handle repetitive product research while the person retains the visual context and final purchasing decision. How I built it ShopNearMe uses React, TypeScript, and Vite for the frontend. Live product and local-store data are fetched through server-side search endpoints so provider credentials are not exposed to the browser. Search data includes Google Shopping and Google Maps local results through SerpApi. The location picker uses Leaflet and OpenStreetMap, with geocoding and reverse geocoding for address search and direct map selection. Search results are normalized into a shared offer model. ShopNearMe calculates total prices including shipping when available, derives product-specific filters from the returned data, separates different purchase methods, and handles offers whose prices cannot be verified. WebMCP is implemented directly with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The tools operate on the same state used by the normal interface rather than functioning as an unrelated API layer. The project is deployed on Vercel. GitHub Actions runs linting, TypeScript checking, tests, and a production build. Challenges I ran into One of the main challenges was normalizing inconsistent commerce data. Different listings provide different levels of information about shipping, price, availability, attributes, location, and store details. Local shopping also behaves very differently from online shopping. A local store may be highly relevant to a product even when no trustworthy price is available. Instead of presenting that data as equivalent to a verified listing, ShopNearMe exposes unverified local offers separately. Another challenge was making product filters truly dynamic. Hard-coded filters would only work for predefined products, so ShopNearMe derives useful facets from the actual results. The WebMCP integration also required keeping agent actions synchronized with the visible interface so that the user and the agent are genuinely operating the same application. Accomplishments ShopNearMe is a working, deployed WebMCP application rather than a WebMCP proof of concept. Its five WebMCP tools cover the core shopping workflow and operate on the same state as the human-facing application. The project also includes: Live arbitrary-product search Nearby physical-store results Online and second-hand offers Shipping-aware total prices Dynamic product-specific filters Two-way price sorting Current-location support Searchable interactive map selection Explicit handling of unverified prices Responsive desktop and mobile interfaces Automated tests and CI A live desk clock search around Tel Aviv, for example, returned local stores together with online and second-hand offers. What I learned The main thing I learned is that an agent-native website does not need a separate AI interface. WebMCP can expose the semantics behind an existing human interface while keeping both interaction models synchronized. I also learned that useful WebMCP tools should represent meaningful user actions rather than simply wrapping backend API endpoints. The project also required learning more about normalizing commerce data, location-aware search, dynamic filtering, geocoding, handling uncertain data, and testing agent interactions in a real browser environment. What's next A production version of ShopNearMe could add more commerce providers, direct retailer integrations, stronger stock verification, better cross-store product matching, broader international support, and improved ranking of physical stores. Future WebMCP tools could also support saved comparisons, watchlists, product availability monitoring, and multi-product shopping plans.  Inspiration 

 AI agents are increasingly capable of helping people research products, compare options, and make purchasing decisions, but most ecommerce websites were designed exclusively for humans. 

 An agent visiting a storefront often has to scrape the website to get context. Interpret buttons and forms, scrape product information, or rely on a separate API that may not represent the experience available to the shopper. 

 We built SuggestAPI around a simple idea: merchants shouldn't have to rebuild their search and product discovery infrastructure for every new AI interface. We bring Agentic Commerce to any ecommerce platform without replatforming. 

 WebMCP gave us an opportunity to bring that idea directly into the browser. 

 Instead of making an agent guess how a storefront works, the website can explicitly expose the actions it supports as structured tools. Humans continue using the normal storefront while agents get a reliable interface to the same underlying product catalog. 

 What it does 

 SuggestAPI adds an agent-ready product discovery layer to existing e-commerce search infrastructure. 

 For our WebMCP implementation, a participating storefront exposes structured browser tools that an AI agent can discover and invoke while visiting the website.

 catalog_search — search a merchant's catalog using natural-language shopping intent

title: WordLift AI Audit
pitch: The machine reads the website. The human knows the business. ChatGPT compiles both into a governed service map for agents.
about_excerpt: The machine reads the website. The human knows the business. ChatGPT compiles both into a governed service map for agents. Like Comment Story Updates The machine reads the website. The human knows the business. ChatGPT compiles both into a governed service map. WordLift AI Audit turns a public website into an evidence-backed service map for AI agents. It reads representative pages, classifies the business, extracts domain entities and vocabulary, compiles the actions an agent should be able to perform, and verifies which machine interfaces actually work. But the machine output is deliberately a draft. Pages cannot prove every operating role, important entity, business term, or responsibility boundary. ChatGPT therefore interviews the human and compiles that judgment into a new immutable, human-refined service map. The problem Websites were designed as pages for people. Agents need explicit knowledge about the things a business offers, the functions they may call, the boundaries around those functions, and evidence that the interfaces really work. Most AI-readiness scanners stop at crawlability, metadata, or declarations. They cannot answer: Which action applies to which entity? Can people perform it today? Can an agent perform it? Who owns the action: the organization, a partner, or nobody? What evidence proves the conclusion? What governed contract would close the gap? What WordLift AI Audit does Analyzes up to four representative pages rather than only the homepage. Preserves the complete bounded WordLift foundation audit behind progressive disclosure. Classifies the site as commerce, publishing, travel, finance, SaaS, or a conservative fallback. Builds the Context Engine: domain graph — organizations, products, services, places, articles, offers, and provenance; lexical graph — categories, names, terminology, meanings, and aliases; action layer — expected actions, entity bindings, interfaces, boundaries, evidence, and contracts. Separates human-facing support from agent-facing declarations and successful invocation. Produces a machine-generated service-map draft with three priority gaps. Lets ChatGPT inspect that draft and interview the human about the business role, primary entities, terminology, and every expected action boundary. Compiles the human decisions into an immutable child report without altering the original evidence or allowing a human assertion to mark an action agent-ready. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is not an accessory to the interface; it is the collaboration protocol. The application exposes six generic tools: audit-website starts an audit of any safe public URL. get-audit-report follows a long-running audit through progress to completion. inspect-service-map gives ChatGPT the full machine review brief. explain-capability retrieves deeper evidence and the governed contract for one action. explain-foundation-audit returns the complete safe WordLift foundation audit. refine-service-map submits typed human judgments and returns the immutable refined report. The tool descriptions encode the intended protocol: audit → inspect → interview → explain where unclear → refine This creates a form of human–agent collaboration that was difficult before WebMCP. The machine contributes observation and inference. The human contributes business meaning and responsibility. ChatGPT mediates the conversation and turns both into structured symbolic commitments. Honest readiness A declaration earns zero readiness points. Structured data, OpenAPI, MCP, WebMCP, and other declarations remain unverified until the relevant interface is invoked successfully. Human decisions can change applicability, vocabulary, entity priority, and governance boundaries, but never evidence-based readiness. The report therefore keeps two scores separate: WordLift foundation readiness; verified agent action readiness. Example A tourism website may contain booking forms, accommodation pages, and hotel links. The machine can infer that availability matters, but it cannot safely conclude that the destination organization owns hotel inventory. The human can tell ChatGPT that the organization owns discovery and recommendations while availability is a partner handoff. The refined report then promotes the correct organization and destination entities, clarifies the terminology, changes the action boundary, updates the entity–action bindings and contract, records the rationale as human-provided provenance, and preserves the original machine draft for comparison. Implementation The application is a React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Express, and Node 22 service deployed on Google Cloud Run with immutable Firestore report revisions. It uses Zod contracts, a deterministic versioned action compiler, JSON-LD, Schema.org, Google Natural Language classification, and the WordLift AI Audit provider. Tools register on the top-level report document through the WebMCP imperative API on document.modelContext , with a compatibility alias for Chrome's current preview surface. Report-scoped tools register as soon as the route loads, before the report has finished rendering. Security controls include SSRF protection, DNS and redirect validation, response limits, sanitized evidence, rate limiting, bounded storage, server-only credentials, and truthful partial or failed states. New work created during the challenge The private WordLift AI Audit existed before August 25. The following public implementation was created during The WebMCP Challenge: a new open-source deployable application; the versioned six-archetype action compiler; multi-page context extraction and provenance; domain, lexical, interface, and entity–action schemas; verification-only readiness and safe invocation probes; six generic WebMCP tools; the inspect/interview/refine collaboration protocol; typed human assertions and immutable refined reports; the Context Engine and capability-map interface; deterministic fixtures, security boundaries, and the complete test suite. The challenge contribution is not a wrapper around the previous product. It is the new public context compiler and human-guided WebMCP experience. Testing The current release passed strict TypeScript checks, 323 unit/integration/component tests, the production build, and 12 Playwright browser scenarios. The browser suite includes the full Cyborg journey: audit, inspect, refine, open the immutable child, verify embodied human judgment, and confirm the original machine draft remains unchanged. No account is required.  Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was shifting from a traditional dashboard mindset to an agent-first architecture . 

 Designing software for humans is familiar. Designing software that humans and AI agents can use together required us to rethink how every business capability should be exposed. 

 Another major challenge involved production deployment. Coordinating a Next.js frontend with a FastAPI backend required resolving API routing, environment variables, HTTPS communication, CORS configuration and production deployment across multiple cloud platforms. 

 We also spent considerable effort making the interface feel like real enterprise software while ensuring the backend remained modular and scalable for future agent capabilities. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're especially proud that BoardMind evolved far beyond its original concept. 

 Highlights include: 

 
 Successfully integrating WebMCP into a practical enterprise workflow 
 Designing an executive-focused multi-agent collaboration system 
 Building interactive dashboards instead of static business reports 
 Creating explainable recommendations supported by evidence 
 Implementing business simulations for decision planning 
 Deploying a complete production-ready frontend and backend 
 Building an interface that feels like modern enterprise software instead of a hackathon prototype 
 

 Most importantly, BoardMind demonstrates a real-world scenario where WebMCP genuinely improves the user experience instead of simply being included as a requirement. 

 

 What we learned 

 This project fundamentally changed how we think about AI-powered software. 

 We learned that the future isn't about AI replacing decision-makers—it's about enabling humans and AI agents to collaborate through well-defined capabilities. 

 Technically, we gained practical experience with: 

 
 WebMCP 
 Agent-oriented application architecture 
 FastAPI 
 Next.js 
 Production deployment 
 Docker 
 Cross-service communication 
 Enterprise workflow design 
 Secure API development 
 

 Perhaps the biggest lesson was that exposing structured capabilities through WebMCP produces a significantly more reliable interaction model than expecting AI systems to interpret complex graphical interfaces. 

 

 What's next for BoardMind 

 BoardMind is designed as the foundation for a much larger enterprise decision platform. 

 Our next goals include: 

 
 Native WebMCP support across every business module 
 Live integrations with Salesforce, Jira, SAP, Slack and Google Workspace 
 Persistent long-term agent memory 
 Multi-step executive approval workflows 
 Autonomous monitoring of live business events 
 Predictive planning using real company data 
 Multi-organization enterprise deployment 
 Secure organization-level permissions and governance 
 

 Our long-term vision is to build an operating system for executive decision-making where humans and AI agents collaborate naturally through WebMCP, enabling organizations to make faster, more transparent and better-informed decisions.
