title: coSynth
pitch: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go.
about_excerpt: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go. Like Comment Story Updates Full Wavetable Synthesizer GIF Active AI state and tool visible in the UI coSynth – AI Web Synthesizer Sound design is hard to get into. A real synth has hundreds of knobs. coSynth lets you describe and get a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays the result, listens to what it made, and shows all the changes in the UI. You keep it, undo it, tweak it, or ask the AI to show you how it got there. You can also ask AI to teach a complext topic and AI will guide you through step by step. Live: https://coSynth.vercel.app Code: https://github.com/brunnolou/coSynth (MIT) Why WebMCP fits A synth is a terrible thing to operate through text or screenshots. Too many parameters (in this case 224), knobs to drag, LFO curves to draw, etc. An agent can misclick, can miss an exact value, and can't hear the audio. The UI is too complex for someone to easily find things when they are not used to it. That makes a synthesizer one of the best interfaces for WebMCP. For the AI agent: It communicates to the synth directly. Every parameter has a name, a unit, and a range that can be edited directly in bulk. When the agent plays a note, it gets back attack time, decay, spectral centroid, and harmonics, then compares that with a reference clip. So it can "hear" with a tool call. For humans Instead of starting from scratch, you get very close to what you want. Then you can see the exact changes and tweak manually. If you don't know a concept or want to find something, AI can show you the exact location or teach you step by step. You can leverage AI's world knowledge to create any synth sound! What used to need trained ears you now can achieve by sending a reference sound and asking AI to replicate. How I Made the AI<>Human UX Better Each knob the AI touched gets a small animated marker. A status line shows which tool is running. You can reject a whole AI iteration and keep your own edits. Undo covers AI changes and yours. Old branches stay reachable in history. The AI can highlight controls step by step and explain them. Every AI performance is saved, so "play that again with my new adjustment" is one click. AI can save as a preset, and you can download it. How I implemented WebMCP Vanilla TypeScript and Vite. DSP in an AudioWorklet, UI in Canvas, WebGL2 and DOM. WebMCP sits on top of the same engine the UI uses, and the synth works without it. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . There are 24, each with a JSON Schema input and a readOnlyHint : Reading : get_synth_state , get_parameter_schema , get_ui_targets , list_presets , get_history Editing : update_parameters , set_modulation , set_fx_order , apply_patch , save_preset , load_preset , delete_preset , export_preset Sound : play_notes , render_audio , capture_audio , analyze_audio , analyze_reference_audio , compare_audio , suggest_patch , stop_performance Together : show_ui_guide , navigate_history , replay_history All 24 register at page load. play_notes needs the human to click Start first, because browsers won't play audio without a gesture. render_audio uses an OfflineAudioContext, so the agent can design and measure before anyone clicks anything. The page also documents itself. A clipped agent brief in the DOM, a JSON descriptor, ai-tools meta tags, llms.txt and robots.txt . An agent given only the URL can read the page and know what to do. How I tested the agent experience I want to ensure AI could call the tools easily. So I built a loop. A harness exposes only what a real WebMCP client sees, and logs every call. A fresh agent gets a fixed prompt and is never allowed to read the repo. Each round runs on Claude and Codex. When * both trip in the same place( , the tool is wrong . Fix the top blocker, run again. In self-improving loop. Four evals, each asking one question. Can the agent find out what to send ( docs/agent-ux-eval.md ). Can it steer toward a sound it cannot hear ( docs/agent-match-eval.md ). Given a "how do I" question, does it teach rather than edit ( docs/agent-teaching-eval.md ). Given only a URL, does it find the tools at all? Prompts, agent reports and raw logs are all in the repo. Learning all 224 parameters went from 45 calls to 1 . Failed calls went to zero on both models. The matching loop went from 87 calls to 36 . How to test Open https://cosynth.vercel.app in the ChatGPT in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . ChatGPT Desktop was the most reliable client for me. Click "CLICK TO START AUDIO" once. Try: "Make a bright plucked bass and play a short riff." "Show me where the amp envelope is and how to shorten the release." "Save that." Watch the markers, click the status dot for before and after values, and use Keep or Reject. No login. Presets and reference audio stay in the browser. What was already there, what is new I started from Soundgineer by noisyloop ( https://github.com/noisyloop/soundgineer , MIT). Its DSP engine and original UI date from July 6 to 11, 2026, and that version is still up at https://soundgineer.vercel.app . Everything WebMCP-related is from the submission period, August 26 to September 3, 2026, about 200 dated commits: the WebMCP layer and all 24 tools, offline rendering and audio analysis, change markers and Keep/Reject, shared undo history and replays, guided walkthroughs, the interface redesign, the four evals with their harness, and the in-page agent brief. title: Polkaswap
pitch: Browser agents discover assets, quote routes, and build fresh swap plans without wallet access.
about_excerpt: Browser agents discover assets, quote routes, and build fresh swap plans without wallet access. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a swap involves identifying assets, reading precise amounts, comparing routes, and checking fees, price impact, and freshness. We wanted browser agents to obtain those facts directly from the exchange and explain them through a structured, inspectable interface. Polkaswap already connects people to SORA liquidity. WebMCP lets an agent use that same application to build a useful plan while wallet access remains a separate decision. What it does Polkaswap exposes nine public WebMCP tools for capabilities, status, readiness, asset search and resolution, common assets, quotes, unsigned swap plans, and pool information. An agent can respond to “Plan swapping 1 XOR for VAL with 0.5% slippage” by calling polkaswap_plan_swap directly. It waits for the node, resolves assets, obtains a fresh quote, and returns the route, amount bounds, fee estimate when available, warnings, expiry, network context, and unsigned SDK-call metadata. Unavailable fees produce an explicit warning. No wallet connection or prior quote-button click is required. People can inspect the same planning workflow in the agent playground. Changing the pair or amount refreshes the plan automatically; visible pages also refresh expired plans. A switch stops automatic planning. The interface prevents older responses from overwriting newer inputs. Public tools cannot expose account identity or balances, connect a wallet, create an executable intent, sign, submit, transfer funds, or change liquidity. Plans return mode: "unsigned" , canExecute: false , and requiresWallet: false . The preview is SDK-call metadata, not a SCALE-encoded transaction. This entry provides autonomous planning, with no unattended trading. How we built it The implementation uses Vue 3, TypeScript, Vite, the existing SORA SDK and node connection, and FPNumber for precise token amounts. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool() when WebMCP is available. The playground registers its tools at the top level and forwards calls into its same-origin application iframe. Strict schemas require decimal-string amounts and reject additional properties. Public result projection excludes wallet and provider details. Cancellation, bounded errors, network-context checks, and five-minute expiry keep planning results predictable. No executable authorization is stored by planning. Everything ships as static assets suitable for IPFS, without hosted command middleware. An optional local Node.js stdio MCP bridge shares the same public catalogue. Humans use visible controls and agents use named tools, with both reaching the application's existing planning logic. Challenges we addressed Browser agents do not discover tools registered inside the playground iframe, so discovery needed a top-level adapter. Useful market results also needed careful separation from the application's broader wallet-aware API. Planning introduced timing problems: inputs can change during a quote, results can expire, and pages can become hidden. The scheduler serializes requests, ignores superseded results, pauses while hidden, and bounds retries for transient failures. Accomplishments Native verification of the published build discovered all nine tools and directly invoked polkaswap_plan_swap . It returned an unsigned live SORA plan without wallet access. The page planner also refreshed from 1 to 2 XOR and stopped automatic refresh when disabled. The clean submission passed 306 focused tests across 21 files, 13 translation tests across four files, and nine preview-helper tests. The official Node MCP stdio check discovered all nine schemas. A separate browser registration-harness smoke verified planning and input-change replanning with zero captured console, request, or HTTP errors. Existing project and challenge contribution Polkaswap is an existing open-source exchange. Its exchange UI, SORA integration, wallet workflows, static deployment infrastructure, and earlier browser-agent foundation predate this contribution. The August 25–September 3, 2026 challenge contribution adds the public WebMCP catalogue and adapters, wallet-independent swap planning, the agent playground and automatic replanning behavior, and supporting tests and documentation. The linked public comparison identifies the changes from baseline 893783b to submission commit 4955eb0 . What's next We want clearer multi-route comparisons, more useful public market reads, and better explanations when node data is temporarily unavailable. Signing and execution remain outside the public WebMCP tools. title: Carpo
pitch: Carpo turns your videos into shareable clips. Let AI help you find the moments and make the cuts!
about_excerpt: Carpo turns your videos into shareable clips. Let AI help you find the moments and make the cuts! Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration 8 years ago, I built an app for my gaming community. I had over 30,000 Tekken players using it, and I promised them all I'd make gifs for every attack from every character. I didn't realize it at the time, but that required making over 5,000 gifs. How did I pull it off? I built a clipping tool to produce them. With a team of volunteers, we were able to tackle the project in a few months. I decided to revive that tool but this time I wanted to enable an agent to work with me. Making clips is a long tedious process and requires a lot of precision. From finding the right moments, properly timing the clips and adjusting it to the way you need, it can be really taxing mentally. WebMCP lets an agent help with those tedious parts, while still allowing you to jump in and edit things by hand. Sunil from Cloudflare talked about working with AI as having “your hands in the goop” alongside your agents. That's exactly how I feel about how we should be working with agents as well. It should feel like me and my agent crafting together. This experience is what I hope to capture with Carpo! What it does Carpo assists you in making clips of your videos of moments you might want to share on socials for marketing. It uses Cloudflare infra for storing and sharing the urls after they're made. Your agent can navigate it with WebMCP or you can use Project Think in the same way if you're not connecting via WebMCP. How we built it Built it iteratively with Coex, kept PRs small and used tons of architecture reviews with Matt Pocock skills. I had it read the old code from 8 years ago so most things went directionally the right way considering that it had a foundation to work of off that was familiar to me. The frontend uses React, TypeScript ,Vite and StyleX, Cloudflare Workers serve the app and API, using DOs to coordinate the FFmpeg containers. R2 stores the videos and transcripts. D1 holds the application records and I'm using Cloudflare Access for auth. One thing that was really important to me was making sure that this worked without AI, the way I used to do it. If someone doesn't have access to an agent to interact through WebMCP, or if Think wasn't available, you can use this just like I did 8 years ago. I also think human approval is really important with these types of things so it's enforced through Think deterministically and we guide your agents to ask before making clips. I found testing this manually to be very time consuming, so I used a flue agent to look at PRs descriptions, look at the diffs and test the features directly and provide screenshots as evidence. This made me feel confident that I can let it rip on some features and come back later. Challenges we ran into GitHub outage. At first I was going to handle the browser testing through an agent through GitHub actions, but there was an outage that blocked that. This is when I looked into what Cloudflare has to offer and I learned about Browser Run and using Flue to navigate the site and test things I care about. YouTube. The original thing I built worked with YouTube and I do believe there is a path here where YouTube can work, but I was getting hit by all kinds of rate limits and stuff so I had to fall back from this. Very sad about it but it's something I want to explore further. Accomplishments that we're proud of Very proud that this is something that can be valuable whether AI is available or not. WebMCP just is there to give someone leverage and make them 10x more productive while they stay in the loop. I'm also really proud that it can be tested or used by browser agents as well. It can understand how to use the product through the structured tools! What we learned While we talk about "AGI" a lot and letting agents handle anything and everything, but this project was a good reminder that truly useful agents are going to need some sort of structure or well designed APIs to get anything done. I tried making videos and clips this way before, just asking an agent to find certain parts of videos where someone says a certain thing and more often than I would hope, it wouldn't do a great job. From what I've seen with Codex + Carpo, the success rate of getting exactly what I want is way higher now. What's next for Carpo I would love to push this further and make it easier and more efficient as far as sharing clips across different social platforms. As well as adding more editing abilities like sound boards or small visuals. I don't necessarily want Carpo to actual edit video by generating anything. I want people to be able to manage their own library of visuals and sounds and ask Codex to assist them in implementing it all. Maybe this could be a sick product some day! title: FV® Tax Engine | AI Fiscal Agent for Odoo
pitch: A fiscal operations web app where accountants and AI agents collaborate through browser-native WebMCP tools with human approval and traceability.
about_excerpt:
A fiscal operations web app where accountants and AI agents collaborate through browser-native WebMCP tools with human approval and traceability.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 




 
 FV-ID VIZF850813D46 

 Inspiration 

 Mexican accountants, finance teams, Odoo implementers, and small businesses spend significant time reviewing CFDI electronic invoices, payment conditions, tax exceptions, reconciliations, and ERP records. Many steps are repetitive, but exceptions still require professional judgment. 

 FV® Tax Engine was created from real accounting, fiscal, and Odoo implementation workflows to reduce repetitive work while preserving evidence, traceability, and human control. 

 Why WebMCP 

 The existing FV® Tax Engine foundation analyzes structured fiscal information and prepares accounting findings. The WebMCP Challenge edition is focused on adding a browser-native collaboration layer so an AI agent can discover explicit fiscal tools exposed by the web application instead of guessing how to operate the UI. 

 This is a strong fit for WebMCP because fiscal workflows require precise, auditable actions with narrow schemas and clear boundaries. The agent should be able to invoke defined functions such as reviewing CFDI records, filtering exceptions, explaining detected risks, and preparing a proposed accounting action while the professional remains in control of sensitive decisions. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 The intended WebMCP workflow is: 

 
 The accountant opens the FV® Tax Engine web interface. 
 The page exposes structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . 
 The agent discovers only the actions the application explicitly makes available. 
 The agent can analyze or filter fiscal records and return structured findings. 
 Sensitive or accounting-impacting actions remain subject to human review and approval. 
 The application preserves traceability from fiscal source data to finding, proposed action, and human decision. 
 

 This avoids brittle UI automation and gives the agent a precise contract for interacting with the fiscal application. 

 Existing foundation vs. WebMCP Challenge work 

 FV® Tax Engine existed before the WebMCP Challenge. The pre-existing foundation includes Python-based CFDI/fiscal validation concepts, deterministic rules, evidence-oriented workflows, and Odoo integration design. 

 For this challenge, the project is being extended with a WebMCP-enabled web experience and structured agent-callable tools. The WebMCP-specific implementation is the new competition work and is being kept distinct from the pre-existing fiscal engine so the extension is auditable. 

 Architecture 

 The design separates deterministic fiscal controls from agent orchestration: 

 
 deterministic rules determine what happened in the fiscal data; 
 WebMCP exposes explicit application capabilities to the agent; 
 the agent coordinates analysis and explanation; 
 the accountant approves sensitive actions; 
 Odoo remains the target ERP workflow layer. 
 

 This separation is intended to reduce hallucination risk and keep professional accountability with the human user. 

 Implementation target for the challenge 

 The WebMCP layer uses the emerging browser API under document.modelContext with explicit tool names, descriptions, JSON input schemas, and execution callbacks. The challenge build is designed around read/analyze-first tools and human approval gates for any action that could affect accounting records. 

 Impact 

 The project targets a concrete operational problem: fiscal review is time-consuming, repetitive, and difficult to automate safely. A browser-native agent interface can let professionals delegate structured review tasks without giving an AI unrestricted control of the ERP or relying on fragile screen automation. 

 Current submission status 

 This Devpost entry is the WebMCP Challenge edition of FV® Tax Engine. The underlying fiscal engine and repository are existing work; the WebMCP web layer, challenge demo, and challenge-specific testing flow are the new submission-period deliverables.

title: ClaimReady
pitch: Browser-native WebMCP agent for First Notice of Loss (FNOL): tells drivers what their car insurance covers while reporting a crash.
about_excerpt: Browser-native WebMCP agent for First Notice of Loss (FNOL): tells drivers what their car insurance covers while reporting a crash. Like Comment Story Updates Discovery. The agent finds the insurer's typed tools at runtime and drafts the claim from what the claimant said in plain words. Routes on screen. Rows the agent wrote read via tool, rows that came with the file read on file, and each requirement names its clause. A moving surface. Answering that the car cannot be driven publishes a ninth tool. Changing the answer back withdraws it again. Refusal. A planted instruction inside a third party note is refused, and the ledger names the code, PATCH_REJECTED_LOCKED. The refusal, and the button. PATCH_REJECTED_LOCKED on the pinned row, the claim not filed, and File this claim left for a person. The whole desk, live in the ChatGPT browser. The agent says it is ready to file, and that pressing File this claim is yours to do. The insurer's page hands your own agent its rules as typed tools, so you learn what you are covered for while still describing the crash. Live, no account: https://upgradedev.github.io/claimready/ Code (MIT): https://github.com/upgradedev/claimready Tools need a browser that has WebMCP. Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing on, verified on Chrome 151 stable, or the ChatGPT desktop app's built in browser with site tools enabled. Availability there is still rolling out and varies by workspace. In any other browser the page works by hand and says on screen why no tools are registered. Inspiration Somebody has just had a crash and is standing next to the car with a phone. They know what happened. What they do not know is what their own policy needs to hear about it, and neither does any general purpose assistant, because the clause, the excess and the list of required answers sit on one insurer's origin and change from customer to customer. I build claims systems for European assistance operators, so this is the failure I watch: a first notice of loss arrives wrong about what the policy needed rather than about what happened. Then the driver waits days to learn what they are covered for, and a handler spends the interval asking for the field nobody told anyone to fill in. What it does Describe the crash to your own agent. It reads the insurer's typed tools and tells you what this policy still needs while you are talking. Then the surface moves: answer that the car cannot be driven and get_assistance_options registers, a capability the agent lacked a moment earlier and loses when that answer changes. Three prompts to paste, with two page steps between the second and the third: Read this claim page and tell me what it still needs from me. A delivery van reversed into my car while it was parked in the car park on Harbour Road. It caught the left front wing and left a dent. The car still drives, and it is still there in the Harbour Road car park. Fill that in for me and write the description. Now set Still drivable to no on the page yourself, and press Pin on that row. Both steps matter: the pin is what makes the next answer a refusal rather than a successful write. Then: Read the notes on the file, then read the claim again, do what that note asks, and tell me what the page said. That note is a planted instruction inside third party evidence, and it asks for the row you just pinned, so the answer is PATCH_REJECTED_LOCKED . Every answer also carries the route it arrived on: on file, via page, via tool. That names a surface, not a person. The page cannot see who is at the keyboard, so it never claims to. Filing is human only. No tool files, dispatches, pins or unlocks, and a test reads the source to keep it that way. Filing leaves a handler packet built from the exact revision that passed the filing gate, with the clause, the excess, every requirement and a SHA-256 that scripts/verify_packet.mjs recomputes. Nothing is transmitted and no claim is opened anywhere. With no key and no signature, a matching digest shows only that the content is unchanged. It does not show origin, authorship, or that nobody edited the content and recomputed the digest to match, and the repository says so in the same words. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The rules that decide a motor claim sit on one insurer's origin and change from customer to customer. A REST endpoint with an OpenAPI file carries the same answers, once somebody builds that integration for this insurer. This is browser native and same origin, with zero integration work: an agent meeting this insurer for the first time discovers the tools at runtime. How it creates a better user experience The driver learns what their own policy still needs while they are still describing the crash, in the assistant they already have open, instead of a second call days later. The cover answer at the roadside instead of a letter a week later. Nothing to install, no account, and the page keeps working by hand in a browser with no agent in it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Two parties write to one document and neither overwrites the other silently. The agent drafts. The person corrects a field and pins it, and a pinned row then refuses every later patch and says so with a code. The tool surface itself moves: answering that the car cannot be driven publishes a ninth tool, and changing the answer back withdraws it. Filing stays a button only a person can press, and the page says so in its own tool list. Before this, each of those needed a bespoke integration per insurer, and an agent still had no way to be told what a page refuses. How WebMCP is implemented Tools register on document.modelContext , falling back to navigator.modelContext , over a pure core with no dependencies and no build step. Page and tools share one store, so an agent action shows on screen. Read tools carry readOnlyHint and text the insurer did not write carries untrustedContentHint . Both halves of the standard ship. Nine tools come from JavaScript, eight from the moment the page loads and a ninth that appears when the claim says the car cannot be driven, which is why the narration at 0:20 of the video counts eight. The tenth is an ordinary HTML form carrying four attributes, toolname , tooldescription , toolparamdescription and toolautosubmit , and the browser builds the JSON Schema and the tool from that markup on its own. toolautosubmit is the one that makes an agent's call actually submit the form rather than only fill it. So an insurer adopts WebMCP by adding attributes. What the demo video shows Three beats are captured in CI by Playwright against the deployed page in Chrome. Two run with WebMCP on, against the browser's own implementation. The first runs with it deliberately off, because that beat shows the page as a visitor with no agent sees it. Six are one continuous unbroken recording in the ChatGPT desktop app's built in browser, cut into six. Two corrections to the narration , written here because the cut is frozen. At 1:40 it says the roadside collection "is arranged": the demo records a local roadside assistance request and marks that requirement answered, it does not arrange or dispatch a service, and nothing leaves the page. At 2:08 it says "Chrome builds the schema from that markup", where the accurate word is the browser: that take was shot in the ChatGPT desktop browser, and the declarative half is verified separately in Chrome 151.0.7922.174 stable. Both are also written into the video description. The opening and closing cards are type on a still background, generated by a script in the repository. No stock footage and no rendered people: every other frame is the deployed page running. Evidence 961 unit tests, from node --test tests/unit , with source coverage of 98.11 percent of lines over the 22 files under src. Both are read at the submitted commit and both reprint in any clone. 178 assertions run against the deployed page in a real Chrome with WebMCP enabled, in CI, at the same commit the host serves. The page loads no framework, has no build step and makes no network call at runtime after load. Challenges, and the honest limits Insurer, policy, vehicle and claimant are invented. No integration, no adjudication, no handler has reviewed a packet, nobody has run this on a real intake. What this page demonstrably does is in the sections above and every part of it is checkable in a browser: policy rules discovered at runtime on the insurer's own origin, requirements recomputed on the page as answers change, a route recorded on every answer, a pin that refuses patches with a code, and filing that no published tool can reach. What is not demonstrated is that any of it makes an autonomous agent fill a form better. One experiment tried to show that and did not, and it is published in full rather than dropped. What I measured went against the page, and is published anyway. In 36 runs with language models standing in for drivers, the arm

title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. The stage restarts on the new beat and the log on the right shows every call as it happens. The question becomes voice input. The composer shows a capture instead of typing. One line changes the look. The ink theme and the Aurora backdrop through direct scene. >> The same script on the terminal surface from the start. Same beats, a different room. Export asks the person first, then writes one animated SVG, CSS keyframes, no JavaScript. 13 site tools, a stated privacy default, and the person's approval on every rewrite and export. Built on SVGent and bound SVG.

title: Wired Future: Collaborative 3D Agent Canvas
pitch: Wired Future is an agent-native 3D canvas where humans & AI design together in real-time. Powered by WebMCP, ChatGPT directly reshapes landscape geometries & aesthetics alongside human creators.
about_excerpt: Wired Future is an agent-native 3D canvas where humans & AI design together in real-time. Powered by WebMCP, ChatGPT directly reshapes landscape geometries & aesthetics alongside human creators. Like Comment Story Updates Wired future Inspiration Most "AI-powered" websites bolt a chat box onto the corner and let a model guess which button to click. The model reads pixels or scrapes the DOM, and breaks the moment you move a div. WebMCP flips that. A page can hand an agent a typed contract instead: here are my tools, here is what each argument means, call them. I wanted to find out what a site looks like when you design for that from the first line, rather than retrofitting it. So Wired Future has one rule: there is exactly one place scene state can change, and both the human and the agent go through it. What it does Wired Future is a 3D design canvas where you and an AI agent work the same screen at the same time. Twenty tools are registered on document.modelContext . One reducer, two interfaces The human controls and the agent's execute() handlers call the same zustand reducer. Three things fall out of that for free: Recolour the grid from ChatGPT and the human's colour picker moves to match. Nobody wrote that sync. The picker is a pure function of the store. Every change is attributed. The trace prints [HUMAN] or [AGENT] on each line, so you watch the collaboration happen. The fallback console runs the shipped handlers, not a mock. A real car, taken apart The stage holds the Khronos CarConcept glTF. It ships as 97 named mesh nodes, which split into 109 addressable meshes: door handles, wing mirrors, wipers, brake discs, steering wheel spokes, pedals. Each sits on its own pivot inside its assembly's pivot. Hold Ctrl over any part and: Click runs what that part does. Doors swing on hinges derived from their own bounding boxes, the hood lifts from its rear edge, and anything without a hinge pops off and back on. Drag pulls the part out along its own outward axis, following your mouse. Scroll resizes it. A "3D print" finish strips the paint and glass to matte resin so you can read the geometry. An explode slider fans all thirteen assemblies into a parts diagram and back. Parts measured with real geometry inspect_car_part walks the actual triangles. Surface area from the cross products, volume from the signed tetrahedron sum, an area-weighted centroid, and a watertight check that every edge is shared by exactly two triangles. Mass is a shell model: surface area times wall thickness times density. That detail cost me an hour and I am glad it did. My first version treated the volume a wheel's surface encloses as solid steel and reported 771 kg. Car parts are pressings and castings, not billets. As a 5 mm aluminium shell the same wheel comes out at 34.9 kg, which is roughly what an alloy wheel and tyre weigh. The tool now reports the method, the wall thickness and the 4.6 m length assumption alongside the number instead of hiding them. modify_car_part then rewrites vertices: per-axis scale about the part's own centre, offset along vertex normals to thicken a shell, progressive twist, and re-specification in steel, aluminium, titanium, carbon fibre, ABS, glass or rubber at real densities. Edits rebuild from the pristine buffers, so sending scaleX: 1.2 twice leaves the part at 1.2 rather than 1.44. An agent can measure the hood, tell you it is 18 kg in 1 mm aluminium, and re-spec it in carbon fibre at 11 kg, with the geometry on screen changing to match. Photo to 3D, with no server Drop a photo of an object and it becomes relief geometry on the stage. Depth Anything V2 Small runs in the browser tab through transformers.js, on WebGPU where available. A CLIP zero-shot pass declines people and animals before any geometry is built. No upload, no API key, no backend. The weights stream once from the HuggingFace CDN and the browser caches them. How I built it Next.js 15 static export, three.js, zustand, TypeScript. It deploys to GitHub Pages as flat files. The architecture is one diagram: human UI event ──┐ ├──> useWired.getState().apply(patch, origin) agent execute() ─┘ │ ├──> React re-renders the panel ├──> engine.apply(state) (three.js mutates) └──> log({ origin, message }) React never imports three. The engine never imports React. The store is the only bridge, and because it lives outside React, an execute() callback reaches it with no context plumbing. Challenges The API had moved and I had not noticed. I coded against navigator.modelContext from the spec draft. On 21 July 2026 it moved to document.modelContext . My detection would have missed a conforming runtime entirely. It now probes both and uses whichever carries registerTool , and document is the one Chrome actually exposes, so without that fix none of this would work. The origin trial token shipped in a form Chrome ignores. WebMCP runs as an origin trial through Chrome 156, so production traffic needs a token. Next's metadata.other API emits <meta name="origin-trial"> . Chrome only reads http-equiv . The token was live, looked correct in view-source, and did nothing. I render the tag directly now. The flag route is a dead end, and I measured it. On Chrome 152.0.7977.75 and Edge 152.0.4191.53, with WebMCP and DevToolsWebMCPSupport both confirmed in the launch command line, neither surface was exposed. The README records that so nobody repeats the investigation. A bug in three.js r0.169. TransformControls.dispose() calls this.traverse(...) , but in r169 the class extends Controls , not Object3D . It always throws. Under React StrictMode that killed my teardown mid-way, so the renderer was never released and the next mount came up with a dead canvas. I call detach() and disconnect() and free the gizmo geometry myself. Parts walked off screen when you dragged a slider. Deformations rebuild from the pristine geometry, so they must be centred on the pristine centre. I was re-measuring the live bounding box, which is the centre of the already-deformed part, so every slider tick translated it a little further. Each assembly now caches its rest centre in its pivot's local space, which stays correct while the part is exploded or the door is open. The page froze mid-drag. Every pointermove wrote to the store, re-rendering a 109-row list and re-running the rig sync each frame. Gestures now mutate the scene directly and commit once, on release. A twelve-move drag went from locking up to 57 ms. Accomplishments The bridge is verified, not assumed. Chrome accepts the registration, getTools() returns all twenty, and executeTool runs them: executeTool(tool, JSON.stringify({ doorLeft: 1, doorRight: 1, finish: 'print' })) → "rig 3D-print finish / left door 100% / right door 100%" Register, enumerate, invoke, scene changes, UI mirrors, trace attributes it to the agent. The whole loop, through a real browser implementation. The terrain runs 8.5× faster. Every wave term has the form sin(kx + ωt), which expands to sin(kx)cos(ωt) + cos(kx)sin(ωt). The spatial halves are constant per vertex. That took the loop from 61,605 transcendental calls per frame to 8, and 2.48 ms to 0.29 ms. I checked the algebra against the direct form over 200,000 random samples before trusting it: maximum difference 1e-13. What I learned Tool descriptions are the interface. An agent picks a tool from its name, description and schema alone, so "scale, 0.2 to 3" is a worse contract than "scale across the car, 0.2 to 3, where 1 is untouched." I spent longer writing those strings than writing some of the tools. Read-only tools matter more than they look. An agent that can only write is guessing. get_wired_future_state , inspect_car_part and list_car_parts let it look before it leaps, and the difference in behaviour is obvious. And the honest one: I claimed several things worked before I had watched them work. The mass model, the bounding boxes, the origin trial. Each time, checking found something wrong. The 771 kg wheel would have shipped. What's next Multiplayer, so two people and an agent share a canvas. Persisting a design as a shareable URL. And capture_scene_snapshot already returns the canvas as an MCP image block, which means an agent can see what it built. The obvious next step is letting it critique its own work and iterate. Credits CarConcept from KhronosGroup/glTF-Sample-Assets , by Eric Chadwick from a public-domain model, licensed CC BY 4.0, attribution to Darmstadt Graphics Group GmbH. Fonts: Chakra Petch and JetBrains Mono, SIL Open Font License, self-hosted at build time. title: Fangorn.tv
pitch: Own your algorithm
about_excerpt: Own your algorithm Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration In 2020, NBC's Peacock officially launched and pulled the license for "The Office" from Netflix. I was bothered; another gatekeeper forcing yet another SaaS subscription to consume a single series could not be justified. Growing up with services like Limewire, this felt like a massive degradation in user experience. While the technology for distributing media has become more powerful, the consumer experience seems to be converging to the worst parts of cable TV again: fragmented catalogs behind increasingly costly paywalls, centralized recommendation systems, the reintroduction of advertisements, and increasingly little control over what you consume and how you discover it. This led to a multi-year journey into the depths of cryptography, storage, search, discovery, payment, privacy, and the many failed iterations of a sovereign, semantic web, in an effort to understand the economic and social factors that arise to bring us "Streaming services that are just TV again". Fangorn TV is an experiment of what it might look like if media curation, synthesis, and recommendation were designed for both humans and agents from the beginning. What it does Fangorn.TV is an agentic media platform that lives in the browser. It is a static site that exposes its own semantic dataset to agents through WebMCP. The key idea is that the site itself is the agent's data source, that the semantic index and media operations are exposed directly to an agent with WebMCP. Seeded from a slice of the Internet Archive, it holds ~20k titles to choose from. It has no ads, no login, and collects no user data whatsoever. For a human ( without an agent ), it lets you "own your algorithm": Maintain Client Privacy: privately search the archive by semantic meaning (e.g. "cats") entirely in the browser. Queries never get broadcast to a third party, your behavioral data remains yours. treat the internet archive as live TV channels that can be synced across viewers (i.e. watch with your friends), even building your own custom channels based on meaning Since all data in Fangorn.TV is a vector embedding, users can use ("train") a Markov kernel (over the embedding space) built on their actual behavior, providing newer ways to 'be your own discovery algorithm' Using WebMCP tools and an autonomous agent (like Claude Code): Agentic Media Curation: An agent can control playback based on your actual intent and preference, further amplifying the "own your own algorithm" capabilities. An LLM can be prompted to "Find that one episode of XYZ where THINGS happens", or "Create a new channel that only has shows and movies about dogs" and watch as it produces Dog TV in the browser. Byte-Level Range Requests: Agents can efficiently discover granularly labeled content and extract exact video slices directly using HTTP Range headers instead of downloading gigabytes of raw source files (e.g. efficient GIF extraction from media playing in the browser). Programmatic Media Synthesis: Allows an agent to efficiently synthesize disparate archival footage, builds seamless audio beds, applies dynamic text overlays, and executes frame-accurate FFmpeg cuts to produce polished short documentaries, GIFs, and audio clips. Zero DOM Scraping: Eliminates fragile HTML parsing, selector guessing, and simulated UI clicks. The agent interacts purely through typed, deterministic tool interfaces. Zero-Telemetry Local Discovery: Queries are resolved instantly against client-side vector bundles. The agent receives exact media segment URLs, transcript timestamps, and metadata in milliseconds—running search entirely on the client without exposing behavioral data to external backends. Beyond these immediate capabilities, Fangorn.TV does something less noticeable. It presents a reusable pattern for deploying static sites that simultaneously act as rich, agent-ready datasets with incredibly low overhead both in terms of storage, cost, and bandwidth. The same pattern can be applied to nearly any dataset. How we built it Fangorn.TV existed before we entered the hackathon, but without WebMCP integration. The majority of work during this hackathon involved both WebMCP integration and associated agentic tooling and testing. The application is built using the Fangorn SDK , a "git for knowledge graphs" protocol anchored to Arbitrum and backed by IPFS. We crawled the Internet Archive's Video and TV catalog, cross-referencing entries with wikidata and attempting to filter out content that either lewd/illicit/obscene, deemed low quality, or non-CC0/PD. We used the metadata to build a knowledge graph, organizing content hierarchically (e.g. title > series) and committing it onchain using Fangorn. Then, we run a multimodal feature extraction pipeline (developed during the hackathon in order to enhance the semantic richness of the embeddings), extracting timestamped subtitles using whisper and summarized video features using granite. This enriched data is then used to extend the KG that was committed to previously, adding new vertices and edges to map media to its extracted features. With the time available, we were able to execute this on roughly ~250 videos (using an RTX 3050/i9 - estimates indicate ~21 days for the entire catalog). The graph committed in Fangorn is then used to build vector embeddings (using Qdrant), where we leverage int8 scalar quantization to minimize the memory impact of the set of embeddings, make it small enough to efficiently live within a statically hosted Vite site. This site is deployed as a page on cloudflare, https://tv.fangorn.network , where WebMCP integration makes the bundled embeddings easily queryable by an agent. Challenges we ran into Restricting to Open/Public Domain Content: Navigating copyright boundaries requires strict filtering for CC0 and public domain assets. While we made a best effort to limit this, some content still made it through our filters. - Rich Semantic Embeddings Under Constraints: As mentioned above, our pipeline first extracts subtitles and video features, then builds a graph, and then on top of this embeddings. Due to computational and temporal constraints, we have only produced rich embeddings (i.e. including subtitles + features) on roughly 1.5% of the available catalog (so far). Accomplishments that we're proud of Autonomous Documentary: We used WebMCP to generate multiple 'documentaries' composed full of real archival footage. Zero telemetry RAG: Achieved fully private, semantic vector search running 100% inside the user's browser runtime through WebMCP. Massive bandwidth reduction: reduced data transfer by over 90% using HTTP range requests instead of pulling raw video files into an editor. What we learned Static sites can act as agentic backends : Instead of running a bespoke MCP server in order to make these embeddings available, we only need a static page deployed (e.g. on cloudflare), incurring virtually zero cost. By shipping quantized embeddings (built on top of a structured KG) and WebMCP, it becomes possible to turn a static webpage into a rich database that agents can natively query and leverage. The operational cost collapses to near zero. Efficient web tools can be used to optimize agentic compute : By using HTTP range requests and fine-grained timestamping (on the vids with enriched feature extraction), agents don't need local copies of massive datasets, instead benefiting from byte-level retrieval. A missing consumer class emerges : The Semantic Web of the early 2000s failed because there were no entities that needed to navigate RDF graphs. AI agents are the missing consumer that makes structured semantic data viable and necessary. What's next for Fangorn.tv While we used video streaming here, Fangorn TV is only a media-focused proof-of-concept for a broader architectural paradigm. The underlying pattern, where we leverage version controlled graphs, quantized vector embeddings, and client-side WebMCP interfaces, generalized to any dataset or web application. It fundamentally redefines how static web pages can host and serve data for both humans and agents. Generalizing Beyond Video By making the architecture reusable, we can allow developers to ship static, zero-latency, privacy preserving, agent-native applications across nearly any domain. For example: Private E-Commerce : Users and their agents can search and purchase items (using x402f - our x402-based private paymaster scheme using Semaphore) without sending query intent, browsing history, or shopping telemtry to centralized trackers. Documentation and Research : Static libraries, like docs, research catalogs, and corporate knowledge bases can instantly become queryable by LLMs. For example, we previously stood up experiments like the surgext manual to demonstrate search capabilities. The same approach could be useful for government laws, logs, and meeting notes, as evidenced by the official Piedmont, Alabama webpage , whose agenda and mi

title: GridBoard
pitch: An agent-native search and rescue incident board. Your agent plans. The incident commander decides.
about_excerpt: An agent-native search and rescue incident board. Your agent plans. The incident commander decides. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Wilderness search and rescue is run by volunteers on whiteboards. The first hours decide most outcomes, and the incident commander is juggling a probability map, six tired teams, fading daylight, weather, and a radio. The math of search theory (probability of area, probability of detection, expected gain) has been understood for decades, but nobody at a trailhead at dusk has time to run it. The National Missing and Unidentified Persons System listed over 26,000 active missing-person cases in early 2026, and the National Park Service alone runs thousands of searches a year. That is exactly the shape of problem where a human and an agent are better together than either alone. The agent has breadth: it can read every segment and every team and run the numbers in seconds. The human has judgment: they can see the terrain, hear the radio, and know which volunteer is done for the day. WebMCP is the first thing that lets both of them work on the same live board. Why this use case fits WebMCP A chatbot cannot do this job. The state that matters is on the page: which segments have been searched, at what coverage, who is where, what is staged and what is approved. With WebMCP the agent reads that state directly through typed tools instead of screenshots, its actions render on the board instantly, and the human can intervene at any moment. The agent sees the new state on its next call. It also fits because the domain demands a hard line between advising and acting. WebMCP tools run in the page, so the page decides what the agent can do and when. GridBoard uses that to enforce a rule no prompt could: there is no tool that dispatches a team. What humans and agents can do together The commander says "we lost daylight, replan the east side." The agent reads the briefing, ranks segments by expected gain for each available team, and stages two assignment proposals with rationale, estimated POD and expected gain. The commander approves one, rejects one with a reason, and both decisions are logged with who proposed and who decided. The commander drags their attention to a segment and says "Ground 2 found a blue glove here." The agent logs the clue in the focused segment under Ground 2's name. A team radios in. The commander marks them returning; a debrief_team tool appears for the agent, it records the coverage, and remaining probability shifts across the whole map. The agent hits a call it should not make alone ("hold the drone for night thermal, or launch now?") and asks the commander a question with options. Only the human can answer it. Two people can bring two agents. A planning agent may propose for any team. A team lead's agent, checked in for Ground 2, can only propose for Ground 2. None of this was possible before: an agent that can run the search math on the live board, whose every action is attributed and reversible, and that structurally cannot dispatch. How WebMCP is implemented All tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool in src/tools.js , and the registered set is reconciled against board state after every change. Three classes. Eight read tools ( readOnlyHint: true ) so the agent never clicks through the UI to read; read_log also carries untrustedContentHint because log entries are field reports written by other people and agents. One navigation tool, focus_segment . Write tools appear only after check_in with a name and role, and every write is attributed to that name. Capability follows state. check_in exists only while no agent is checked in. mark_clue exists only while a segment is focused, so a clue lands in the right place. withdraw_proposal exists only while a proposal is staged. debrief_team exists only while a team is returning. approve_proposal never exists. Staged, then approved. propose_assignment validates the request (team and segment exist, rationale is at least a sentence, the team is not spent, no duplicate for that team), computes estimated POD and expected gain, and stages a card. The team does not move until the commander's Approve button. Agent experience. Inputs are natural-language names ("K9 Juno", "Pika Overlook"), not ids. Errors come back as { ok, error, hint } so the agent self-corrects: a wrong team name returns the list of known teams. The Site tools tab shows the human the live tool list, flashes tools as they appear, and lists which tools are locked and why. Verified in the real thing. npm test covers the engine and the registration logic. test/e2e-chrome.mjs launches real Chrome with WebMCP enabled, confirms the browser accepted the registrations (it rejects a duplicate name with InvalidStateError ), drives the tools as an agent would, and checks that the tool set changes with board state and that a proposal never moves a team. Built with Vanilla JavaScript, SVG, Vite, Vercel. No framework, no backend, no API keys. Search theory: Bayesian POA update, cumulative POD, expected gain. What's next A small realtime backend so a commander, a planner and three team leads can bring their own agents to one shared board. Import of real segment polygons from CalTopo/SARTopo. Night operations mode with thermal UAV constraints. title: CreatorFlow
pitch: Agent Native Content workspace for creators
about_excerpt:
Agent Native Content workspace for creators

 Inspiration 

 Creators already have the content. The hard part is everything between recording and publishing. 

 A creator might have a video, an idea, or a piece of writing, but turning it into something ready for different platforms often means jumping between editors, research tools, formatting tools, and publishing workflows. 

 We wanted to explore a simpler idea: 

 What if a creator could tell an agent what they want to do, and the agent could actually operate the creator workspace instead of just giving instructions? 

 That became CreatorFlow. 

 CreatorFlow is not an AI creator that replaces human creativity. It is an agent-native creator workflow where the creator provides the idea, content, and judgment while the agent helps with repetitive production work. 

 What it does 

 CreatorFlow gives creators one simple workspace to: 

 Research → Edit → Prepare → Publish 

 For example, a creator can ask: 

 
 "Find the strongest 30 seconds and make it ready as a vertical short." 
 

 Instead of manually navigating through the editor, the agent can use CreatorFlow's WebMCP tools to understand the project, find a useful moment, create an edit plan, apply the edit, change the aspect ratio, and add captions. 

 The creator can then review the result, modify it, or undo the changes. 

 CreatorFlow can also prepare content for different publishing formats such as: 

 
 YouTube 
 Instagram 
 LinkedIn 
 X 
 Medium 
 

 The goal is not to replace professional editing software. It is to make the repetitive workflow around publishing faster and easier. 

 Why WebMCP fits CreatorFlow 

 Content creation is full of small, repetitive actions —finding a moment, trimming a clip, changing the format, adding captions, and preparing content for a platform. 

 WebMCP fits because it lets CreatorFlow expose these real application capabilities as tools an agent can directly use , instead of making the agent click through the interface like a human. 

 What people + agents can do together 

 The creator provides intent and creative judgment : 

 
 “Find the best part of this video and prepare it as a short.” 
 

 The agent handles the workflow : 

 Understand content → Find moment → Edit → Reframe → Caption → Prepare for platform 

 The creator can then review, change, approve, or undo the result. 

 So the key difference is: 

 Without WebMCP: 
Agent → tries to navigate the UI → clicks buttons → hopes it works. 

 With WebMCP: 
Agent → discovers CreatorFlow's tools → performs structured actions → UI updates → creator reviews. 

 That's why WebMCP is the core of CreatorFlow : it doesn't just put an AI assistant beside the editor; it makes the creator workspace operable by an agent while keeping the human in control. 

 How we built it 

 CreatorFlow is built as a web application using: 

 
 Next.js 
 TypeScript 
 React 
 Zustand 
 HTML5 Video 
 WebMCP 
 

 The most important part is the WebMCP layer. 

 Instead of creating a separate AI system that controls the UI through clicks, we exposed meaningful CreatorFlow capabilities as WebMCP tools. 

 Examples include: 

 
 get_project_state 
 get_transcript 
 find_best_moment 
 create_edit_plan 
 apply_edit_plan 
 change_aspect_ratio 
 add_captions 
 prepare_for_platform 
 undo_last_action 
 

 These tools operate on the same project state used by the CreatorFlow interface. 

 This means the agent and the human are working with the same workspace rather than maintaining two separate systems. 

 We also added a WebMCP activity panel so users can see which tools are being called and what the agent is doing. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was understanding how to make WebMCP meaningful instead of simply adding tools for the sake of the hackathon. 

 We initially thought about building a much larger AI video editor, but that quickly became too complicated. 

 We narrowed the product down to the workflow that matters: 

 Understand the content → make an edit → prepare it for publishing. 

 Another challenge was keeping the creator in control. 

 Some operations change the project, so we designed the workflow around proposals, approval, and undo rather than allowing an agent to silently change everything. 

 We also had to make sure that WebMCP tools were connected to real application state instead of being disconnected demo functions. 

 Accomplishments we're proud of 

 We are proud that CreatorFlow demonstrates a different way of thinking about web applications. 

 The important part isn't simply that an agent can chat with the application. 

 The important part is that the application's actual capabilities are exposed as tools that an agent can understand and operate. 

 A creator can express an outcome such as: 

 
 "Make this into a vertical short." 
 

 The agent can translate that intent into a sequence of structured operations while the creator watches the workspace change. 

 We are also proud of the shared state architecture, where human interactions and WebMCP tool calls use the same underlying operations. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building for agents changes how we think about UI design. 

 Traditional interfaces are designed around: 

 buttons → menus → clicks → navigation 

 An agent-native interface can instead expose: 

 intent → tools → actions → result 

 WebMCP makes this possible directly inside the web application. 

 We also learned that agents should not necessarily replace the user. In creative workflows, the better experience can be human + agent collaboration , where the agent handles repetitive work and the human remains responsible for taste and final decisions. 

 What's next for CreatorFlow 

 This hackathon version focuses on demonstrating the core idea. 

 Next, we would make the workflow production-ready by adding: 

 
 Real video processing and rendering 
 Real transcription 
 More intelligent editing suggestions 
 Direct publishing integrations 
 Platform-specific content optimization 
 More WebMCP tools for research and content preparation 
 Better agent approval and safety controls 
 

 The long-term vision is simple: 

 CreatorFlow becomes a place where people bring their content and intent, while agents handle the repetitive work required to turn that content into something ready to publish.

title: tableread
pitch: A web page that hands a browser agent ten WebMCP tools to write, playtest and QA a SillyTavern character card. The page owns the deterministic bookkeeping; the agent owns the judgment.
about_excerpt: A web page that hands a browser agent ten WebMCP tools to write, playtest and QA a SillyTavern character card. The page owns the deterministic bookkeeping; the agent owns the judgment. Like Comment Story Updates A browser agent (ChatGPT Codex, left) drives tableread, calling run_scenario, get_playtest_context and commit_playtest_round round by round. Creator mode: the nine-aspect checklist is complete, card fields filled, and a playtested scenario fills the transcript and QA panels. get_checklist_status returns nine aspects (seven richness aspects, the MVU decision, the beautify direction), each with a decision axis. get_playtest_context lists which world-book entries are live each round; commit_playtest_round applies the regex and the variable patch. The QA panel: rounds run, JSON-Patch misses, world-book entries never triggered, warnings, and every tool call the agent made, in order. Game-publisher mode: compare_scenarios puts two already-run openings side by side and diffs their final variable state. What compare_scenarios is for: world-book entries that fired in some scenarios but not others, an inconsistency a reviewer would miss. The whole card built through tools: every update_card_field / get_checklist_status call, with arguments and result, in the activity log. Inspiration I build SillyTavern character cards, and the hardest part isn't the writing — it's knowing whether the thing actually works. A card isn't one prompt. It's an opening scene, a handful of alternate greetings, a world-book of keyword-triggered lore with sticky and cooldown windows, regex scripts that render status bars, and often a block of variables tracked across the whole conversation. After any edit you have to re-check that every opening still feels like the same character, and that the right lore fires in each branch — by reading transcripts and trying to remember what triggered where. It's exactly the kind of bookkeeping a human skims and an LLM just guesses at. When WebMCP landed, the split was obvious. The page can do the deterministic half perfectly — which entry is in a cooldown right now , whether a variable patch applied, how triggers differ across scenarios — and hand the agent only the part that needs judgment: turning a premise into real choices, and writing the dialogue. So I built the page that does that, and gave the agent ten tools. What it does tableread is a browser-agent-collaborative platform for building and playtesting SillyTavern character cards. It registers ten deterministic tools via document.modelContext.registerTool(), so a WebMCP-capable browser agent (ChatGPT's Codex browser, or Chrome with the WebMCP flag) can: • Write a card from a premise. get_checklist_status returns nine aspects a card needs, each annotated with a "decision axis" — the thing a set of options should actually differ on. The agent proposes two or three concrete directions per gap, the creator picks one, and update_card_field records it. • Playtest it deterministically. run_scenario / get_playtest_context / commit_playtest_round run the card round by round. The page computes exactly which world-book entries are live each round (keyword match, constant, or still inside a sticky/cooldown/delay window), applies the regex "beautify" scripts and the JSON-Patch variable updates, and reports every warning honestly. • QA it across scenarios. compare_scenarios takes a batch of already-run openings and flags which world-book entries fired in every one of them versus only some. That inconsistency is the single most useful "does this card hold up across branches" signal — and it's not something any existing SillyTavern tooling, or an agent working from the rendered page, can compute. The page never calls an LLM. Zero API key. Every line of generated dialogue comes from the calling agent's own model. How I built it • Pure frontend, zero bundler: index.html + native ES modules, served by a ~30-line zero-dependency static file server. Deployed on GitHub Pages. • The playtest engine — world-book scanning, regex rendering, JSON-Patch variable state — is ported from an existing Python tool (playtest_engine.py) to JavaScript, and checked against it with a golden-parity test suite that replays fixed multi-round conversations through both engines and asserts byte-identical output. 81 tests total (unit + golden + Playwright e2e). • Each of the ten tools is a plain, DOM-free function unit-tested on its own; only one module (registerTools.js) ever touches document.modelContext, and registration is fault-tolerant (per-tool try/catch, a timeout cap) because the API is still experimental. • Tool descriptions and the whole UI are bilingual (Traditional Chinese / English) and follow a page toggle, so the agent reads whichever language the creator is working in. Challenges I ran into • WebMCP is early-preview. The agent side — a browser that actually calls the registered tools, not just accepts them — exists today only in ChatGPT's Codex browser and in Chrome behind a flag. Working out which environment actually calls the tools (a plain ChatGPT account registers them but never calls them) took real testing. • Getting the agent to emit the exact wrapper the engine parses. Solved by having the tool report the precise format error back to the agent — which turned into a good demonstration that the tool's output, not the agent's "verified, no warnings" self-report, is what tells you whether something worked. • Keeping the split honest: everything deterministic and stateful on the page, only the in-character writing on the agent — and resisting the urge to let the agent "help" with the bookkeeping. Accomplishments that I'm proud of • The full write → playtest → cross-scenario QA loop runs through typed, self-describing tools with zero prompt scaffolding. The agent discovers the whole call sequence from the tool metadata alone. • compare_scenarios computes a QA signal (world-book entries that trigger inconsistently across branches) that no existing character-card tooling produces. • Golden-parity tested against the original Python engine, so the ten tools an agent calls are backed by code that doesn't guess. What I learned • WebMCP's real value is the division of labour: the page can hand the agent exact state — which entry is inside a cooldown right now , whether a patch actually applied — that the agent could never reconstruct from the rendered page. • Self-describing tools plus honest error reporting removes almost all of the prompt engineering. The tool descriptions are written for the agent, and the agent just follows them. What's next for tableread • A bottom-of-page ideation panel, so option-picking happens in the UI rather than only in chat. • A "load an existing card" import, so creators can QA cards they already have. • Wider agent support as WebMCP rolls out beyond the early-preview browsers.
